speechtext: Mr.* Speaker, on Thursday last I gave notice that when motions were called I would move that Bill 118, letter E of the Senate, for the relief of Charles Isaac Alexander, he referred back to the Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee. My reason for asking that the Bill be referred back to the committee is this: The Bill went through the Senate Committee unanimously and came down to this House, and went before the Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills of this House. That committee required a quorum of ten members. There were 13 who took part in the vote, 7 against the preamble and 6 in favour of it. In view of the small number present, and in view of the history of the Bill up to the present time, I would ask that it he referred back to the committee for further consideration.

Surely it would be
most objectionable to adopt this proceeding. I was a member of that committee. That Bill was considered and considered carefully; there was a great deal of discussion. There is absolutely no use of putting members on committees if their findings are not going to be adopted, and it Bills are going to be thrown back on them. I protest against this procedure.

On the other hand, I have not yet heard that this House exists for the purpose of handing over its authority to any of the committees. The committee is a convenient means of 'bringing out evidence, but it is the House that renders its decision. As a member of the House, not a member of the committee, I do not wish to be held responsible for the decision of the committee.

As a member of that committee and one who listened carefully to the discussion by counsel representing the parties, and who voted against the Bill, I feel that this proposition is a reflection upon the members of the committee. Some hon. members who have voted against the Bill have gone home and intend to remain. Consequently, if the Bill is referred back, we have no chance to get another expression of opinion by the committee. I think the motion should stand over.

My attention was directed to this case by Mr. Lougheed, the Chairman of the Divorce Committee in the Senate, and by my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. MeCraney). 1 read over the evidence, and, if it is to be believed, there is absolutely no question that a divorce'ought to toe granted. The question of [DOT] the credibility of witnesses is usually left to those who have had the opportunity of observing their demeanour and judging by that as to whether or not they are telling the truth. The Senate committee which heard the witnesses in this case seem to have 'believed those who were called on behalf of the petitioner. The circumstances put forth by respondent, who was the only witness called in her own behalf, are corroborative to some extent of what was alleged by witnesses for the petitioner. I think the result of this case indicates the absolute necessity of some reform in the methods by which Bills for divorce are considered, because it is manifestly incongruous that a case which depends upon the credibility of witnesses should be decided in favour of the credibility of those witnesses by a committee which heard them and should be decided against the credibility of those witnesses by a committee which did not hear them. There is much in the result to indicate the necessity of some effective reform in the methods by which these Bills are heard. When the case was brought to my attention I took the opportunity of reading the evidence very carefully. It is no reflection whatever upon the members of the Private Bills Committee that any one in this House might entertain an opinion of the result of that evidence different from that which they entertained. The evidence seemed to me to indicate circumstances as strong as any I have ever seen brought forward in this Parliament in favour of a divorce, unless we are absolutely to disbelieve the two witnesses who were called for the petitioner. The evidence was most direot and circumstantial. In so far as I am personally concerned, and with every possible respect for and deference to the opinions of those who entertain a 'different view,
1 would be disposed to think ithat the case might very well be referred again to the Committee on Private Bills.

On the Orders of the Day being called:

I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Militia to an anachronism or perhaps a blunder that has occurred in the attestation papers required to be signed by recruits previous to enlistment in the overseas expeditionary force, and also in the permanent force of Canada. This error has caused some discussion and perhaps a little irritation on the part of a large body of our citizens. In the particulars which are required to he given in these papers, the recruit has to state the religious denomination to which he belongs, and the religious denominations set out are: Church of England, Presbyterian, Wesleyan, Baptist, Congregationalist, other Protestants, Roman Catholic, Jewish. There is no mention in this list of the Methodists.

That may be accounted for, perhaps, by the fact that the theological section of the Department of Militia has been, like Rip Van Winkle, asleep for about forty years. There was in Canada, over forty years ago, a religious denomination called Wesleyans, but it has ceased to be, and I am quite sure that the Methodists, who are as large a body in Canada as those of the other Protestant denominations specified, are quite as loyal and quite as deserving of being mentioned. I call the attention of the Minister of Militia to this in order that [DOT] the error and its consequences may hereafter be obviated.

It is quite evident that my good friend (Sir James Aikins) has been asleep himself. It is true that the attestation paper does not contain the word " Methodists," but every one knows that the Methodists are always to the front in every loyal and patriotic cause. No one would suspect that either my good friend or myself, both of whom occupy front seats among the orthodox Methodists at least once a year, would-intentionally cast any reflection on the Methodist body. The mistake has been made through our following the English attestation sheet. When I asked for an explanation of it some weeks ago, I was told that our men here simply copied the English sheet, and I, being the head [DOT] of the theological branch of the Militia Department, was not consulted, or I would have noticed it. The other officers in the department, being only military men, did not observe the effect of the mistake. I may, however, inform my Hon. friend that the Wesleyans are not dead, because there are in England hundreds of thousands of the very best citizens who still hear the name of Wesleyans. As I say, we followed the English form, but I can promise my hon. friend that the word " Methodist " will be found in the papers in future. 1 may say also that there is nothing in the world to prevent a man writing in the word " Methodist," as many of them do, if he wishes to.

1.	I am a director of John Millen and Son, Limited.

On or about September 15, 1914, and for some time previously, I alone had full charge of the negotiations, the purchase, and all matters appertaining to the purchase of letters patent No. 114,110, for an improvement in trolley wheels, issued under the seal of the Patent Office of Canada and dated the 15th day of September, 1908, the full right, title and interest in and to which was vested in the Lumen Bearing Company, of the city of Buffalo, in the state of New York, U.S.A., and transferred by the said purchase to the said John Millen and Son, Limited.

4.	During the negotiations and for some time previously it was believed by me that the said letters patent of Canada were fully paid up and that no payment of Government fees was required to maintain the patent in full force and effect.
5.	During the time from September 1, 1914, to September 14, 1914, I was absent from Montreal on a vacation and could not be reached for instructions before my return to Montreal.
6.	During my absence from Montreal there was a large accumulation of matters requiring or believed to require my personal attention, all of which matters were allowed to remain in abeyance until my return on September 14, 1914.
7.	On my return on September 14, 1914, I immediately gave the accumulated matters attention and proceeded to dispose of the same with diligence, and on September 15, 1914, I found amongst the said accumulated matters a notice from the said Lumen Bearing Company that a Government fee had to be paid to the Commissioner of Patents for the extension of the term of duration of the said letters patent of Canada, on or before September 15, 1914.

On section 2-proof of right to be a petitioner:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What change does this make?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The change made is the provision that the production of a copy of the voters' list used in the election containing the name of the petitioner shall be

conclusive evidence that the petitioner could lawfully present the petition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is designed to prevent controversy as to the status of the petitioner, which sometimes causes delay. I should think it is a very proper amendment.
Do you require from the petitioner an affidavit that he is the person whose name appears on the voters' list?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The production of a voters' list certified by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to be a true copy, containing the name of the person presenting the petition, is conclusive evidence as to his status. There is no requirement of an affidavit by him if his name is on the voters' list. It may be that under that provision the court would consider it necessary for the petitioner to prove that he was the same man whose name appeared on the list.

The point is important because, for instance, in my constituency there are many men of exactly the same name who would have to go back to the third or fourth generation to be identified. There might be a dozen Jean Antoines in my constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My impression is that the court would require proof to be made before it that the petitioner was the man ,whose name appeared on the voters' list. That would be a better protection than merely making an affidavit.

Does my hon. friend know if the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is bound to give a
12 noon, certified copy of the voters' list to anybody who asks for it, say
by letter?
It might be well to put in a line, "who, upon request, shall supply the same."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Where a public official is authorized to do a particular act, the court considers him as being under the duty to perform that particular act. Therefore, if he has power to certify a list, it would be his duty to certify a list when called upon to do so.

Under this Bill any party may ask the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery for a copy of the list. I should imagine that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery would be bound to give a copy to anybody asking for it the moment the request was made.
126J

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was endeavouring to meet the point the hon. gentleman has made. If the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is authorized to deliver a certified copy of a document, of which he is the legal custodian, it seems to me to follow as a matter of course that it is his duty to furnish this certified list when so required. While I have no objection to inserting any words to make that plain, I do not think they are really necessary.
Neither do I; I assume that is understood.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, I would suggest that after the word "petitioner" in the second line of subsection 2 words should be inserted in order to make it read:
The production of the voters' list containing the name of the petitioner, as set forth in the petition or of a copy thereof certified-

Should it not be absolutely mandatory on the part of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to deliver this certified copy of the voters' list fortwith? If a petition should be filed, and if the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery should refuse to deliver the certified copy of the list, the object of the petitioner might be defeated because the time for taking proceedings might expire.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The only objection is that, if you make a special provision in this case that he has to deliver a certified copy, it might alter the law in other cases. If there is to be any provision, it should be a general provision that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is bound to furnish copies of all documents of which he is the lawful custodian. I do not think it is necessary, because, without any special provision, I understand that is his duty.
I assume that it is the duty of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. If I am a petitioner in a case and I want a copy of that list he is bound to deliver it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, that is my understanding of it.

Would it not be well to provide that a copy of the voters' list " shall forthwith be delivered by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery?" Although the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is bound to deliver the list on demand, yet should

>
he not do so, does it not strike the right lion, the leader of the Government that there should be something farther in the Act to compel him forthwith, upon application for a certified copy, to deliver the same to whomever might apply for it? It would appear to me that that ought to be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I really do not
think there is any 'danger, but might I suggest a change that would place the matter beyond question? Suppose the section should read in this way:
The production of the voters'list containing the name of the petitioner, as set forth in the petition, or of a copy thereof, certified by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to be a true copy of the voters' list used at the election in the electoral district to which the petitioner relates shall be conclusive evidence that the petitioner could lawfully present the petition.
Then you have the opportunity of bringing the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery there with the voters' list, or on the other hand you have the opportunity to get a certified copy, and if you run any danger in one way certainly any court upon his default in furnishing a copy would order him to produce the voters' list. I therefore beg to move that:
Section 2 be amended by adding in the second line, between the words "petition and " certified," the following words:	" or of a
copy thereof " and striking out the words, " or of a copy thereof " where they were inserted before.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The fact that you call for a copy of the voters' list would not exclude the production of the original. There is no harm in making it perfectly clear that you permit the production of the voters' list.
Does the amendment make it clear as to who is to produce the voters' list? What is the alternative?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would certainly be for the petitioner to produce proof of his qualification, and if he wanted to produce the original it would be open to him to ask the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to appear and produce it.

I gathered from the remarks of the right hon. the Prime Minister that it was in his mind that the effect of the amendment was that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery was to perform one of two duties-either to appear in person and produce the voters' list or to furnish a certified copy of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I thought the amendment proposed by my hon. friend

the Minister of Justice was amply sufficient. Some hon. gentlemen on the other side had some doubt about it. Therefore, I proposed my amendment with a view of giving the petitioner the right to have the Clerk of the. Crown in Chancery either to go through with the original list or produce a copy certified by him to be a true copy. My hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) had some doubt as to the absolute duty of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to furnish such certified copy. I have no doubt, but in order to put the matter beyond question, it seems to me that the amendment that I proposed will meet every possible contingency that could be suggested.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 3-sections 6 and 7 repealed:
What is the object of the repeal of these sections?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 6 required the production of an affidavit by the petitioner that he has good reason to believe, and verily believes, that certain allegations contained in the petition are true and it also required that if any other person was substituted for the petitioner the person so substituted should make an affidavit to the same effect. Section 7 provided for preliminary objection by the sitting member. The purpose of this amendment is to do away with what appear to be unnecessary formalities that only encumber the proceedings and which have been a prolific source of delay in the past.
On section 4-form of petition:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The object of this section is to give the respondent the protection of requiring that the party complaining should set forth the grounds of his complaint with sufficient particularity. The law, as it now stands, permits the petitioners to set forth in the most absolute general terms charges of violation of every section of the statute, and the practice, as I understand it, has been to recite the statute and make the preliminary allegation that the respondent has violated all of its provisions. That was considered 'by the committee to be absolutely unfair towards the respondent. On the other hand, it seems perfectly proper that where a man takes the responsibility of making charges of grave violation of a law so important as this, he should not be allowed to rush into court unless he knows substantially what it is which he vrants to charge the respondent with. It

was considered only a matter of fairness that the respondent should have before him sufficient particulars to enable him to substantially know and answer the charges that are brought against him. Furthermore, it is considered that this amendment would contribute materially to making it possible to expedite the trial.

Under the law as it is at present, the petitioner is obliged to give particulars after he has filed his petition, and he has to prove the petition or to pay costs. What more can you do by this change?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This says to the petitioner at the outset that he shall tell the respondent what he complains of, so that the respondent can properly meet the charges, and so that there can be a prompt trial.
It will be a change theoretically but not practically.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will make a very material and practical change. It may be open to discussion whether it is a desirable change. I myself think it is highly desirable, but there is no question about it being a material change. The court, with the issue before it from the outset, can fix the trial within a limited period, whereas, as it is now, months "and even years elapse, and the petitioner then comes in with particulars that he has dug up in these years to try to support his petition. The considerations which moved the committee to suggest this amendment were, that in the first place it was a matter of ordinary fairness to the respondent, and that in the second place it afforded a means of expediting the trial, which is the great object of this legislation. It seemed to the committee that there is ample law now, Ibut that the principal difficulty was the proper method of promptly enforcing the law. It seemed to us that this amendment is absolutely essential, if we -are going to attain the object of a speedy trial, which we have in view.
Would the petitioner be barred from going loutside the specified charges made in the petition?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The purpose is that a man should get as fair an opportunity to make a defence as he gets in an ordinary action before the courts. It will be for the court to determine whether the particular petition is sufficiently particularized to meet the purpose. The intention of the amendment is to prevent surprise and unnecessary expense to the respondents, and to assure a fair and speedy trial. I should think it would be within the power of the court to make rules, under which further particulars may be ordered, if asked for. I would take it that the court would not allow a petitioner to proceed to prove allegations which are not particularized, to the extent required by the present law.

I am very much afraid that instead of leading to a speedy trial and having the member who is elected by corrupt practices unseated, the section is going to give him a splendid opportunity to avail himself of technicalities and to delay the trial for a long time, or probably to have the petition thrown out. It says:
The petition presented under this Act may be in form " A " in the schedule of this Act. It must complain of the undue election or return of a member, or that no return has been made, or that a double return has been made or of a matter contained in any special return made, or of some unlawful or corrupt act or acts, and shall contain such particulars of the complaint set out in the petition as may be necessary to prevent surprise or unnecessary expense to the respondent and to insure a fair and effectual trial; and it must be signed by the petitioner, or all the petitioners if there are more than one.
Who is to determine as to whether there are sufficient particulars to prevent surprise, and what should happen if the judge should think there are not sufficient particulars? In an election petition you cannot set out the offence with particularity. The offence is usually committed in secret, and while the petitioner and his friends may see corrupt practices all around them, they could not within the time fixed set them out with particularity. But it is difficult to give particulars with exactness, and one cannot do it in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred. It is only by making general allegations and relying upon the evidence that one can contest an election. If you require particulars given in such a manner as will appeal to the judgment of the judge and allow him very great discretion, my impression is that in a great many cases petitions which may be founded upon justice will be defeated entirely by reason of the requirements of this section.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think I understand clearly what the committee had in mind in framing this section. It would be

quite possible that it would work out in the way in which they expected. As my hon. friend knows, the difficulty with petitions in the past has been that, notwithstanding the provision as to the necessity of an affidavit, the practice has always been that the solicitor framing the petition takes practically every section of the Dominion Elections Act and alleges in the terms of those sections that its provisions have been violated by the respondent. In fact, the petition ordinarily has given no more information to the respondent than if the petitioner had said in a few words that the respondent had violated every section of the Dominion Elections Act, and had let it go at that. I remember many years ago arguing before the Supreme Court that a petition in that form was not in compliance with the Dominion Controverted Elections Act. The court reserved judgment upon the appeal; but as it appeared that the petition was in the form that had been ordinarily adopted in the province of Nova Scotia, the court held that it was in compliance with the Act. That judgment was delivered by the late Mr. Justice King. I suppose it was the intention of the committee to make it necessary that there should be some more definite statement than that which is embodied in the mere assertion that every section of the Dominion Elections Act has been controverted. I do not know the precise idea of the committee, but I suppose that in view of the abolition of the affidavit which hitherto has been required they have thought it desirable that some more definite statement of the grounds upon which the petition is presented should be set forth therein. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) has raised a difficulty which of course strikes one immediately, that is to say, the extent of the particulars made necessary by this amendment, and he desires to know how that will be determined. I suppose that would be a question for the court or for the judge trying the petition to determine. For that purpose it would be necessary for him to construe the Act and the amendment and to come to a conclusion in regard to the matter.

This is what I had in mind-that the man, say John Jones, must be named, and that the particulars must be given of the corrupt act which was committed; that is, that so-and-so was driven to the poll, the name being given. If on the trial the petitioner should fail to prove

that particular act, the petition would be thrown out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Although I may be in error, I do not quite understand that the committee intend by this amendment to necessitate the giving of particulars of the character which are required before the trial begins. The practice, as we all know, is that when a case is to be set down for trial, the respondent comes with a motion asking that particulars shall be given before a certain day in order that he may prepare his defence. I would not suppose it was the intention of the committee that particulars of that character should be set out in the petition.

That is what section
5 says.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are to give such particulars as are required by section 11. The court will have to determine in each case the extent of the particulars required to prevent surprise and to ensure a fair and effectual trial. The section does not say that the petitioner shall give the name in every instance. There are circumstances where, perhaps, the name may be necessary to prevent surprise and ensure a fair and effectual trial; there are circumstances where it will not be necessary. The court will appreciate that.

In regard to the form, section 3 of schedule A says:
Here state the grounds on which the petitioner relies, and, in case illegal or corrupt acts are alleged, the particulars of each of such acts as prescribed by section 11.
Surely that must mean the particular person who has been bribed, or the particular person who has been brought to the poll.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It says the particulars as prescribed by section 11.
Of each of such acts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. What particulars are prescribed by section 11? That the petitioner shall give sufficient particulars to prevent surprise and ensure a fair and effectual trial. The judge will determine that point. He may determine it upon a motion for further particulars, if the respondent chooses to take that course. If the respondent chooses to meet the petition and go to trial, then it will be for the judge, when evidence of a particular thing is offered, to determine whether proof of that particular action would under the petition as drafted be a surprise to the respondent-

something which he would not be called upon to expect-and would prevent there being a fair trial. I do not dispute that the enactment of this provision may prevent the making of a certain number of petitions. The situation to-day, as I think the hon. member for St. John correctly describes it, is that, because people think there is corruption in the air, because they think there was a great deal of corruption, although they do not -actually know that there was any, and because the law requires the petition to be filed within forty days, they put in their petition with nothing that one can call knowledge of corrupt acts. Let the law be honest with itself and the people to whom it applies. If the law means as it says, that you must file your petition within forty days, surely it does not mean to say: On condition that on a petition when you know nothing, we shall give you a year or two years to hunt up and find whether you can discover anything. If that is the state of the law, then we ought to repeal that law and say that a man may, whenever he finds out any corruption at any time within the Parliament for which a member is elected, bring in a petition.
I believe that the law as it stands to-day is, on the face of it, an invitation-I do not want to say to perjury-but to the very loosest kind of swearing. Requiring an affidavit has proven absolutely nugatory as a protection for the innocent respondent- and there are some innocent respondents. The other evening we were seriously attacked because it was said we were throwing every member of Parliament to the wolves and facilitating his being unseated.
You are certainly taking him from the wolves by this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are trying to create a situation different from that which exists under the law to-day. To-day a man is an object of suspicion -and prima facie guilty of every sort of corruption. And why? Because he has allowed himself to be nominated for Parliament and a majority of the voters, apparently at all events, have voted for him. And yet this law, apparently so severe against candidates, affords such opportunities for delay that the one thing manifest under our system is that you can sit through a whole Parliament in the face of a protestation, whether you are innocent or whether you are guilty. If under the provisions proposed a few guilty men escape being petitioned against, and yet, on the other hand those petitioned against are
brought to a speedy trial, and the result is actually attained of convicting those who deserve to be convicted, the amendment will be a good thing. Looking at it from the point of view of enforcement of the law, I think it is worth while to create conditions which shall assure the respondent that his case will be tried out promptly, and to actually secure prompt trial in a certain number of cases even though the law should operate to prevent the institution of a certain number of petitions upon which the petitioner gets a year or two to prove that the respondent, or somebody on his behalf, had hired a couple of cabs. As I say, the conception of the committee was that the great thing to be desired was that where there was actual guilt there should be prompt trial and also that measures should be enacted to prevent people, by collusion or combination, spinning out the contestation for a long period of time. It will be seen by the sections that follow that within fifteen days after service of that petition the respondent may file his answer, a copy of which is to be served upon the petitioner. Then, after a ishort delay, the parties ask for fixing the trial, and the court shall fix the time. If the parties do not so ask, then the court itself on the clerk's application shall fix the time. If the parties do not go on at that time, that will end the trial. Sb, every man will have to understand that in making a contestation, he has entered upon something which he must see through promptly if he is to secure his rights. To achieve that end, the respondent must be given notice promptly of what he is to meet, and it must be given in such form as will avoid surprise and ensure a fair trial. This is a point which the courts have to decide in a large number of cases. Under the election law as it stands the bill of particulars must be put in, and if the party objects that the allegations are not sufficiently particular or definite, the court must decide the point.
If the court decides that the statement in the information is too vague, can the court void the proceedings upon that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no provision here for a preliminary objection. As I understand it, this is the way the law would work out now-

But could the
respondent move to set aside the petition on account of the delay involved5

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To my mind he would not need to do that. The respondent asks for particulars. The court, let us say, decides that he is entitled to them. The petitioner does not give them. Then the court would naturally dismiss the petition. But suppose that the respondent says the charges are not particularized sufficiently to prevent surprise and secure a fair trial, and the court decides that the particulars in the petition are sufficient, then the case will go on. If the court is of opinion that the particulars are not sufficient, it may well refuse the evidence.
Does the minister intend that the matters included in the petition shall be the only matters intended for trial?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Then, he must put a clause in this Bill forbidding the court to allow it to go further. Because these gentlemen who are put upon the Bench become exceedingly virtuous-though they may have been politicians before-and they will go far beyond what the minister ex

pect.s and will allow the amendment of the petition until the trial comes on. That is the experience of every one of us. The petitioner comes forward and says: We have found new cases of corruption; broad, wide, strong cases; and we want to have an opportunity to prove them and to that end we wish to amend our petition. The court will allow that unless you put it into this Bill that they shall not allow it. And if you put that in the Bill you practically prevent petitions, for you cannot get the particulars of corruption in forty days as a rule, particularly against the shrewd politicians of the West.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There might still be a fairly wide field of operation. There is no doubt that it is intended that the action shall set forth the causes upon which it rests.
Mr. GERMAN': And the court is supposed to stop at that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think it is the habit of courts to allow amendments for the purpose of setting forth distinct new causes of action. In order that there shall be an "amendment" there must be something '"amended." It does not "amend" a cause of action, to bring in a new cause of action. And you have to remember that we have here a law-and personally I do not think it is an objectionable law- which provides that these proceedings
	*
must be instituted within forty days. I hardly think that any court would conceive it to be within its rights or within its power of amendment to allow a party to come in and allege some absolutely new cause of action, any right of action based upon which is actually extinguished by prescription. I cannot conceive that a court would say to a petitioner:	I am
going to allow you to come in a year after the election and make your petition all over again, basing it on a new cause of action, though the law says that your petition should have been brought within forty days. I quite conceive that the courts may exercise much latitude with regard to amending things that are alleged, but I do not apprehend that they would allow the petition to be entirely remade or an entirely new cause to be alleged. I think that, at the very least, we can wait until the apprehensions of the hon. member in that regard have been justified by the results of the operation of this Act.
There would not be many petitions filed under the Controverted Elections Act if this were decided by the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it would be better to have fewer petitions and more judgments. I think one may fairly say-let the blame be generally shared-that the large number of petitions, when we have contrasted with the number of judgments, when we do have any judgments at all, is in the nature of a public scandal, and is the best justification for trying to bring the law into a condition where a man will only be enabled to make a petition when he has distinct and concrete grounds for doing so.

Why should the hon.
minister assume that the * large number of persons charged with these election offences are guilty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not say the number of convictions; I said the number of judgments or decisions, favourable or unfavourable. What I point out as being the scandal is not that the persons against whom petitions are made are necessarily guilty, hut that when we do have a large number of petitions we do have almost no decisions, in one sense or the other. When a petition is made it should imply that the man who makes it has some grounds for doing so. When the petition and the grounds upon which it is made are put forth, we should provide, as we endeavour to provide by the following sections, that

a trial shall be brought on, and that if the parties will not bring on a trial, that shall be the end of the petition.

Suppose that at the trial the respondent objects that the particulars given by the petitioner are insufficient, will the court have power to adjourn the hearing of the petition in order to enable the petitioner to give fuller particulars?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That brings up a very
large and very wide question. We are proposing now to make a law, and that law will, of course, have to be applied by the courts in accordance with the general rule that governs the power of the courts to allow an amendment of the petition or to allow an adjournment. The only answer that I can give is that the court would determine, according to the circumstances put before it, whether the justice of the case required that that should be done. The hon. gentleman has really asked me to place myself in the position of the court and to give one judgment to be applied to all possible cases; that I would not venture to do. It seems to me that the court would, in each particular case, have to determine whether the justice of the case required that the court should permit the adjournment, or permit, possibly, an amendment within the limits which I have just endeavoured to indicate to the hon. member for Welland. There would be cases, I presume, in which the court would think that while it would be a fair thing to give the defendant a more clear definition of what was to he anticipated, at the same time it could not pro-erly be said the defendant was absolutely taken by surprise and that a fair trial was prevented by reason of the vagueness of the allegations of the petition. The necessity for determination of the result of this provision would arise accordingly as a petitioner offered evidence of particular acts on which he based his petition. The respondent would naturally, I suppose, if he saw any ground for it, urge that what was sought to be proved was not sufficiently particularized to lead him to expect evidence of facts of that kind.

Let us suppose that in the petition, bribery, impersonation, treating, and so on, are alleged. Was it the opinion of the committee that it would be sufficient for the petition to state that one or more of these things had been illegally committed by the candidate or his agent, or would it be necessary to say that the candidate or his agent treated John Brown or
bribed William Smith, and so on? Would it be sufficient to make the general charge, as was formerly done in election petitions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In my judgment, the
general charge of bribery would certainly not be sufficient. How far you would have to go in the matter of giving particulars would depend largely on the circumstances of each case. I do not think that you could lay it down as a general rule that because I am required by law sufficiently to particularize in order to prevent surprise, that necessarily means that I must name each particular voter to whom I allege that bribes were offered.
Why this change?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This change is to pro-[DOT] vide that when I allege bribery, I shall give such circumstances surrounding it as in the judgment of the judge will prepare the respondent fairly to meet evidence of the facts as that evidence is offered to the court.
Only of specific facts under the petition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
No others could go in.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No others could go in, certainly. It is the ordinary rule; as I understand it, of every legal proceeding, that you are entitled to prove what you have alleged, and what you have alleged with sufficient particularity to enable your defendant, the man against whom you make your allegations, to go to the court called upon to expect proof of matters of that kind. But it certainly does not imply that in every case you must give the name of the man bribed.
Or the man who gave the bribe.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Or the man who gave the bribe. To ask any man to stand up here and lay down a general rule saying what are sufficient particulars to enable a man not to be taken by surprise and to have a fair trial, is asking the impossible. But I may say that foT a great number of years, day after day, I have heard men determining that question in particular cases and determining it, as it seemed to me, *reasortably and fairly to both parties. I have heard instances where it was considered that names of people were necessary and others where it was not. In my own province we have worked out a perfectly rational method of dealing with these questions, still comply-

ing -with the elementary rule that a man must state the grounds of hi-s complaint with sufficient particularity to enable another man to have a fair trial upon it.

It might be wise, however, to go back to the old section, inasmuch as we have provided for facilitating the trial, that is in connection with the present provisions of the Act. Perhaps there would not be any great objection to restoring the old clause.

You cannot do that if you stick to the first clause, that there is conclusive evidence.
At one o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock, Mr. Sevigny in the chair.
On section 4-form of petition:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It occurred to me that after the discussion on section 4, and having regard to the somewhat sharp division of opinion in regard to it, possibly it would not be an unwise course that we should let this section stand in the meantime and go on with the other sections of the Bill. I think that further examination may throw some light on this section. The same thing will really apply to section 5, as section 5 merely makes for a cross petition the same provision that section 4 makes for the petition itself. The questions involved would be substantially the same.
Sections 4 and 5 stand.
On section 6-how security deposit shall be made:
Why would not an accepted cheque on a chartered bank be accepted as it would be accepted for the deposit in an election?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The difference that is made by this amendment is to substitute the permissive for the imperative form that was contained in that section as it stood, and then, that being done and 'Combining the effect of that with the effect of the next following clause, which I would ask my hon. friend to read, it produces the result that the receipt of the clerk of the court is made conclusive. He is permitted to accept the deposit in the different methods specified but his receipt is conclusive in any event as to the making of the deposit and as to its sufficiency. The hon. gentleman suggests the acceptance of an accepted cheque and there might be something to be said pro

and con in that regard but at all events if the officer gave the receipt that the deposit had been made when ha was merely taking an accepted cheque, although he would not be taking what is permitted to be taken, it would be conclusive, he having taken the responsibility. Whether the Act should expressly include an accepted cheque is perhaps open to some question because you may reduce it down then to the mere matter of a man being able to arrange with a bank to get a cheque accepted where he does not actually have the money. It might be that the party against whom the proceedings are undertaken would have the responsibility of the bank but there are some advantages in not expressly permitting a method that involves anything except the actual money.

I thought it would be more convenient to submit an accepted cheque than the money. In Ontario we have to enter the protest with the registrar of the Court of Appeal in Toronto and we have to send the money there.
On section 9-sections 17, 18, 19 and 20 repealed; service and preliminary ob-objections:

With reference to section 19 providing that within fifteen days after service of a petition, the respondent may file with the clerk of the court a written answer to the petition, I would say that this clause is very general in regard to the nature of the answer to be filed. Is there any special provision giving to the judges power to make regulations as to the nature of the answer or as to what shall be deemed a sufficient answer? Suppose an answer was not sufficiently definite, or suppose counsel for petitioners said: This is no answer at all, it is not a denial with sufficient particularity of the acts which are alleged. They might say that the denial is too indefinite just as the answers in civil cases are frequently ruled out where counsel on the other side attack the pleadings on account of their not complying with some precedent which it is necessary they should comply with. What is the standard as to what a sufficient answer would be?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The provision here is permissive to the party attacked to file a written answer if deemed proper. Assuming the clauses which stand to have been adopted, it would be open, as I understand it, to the respondent in a written answer to raise any question that he thought it was desirable to raise whether as to the suffi-

ciency of the proceedings or the actual truth of the statements of fact. He is by this section permitted to file an answer and no restriction is placed upon the ground which he may invoke as against the petition, the idea of the Act being to reduce the whole thing to one trial. My hon. friend will observe that in the following section. 19a, the provision is that:
After the expiration of fifteen days after the service of the petition, whether an answer is filed or served or not, the petition shall be held at issue and the court may at any time thereafter, upon the application of either party, fix some convenient time and place for the trial of the petition.
Taking the two sections together, the purpose and effect is that within fifteen days it shall be optional with the party attacked to file such written answers as he may desire to the petition thus filed. Failing his doing that, it shall be assumed that issue is joined generally upon the petition. Assuming that the respondent wants to rest upon the ground of the insufficiency of the petition itself, either as not setting up something that amounts to an offence or as not sufficiently particularizing, he would be, as I understand it, at liberty to raise these grounds in that answer without prejudice to his making an answer also upon the statement of alleged facts as made in the petition. The idea is to reduce it down so that upon all the matters that may be raised there shall be just one trial, and that that trial shall be as expeditious as possible.

Then there is no
advantage in the respondent filing an answer for any purpose whatever, because he would have available to him at the trial all matters of defence which he might assert whether he files an answer or not. His objections as to the insufficiency of the petition or any irregularities can be raised at the trial to the same effect, whether he has filed an answer or whether he has not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that would be
the practical result, but we give him the option if he sees any advantage in it.
Mr. PROTJLX; I suppose in his answer he could admit some of the allegations of the petition, and if he did the petitioner need not bring his witnesses to court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He could make admissions if he chose. We have a provision of the law later dealing with the effect of admissions when thev are made.

Do I understand the
effect of the answer of the minister to bo that, where a man did not answer, he could at the trial set out anything he might set out upon the preliminary objections?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, because under this Act there is no provision made for the preliminary objections.

It seems to me that this legislation will have the effect of bringing into play a series of objections at the trial, when the judges on the rota are there to hear the action, when probably one hundred witnesses are gathered, and when possibly counsel may be brought from a distance, so that we are out of the frying-pan into the fire. The air will not be cleared by preliminary objections, and the expense will be enormous of having to fight out at the trial what otherwise would have been settled on a chamber application. This would possibly cause witnesses and counsel and judges to be detained from day to day. The value of this change looks to me to be very doubtful.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no doubt there might be a situation, under certain circumstances, in which the inconveniences which the hon. gentleman suggests might arise. But what we are to ask ourselves is, whether the danger of that and the inconveniences which might result in some cases from that, are greater or less than the undesirable consequences which experience has demonstrated to result from the present provisions of the law, which expressly provide for the making of preliminary exceptions. I might point out that where the party would feel that he had statutory grounds to meet the petition, grounds of insufficiency in one respect or another, he might, in the exercise of his own judgment, make up his mind to rely upon that and avoid the necessity of bringing witnesses, or, the court might order an adjournment. I fancy that is a power which the court would probably feel justified in exercising, in the event of objections in the nature of preliminary objections being taken, which have upon their face the appearance of substantiality sufficient to justify the party who raised them seriously relying upon them. The court might, under these circumstances, if it considered that justice required it, order adjournment to more sufficiently deal with the matter on its merits. We have to rely upon the court for that. As to the expense which the petitioner might go to in bringing witnesses who might prove useless because the peti-

tion failed upon some ground of objection as to its sufficiency, it is true that would be an unfortunate thing for him, but it was for him to see to it that he made a sufficient petition. If the court determines it is not entitled to go into the merits of the case because of insufficiency, then what the petitioner suffers is the result of his own fault. No doubt, if we could obviate the substantial failures of justice which have resulted from the system of providing specially for preliminary objections, and also avoid the possibility of the suggested inconveniences that would be the better system. The members of the committee were not blind to the inconveniences which have been suggested, but they considered that the number of eases in which these inconveniences would arise, and the gravity of these inconveniences even assuming that they did arise, did not compensate for the very serious obstacles towards doing substantial justice which practice has proved to result from the system under which provision is specially made for the making of preliminary objections and of special trials on these objections.
On new section 20-notice of admission:

Does that give the court power to say it will not hear witne ses? I would be somewhat reluctant to give the court that power, because with the highest respect for the judiciary, I think there are some judges w.ho would be very glad to exercise it, and who would refuse to hear witnesses.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They have that power now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think there have been occasions when the courts have decided that once thejr have before them, by admission or otherwise, sufficient evidence to justify a judgment maintaining the petition, they have even questioned whether they have any right to go on and make further inquiries. The purpose of this section is not to extend any power on the part of the court to curtail evidence, but, t" make it quite clear that, notwithstanding the making of admissions, the court may decline to adjudicate simply upon the record constituted by the allegations and the admissions, and may require further inquiry. The purpose is to make it perfectly clear that the court shall have jurisdiction to go on to further inquiries, although the matter before it would justify a judgment.

There is another phase of the situation to be considered.

Suppose a party comes in and admits bribery by agents or some other contravention of the law which would make the election void, and the petitioner says, " I am perfectly satisfied;" all that is wanted is the determination of the court upon the matter, so that the costs may be apportioned. Suppose the court decides to go on, can it impose costs upon the unfortunate petitioner, if the result of the further inquiry should be valueless?
The question of costs is dealt with.

I know that the respondent is not liable for costs if he files the admissions. What I am pointing out is this: supposing the judges should take it into their heads to go on and say: " We -are going to have a roving commission," such as my hon. friend from St. John suggests, and supposing the petitioner says: " I am satisfied with the acknowledgement of the respondent," it is questionable whether under this Bill it should be left in the hands of judges further to impose costs upon a petitioner if no particular advantage is to be gained by that inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as the respondent is concerned, if he has madfe admissions under the first paragraph of section 20, and if any evidence is taken in regard to the matters admitted he shall not be held liable for any costs [DOT] incurred on account of that evidence, unless the result is to produce a conviction against himself of some corrupt act, in which case the court has power to order him to pay costs. ' As regards the petitioner who says that he is satisfied and will not proceed, we have no special provision in this Bill with regard to the costs; but I might point out, as I said a moment ago in answer to the hon. member for St. John, that the purpose of this enactment is to make it perfectly clear that the court has jurisdiction to go on, notwithstanding admissions sufficient to justify the maintenance of the petition. As regards the case where both the petitioner and the respondent decline to provide any further material upon which the court can go on, we gave a good deal of consideration to the question whether w/e should provide machinery by which the court could further go on, and, after a great deal of consideration and of different suggestions, we did not find-that we could work out any practical method of doing that. So that I think the effect of this s'ection in practice, as in

its intention, goes really no further than to make it quite clear that, notwithstanding there being sufficient upon the record, the courts ought to have jurisdiction to go on with a further inquiry. In ord|er that that should be effectually carried out in practice, it would be necessary that one of the parties should concern himself with haying it carried out.

This question of
amending the Controverted Dominion Elections Act along the line of preparing for an independent investigation into all the circumstances surrounding a particular election has been under consideration on previous occasions. I recall some years ago, when I was a young member of this House, that a special committee considered the question of providing for the appointment of an independent tribunal to hold an investigation in any event at th|e request of a certain number of people in the constituency.
A public prosecutor.

[DOT] Yes, something of that kind. We must not forget the power of dealing with controverted elections by the judiciary of this country is a power delegated by this House. Not a great number of years ago both in England and Canada the task of determining the validity of an election of a member to the House was a matter to be determined by a committee of the House. We determined to commit that task to the judiciary, and we have followed that course so far. The task which the judge assumed was the task of reporting to the Speaker of the House whether or not the validity of the election of a certain hon. member which had been called in question had been determined in one way or the other. The giving of this extra jurisdiction to the judge, over and above the determination of the simple issue whether or not a member has been validly returned, opens the door to pretty wide responsibility, as suggested by my hon. friend. It seems to me that the Bill should go further and provide for some person assuming the responsibility, because the man who may be a petitioner against any hon, member may have only one object in view, that is, the unseating of the hon. member. Once his task is fulfilled, that is all he is interested in, and we can well conceive of cases in which a petitioner through his counsel will intimate to the judge that he is perfectly satisfied. We all know the developments
of human nature in regard to these matters, and we cannot eliminate the human element in considering the way in which these things work out. If the judges are to have power over and above the attitude of either of the contesting parties to hold an independent investigation, there ought to be some rule 'to limit that power.
It is limited to the allegations to the judge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As my hon. friend says, it is limited to the allegations before the judge, and moreover it is well to bear in mind that the petitioner, when he institutes the proceeding, although he may set it" in motion for reasons of his own, for example, perhaps, to bring it to a particular end, sets in motion a proceeding in which at .least the people of the constituency concerned have a direct and material interest. He is so little the master of the proceeding that under conditions already existing, if he drops it, some one else may come in and take it up. He has set on foot a proceeding in which the general public are interested, and he has done so because he has taken the responsibility of alleging certain things to be facts. I do not think he has any very serious ground of complaint if at the time he says, I do not want to go on any more, the court says to him: But you have undertaken to make these very serious statements which the public is interested in having cleared up. You have got the court here, you have got the respondent here, you have the proceedings in motion; and I, the court, am not going to shut my eyes to these things; if these things are true-and you have taken the responsibility of saying that they are true-then it is important that their truth should be established. I do not see what ground of complaint a petitioner could have that he is not allowed to take into his own hands absolutely the extent to which this inquiry, in which the whole public is interested, shall be carried. He might complain if it were suggested that the judge should go outside the things he, the petitioner, has alleged; but so long as the judge keeps himself, as he is bound to do within the things alleged, I cannot see that the petitioner has any serious ground of complaint,
I think I ought to add to the observation I made a few moments ago. I did not quite accurately describe the effect of the section. It is not so absolutely restricted as my expression would- convey. As will be noticed power is given to require the summoning of such witnesses, the taking

of such evidence and the production of such papers as to the court may seem requisite or desirable. If the petitioner has taken the responsibility of making the most grave accusations, I think there should 'be power such as is given under this section to go into the matter even to the extent provided for. I do not think it unfair or unjust to the petitioner that if the court deems the matters as brought before it sufficiently serious for earefuly inquiry, those matters should he gone into.

Then the minister ought to add some supplementary words empowering the court to make direction as to the distribution of the costs of the proceedings' otherwise how is the matter to be determined? Suppose the additional inquiry be futile, ought the costs of it to fall upon the petitioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There would be power to deal with that as with the question of costs generally. If the result shows that the respondent is guilty of other corrupt acts than those admitted, that fact would naturally be a determining factor in the question of costs. But if the result is that the petitioner fails to make good his statements-which I assume to be serious, because the court would not investigate other than serious statements-I think there would be no injustice if the court laid the costs upon him. That is a power, which, I have no doubt, judges will exercise with great discretion. The real purpose, as I have said, is to put it within the power of the court, where facts are alleged and are apparently (being suppressed, to inquire into those matters.
On section 10:
Saction 22 is amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
" 2. If at any time, upon an ex parte application of either the petitioner or the respondent, it appears to the court that, in the interests of justice, it is desirable that the examination of any witness should be proceeded with forthwith, the court may grant an order for the examination of such witness, and the provisions of sections twenty-three, to thirty, both inclusive, shall, so far as applicable, apply to such witness, his examination and evidence."
This is a very wide expression. Does this provide for cases of absence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, possibly cases of absence. There are special considerations, it seemed to the committee, which justified giving the court a wide' power for the examination of witnesses. What we have 
in mind is to make a provision under which it would be possible for the court to order the immediate examination of any person believed to be able to give testimony bearing upon the petition. We have perhaps, specially in mind the case that might occur because of the fact that we require particulars to be given in the petition. It was suggested as an objec- * tion to our requiring particulars to be given that the respondent, being made aware of the particular things that were in view, might cause to be spirited away witnesses in a position to establish the facts. This clause was intended in a special way to protect the petitioner against that condition of affairs. Since the petitioner has the obligation imposed upon him by section 4, if that be adopted, to set forth in an intelligible manner the ground on which he relies, if he can satisfy the judge that there is danger that immediately upon that knowledge becoming available, efforts will be made to get witnesses out of the way, he should be enabled to have the witnesses summoned and examined. And it seemed to us that not only in that instance, but speaking generally, wherever circumstances satisfy the judge that the interests of justice require an immediate examination of witnesses, he should have authority to make that examination. There are sections in the present law which deal in a specific way with cases of absent witnesses. There are section 21 which deals with the parties to the petition; section 22 which deals with the person who was the candidate; and sections 23 and 24 which deal with the form of examining the classes'of persons referred to. These sections are made applicable to the class of cases we are now dealing with. There is also another provision, section 45, with regard to special examination during the trial. What we are trying to do is to generalize these provisions with regard to particular persons and particular cases and to create a power in the judge under which, if either party can satisfy him that the interests of justice require it, immediate examination may be ordered of any person able to give testimony bearing upon the petition. And, as I have stated, we had especially in mind the consequence that might result from our provision requiring particulars in the petition. We thought that this would be an effective method of obviating one very serious objection that might be made to the requirements proposed to be made by section 4.

The right hon. leader
of the Opposition has stated that " in the interests of justice " is a very broad term, in regard to which judges may differ. Why not provide that where it is made to appear to the court by affidavit that the evidence of a witness materially affecting the trial may be obtained, an examination may be ordered, so that where a party takes the responsibility of swearing that, according to his belief, a witness may be able to discover material evidence, an examination of that witness may take place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The suggestion made
tends to restrict, not to enlarge the conditions respecting such examinations. We did consider trying to specify the particular reasons, but the conclusion reached was that while by doing that we might make it perfectly clear that under certain conditions this might be done, if we failed to foresee all the conditions in which the interests of justice might require it, we would leave an uncovered case. I cannot quite grasp the idea that any judge would suppose that the interests of justice should require the examination of a witness unless it were shown to him that there was ground to believe that that witness could give testimony material to the matter alleged, or unless it were shown to him that there was reason to apprehend that that witness might not be available at the trial or that there was danger of the witness being tampered with. It seemed to us that the wisest course was to give to the judge power to provide for the examination of a witness wherever the interests of justice require it, and we felt confident that the court would- take that to mean the interests of justice in connection with the particular case under consideration. I do not know whether the hon. member apprehends that under this provision any judge may take unto himself power to have a witness examined with regard to some matter outside of the case. If he thinks there is any danger of that, it may be well to put in appropriate words to make the provision clear, but I think that it is wiser for us not to try to put down in black and white all the possible combinations of circumstances under which the interests of justice may require that examination.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What relation
has this proposed provision to section 45, subsection 1, of the Act, which provides that a witness intending to leave Canada may be examined by order of the court,
made on notice of the parties? This proposed section provides that any witness may be examined at any time under order of the court, made upon ex parte application. What I desire to suggest is, that if a witness desires to leave Canada, under this section an ex parte application may be made to the court for his examination, if it is thought to be in the interests of justice that he should be examined in order that his testimony may be available at the trial.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It seemed to the committee that the provisions of section 45 are applicable only to examination during the trial.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would hardly have supposed that, because it would hardly be presumed that a witness who had been duly subpoenaed would leave Canada during the course of a trial. I would be inclined, subject to the view of the committee, to interpret section 45 as having general application. Of course, if the view which the committee takes is correct, there is no inconsistency or over-lapping, but if the view should prevail that section 45 is of general effect, there would be an inconsistency between it and the proposed provision of this section.

I called the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice to the fact that the words " in the interests of justice '* are very wide, not only in respect of election trials, but of other trials as well. If there is reason to believe that a material witness will not be present at the trial, application can be made to have that witness examined; that is a matter of common law. But, in inserting the words " in the interests of common justice," what case did the committee have in contemplation? If a witness is to be present at the trial, I cannot conceive how justice can be served by his being examined before the trial takes place.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was considering the same question myself, and I assumed that the committee must have had in mind the idea of discovery.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It was represented that our requirement of giving particulars was putting the party making the allegation in the unfair position that his opponent would know from the outset just what he was relying upon and would have full opportunity, between the filing of the petition and the coming on of the trial, of resorting to whatever means his conscience might permit to influence or to

get at the people who could give the testimony. That seemed to us to be an objection certainly deserving of consideration. We thought that this provision would enable the judge, wherever either of the parties could satisfy him that there was danger of anything of that kind, that the interest of justice required an immediate examination to prevent it, to order that examination. There are other methods by which a man may be deprived of his testimony than the absence of the witnesses upon whom he relies. I may say in that connection that as a result of the observations that have been made I think it probably would be a wise provision to require that where any witness had been so examined under an order of this kind, if procurable, he should again be brought forward at the trial and offered for further examination if that was desired. But the real purpose of this provision was to create a situation where at any stage, even a day after the lodging of the petition, if the petitioner can make it clear to the court that there is great danger that once his petition becomes known to the adversary means may be found to deprive him of his evidence by any method, that he may be authorized at once to examine such people as he can show, prima facie, can give material evidence upon the petition. That is what we had in view in using these general expressions, going beyond the provision which had regard to people who may be absent from Canada. As regards the time within which this may be done, I do not think we want to be too absolute in saying that the provision in section 45 applies only to the time of the trial. But there seemed to us, at all events as regards time, that there might be a possible argument made in support of that proposition. In the first place, we find in sections 21 and 22, the sections that deal with the examination of parties to the petition or of the person who may be a candidate, that that examination can only be made after issue is joined. Then we have section 45, which is placed in the subdivision of the statute which is headed " Trial of Petition;" and I think I would be correct in saying that all of the other provisions deal with proceedings at the trial. The section provides :
If it is made to appear to the court or trial judges that any witness intends to leave Canada and will not attend the trial-
Then, on application to the court, the court may grant an order for the examina-

tion of such witness. I am not prepared to say nor do I think the committee meant to commit itself to the proposition that this section only applies during the
4 p.m. trial; but at all events it seems susceptible to argument that this section applies only to the trial and that it further limits the rights to examination after issue joined. It seemed to us that there was no provision in the statute which could clearly be interpreted as entitling one to have an examination at any time after the filing of the petition; and, with regard to the time, we thought, if we were to make this an effective method of meeting the circumstances that might arise, that it should be made clear that the examination could be at any time and further that it might be an examination of persons other than the parties to the petition and other than a person who was about to leave Canada.

If I correctly apprehend my hon. friend, the reason for the amendment of the existing rule is that at present there is the ordinary provision for the examination of a witness who may possibly not be present at the trial. I understand the new provision amounts to this, that either party to the suit may go to the judge and represent to him that there is, for instance, a charge of bribery and that unless the party who ought to have the benefit of this witness, either for or against the petition, has the privilege of at once examining him, he has reason to fear that the witness may be tampered with or that for some other reason his evidence at the trial would not be as unbiased and as genuine as it would be if it were at once taken. I do not undertake to say that the provision should not be adopted, but it is certainly a novel proposition and requires reflection. If we want to have fair and speedy trials, I am not prepared to say that the provision should not be found in the Bill, but my hon. friend will agree that it will be absolutely novel, contrary to anything that we know of, and I think it requires more consideration than we have been able to give it up to the present time.

Why not make the section broad enough to allow either party to bring up a witness for examination before the trial, either before or after issue is joined? We profess-and I trust we are all sincere-that we want to. bring out-the truth in these election petitions, to secure speedy judgment and to unseat or disqualify

any candidate who has been guilty, by himself or his agents, of corrupt practices. Why not give the fullest opportunity to get at all the facts, and why not provide that at any time after the petition is served, upon ex parte application, the petitioner or respondent, upon affidavit stating that in the belief of the deponent material facts may be disclosed by an examination of such and such a party, the deponent shall be entitled to have the party brought up and examined?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is what we meant to do.

My hon. friend does not do it. He throws the burden upon the petitioner or respondent of satisfying the judge that it is in the interest of justice that he should do that. In 99 cases out of 100 the judges would fail to apprehend how it would be in the interest of justice to examine a witness before the trial; they would fail to apprehend that the mere fact that there is danger of a witness being tampered with is a reason for examining him and disclosing what he knows. The judge might think he would be more apt to be tampered with after he had disclosed under oath what he had to say than before. He would be more apt to be removed out of the country. Why not make it broad enough so that upon affidavit any man can be examined?
Ordinary discovery.

There is an obvious and very fair answer to the hon. member for St. John. He knows better than I that the first consideration which affects the mind of a judge is the conduct of a witness in the witness box.
