In drawing this section in the committee W3 did not desire to deprive the court of the benefit of seeing the witnesses except in extreme cases, and these extreme cases I think are met by the further amendment suggested by the Minister of Justice, namely, that if and when the trial comes on the witness that has been examined is still in the country and can be examined, he should, notwithstanding the fact that he has given his testimony, be brought before the court and give his testimony in the presence of the judges, who are thus able to see his demeanour and derive the advantage that one always gets from observing the actual manner in which the witness has given his testimony.
My suggestion would not alter that principle at all; it would be rather an examination for discovery.

My hon. friend knows better than I do that it is at variance with well recognized principles of procedure that all witnesses should be examined for discovery. All witnesses should be examined in court except in the case of the plaintiff and defendant, or as in this case, the petitioner and respondent who may be examined for discovery, or except in the case of a witness who may want to leave the country and who may be examined de bene esse. My hon. friend is aware of the fact that many 'difficulties have been experienced in cases of this kind. Men get out of the country as soon as they find their names in an election petition. They take enforced vacations at the expense of their friends. Sometimes they go to Europe and sometimes they have been known to go to the neighbouring republic and stay away for six months. We have no election petitions in our country, and therefore I can speak on this subject with all the more freedom.
Nor in the county from which the hon. gentleman comes.
They always had a protest, but no trial.
They never have any protest in Northumberland.

I fancy that is because of the extreme purity with which elections are conducted there, oi; it may be the facility with which men change sides, having regard to the history of that county. There is something called the Northumberland deal that my hon. friend remembers and that possibly illustrates the point. What influenced the committee was solely this, that in order if possible to perpetuate the testimony of a necessary witness up to the time of the trial when he himself could not be there to give his evidence, an opportunity should be afforded of taking his testimony, and I agree with the Minister of Justice that this should be done. We should at once permit an ex parte application to be made to the judge, have a subpoena issued and have the witness' testimony taken down, due notice being given to the respondent, or the petitioner, as the case may be, and thus have the evidence perpetuated.
Is the application to the judge to be made as a matter of course or for cause? [DOT]

That brings up a question that engaged the attention of the committee : what are the reasons for providing aa extraordinary procedure of this kind? About that we had many a discussion. One hon. gentleman urged this and another urged that, but the final conclusion we came to was that the words that now appear in the section, "in the interests of justice," should be inserted. Instead of adopting the old language of the Judicature Act, namely, "for the proper conduct of the trial," we have said, "in the interests of justice ". That means that the party making the application to the judge or court will do so believing that it is in the interests of justice, using that word in its broad sense, that the testimony of a particular witness should be taken at once. You cannot define all the cases and, since you cannot define them, what words are you going to use which will cover all of the cases better than the words " in the interest of justice"? The expression, "the proper conduct of the trial," does not comprehend all the cases which would come within the term, "in the interest of justice". The determination of the question as to which particular case comes within the definition is left to judicial discretion. I think we can fairly trust the exercise of so extraordinary a power to the 'discretion of the court as is done under the English Judicature Act which has almost a similar provision. You can take immediate proceedings for the purpose of obtaining the testimony of a witness but the testimony cannot be used at the trial unless it appears that the witness is dead or is out of the country. This whole code approximates closely to the civil code. Examination for discovery, examination de bene esse, examination of witnesses about to leave the country and all that sort of thing are provided for. The committee were not particularly wedded to the words " in the interest of justice " but no other words were suggested which were sufiicientlv comprehensive to meet every condition that might arise.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice can see-and I apprehend that is the principle or rule of this subsection-that this examination can take place even before the petition is served or filed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not before it is filed,
for then there is no proceeding.

Well, then, before it is
served. There is no solicitor on the record to appear on behalf of the respondent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The application may be made at once. There is a provision that this examination must be had after notice to the party or his counsel. The application would be made at once so that the order could issue for the examination of . the witness.

The order is issued for
the examination, but who is to take the responsibility of appearing on the examination? There is no respondent to serve, and there is no solicitor on the record to appear for the respondent. The petitioner can file his petition, he makes an ex parte application, and gets an order for one witness- not one, but fifty, perhaps. It may be a personal charge of corruption, it may be a charge of tampering with an election, of exercising undue influence upon an elector; and suppose you have fifty charges of that kind the petitioner could make application for the subpoenaing of fifty men, get an order, examine the whole fifty, and you have the whole case ready for trial before the respondent has been served or has had an opportunity of taking any action in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The applicant might
make his application, but he could not get this order without giving notice to the party, and he and his counsel would be entitled to be present at the examination. All he can do is to get his order, but he cannot proceed with it without notifying the other party-either himself or his solicitor.

Would it not be easy to spirit away a witness just as soon as the respondent knows which witnesses are to be examined? The witnesses are not notified. Application is made for the examination of ten or twenty witnesses, and the applicant gets his order. Is jt a very difficult matter for these witnesses to be spirited away before they can be served? How are you going to advance the interests of justice there?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The order may be made and at once served on the witness.

It cannot be served the
same day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will admit that we do not pretend that we have been able to devise a cast iron arrangement which will *absolutely prevent the possibility of it

being evaded, but we think we have provided a method which, while it may not reach some cases, will reach a great many. What the hon. gentleman has said is precisely what demonstrates the wisdom of our making a provision that this order should be made only when the judge thinks it is desirable. I understand the objection from the hon. gentleman to be that this is not restricted enough, whereas, the objection of the right hon. leader of the Opposition is that it is too wide. I am quite ready to admit that it is an innovation in the wide scope it gives for this sort of exceptional examination, out just because it is that I fail to see the force of the suggestion of the hon. gentleman, which is in reality that wie ought to throw it wide open without any reference as to whether anybody can satisfy any judge that there is occasion for it, and that we should allow them to subpoena everybody of their own motion and examine them for discovery. I cannot quite grasp the necessity of doing that. I share the apprehension of the right hon. gentleman that this would be extending the thing too far, and from that point of view I believe we should retain the check of requiring the juage to oe satisfied that there is occasion for resorting to this exceptional procedure. If we could find words which would more closely define occasions when this powier should be exercised, and not unduly restrict the power of the judge, I should be very happy to incorporate them in the section. The committee did not put this forward as being an infallible conclusion or one that is not open to consideration, but after having threshed out a great many of the objections which have been raised here, we thought that the words in the Bill expressed the idea as well as we wene capable of expressing it. It certainly did not occur to us that it would be desirable to provide for a general examination on discovery of everybody, at the instance of either party.

This examination cannot certainly take place before a judge, because the witnesses could not be taken to Osgoode Hall to be examined. They would be examined in the county in which they rteside, before the local registrar of the court. The first thing that would have to be done after the order was issued, would bh to file the order with the local registrar where the trial would take place, and tb!en there would have to be an appointment to examine one witness, or as many witnesses as the petitioner or respondent saw fit to 127*
examine. That would take some days, and then there would have to be a number of days before the witnesses could he subpoenaed. How are you therefore to prevent the spiriting away of witnesses and the instruction of witnesses? I hava no serious objection to the section, because what will be sauce for the goose will be sauce for the gander, but I submit that the minister is placing on th1e statute book a law which eventually will be found to be unworkable. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) said it corresponds with the English procedure but it does not correspond with the English procedure any more closely than it corresponds with the Canadian procedure, in the lexamination of witnesses de bene esse. I believe that under the present Controverted Elections Act you can do all that is sought to bb done here.
No.

I think that under section 45, if you can convince a judge that it is necessary to perpetuate the evidence of a witness for use >at the trial, you can got an order for the examination of that witness, but you axe going beyond that in this ease. I am strongly of the opinion that you are doing something which will be regretted even by the members of the committee who reported this Bill to the House. I do not care particularly one way or the other; if the minister is prepared to take the responsibility, he can do so.

Has the minister in any way taken into consideration what I ventured to urge before the members of the committee when they required me to appear before them? The misconduct of people during an election is like any other misconduct, and public opinion is the eventual arbiter in all these things. If a man gets drunk, you arrest him, and you give the evidence and the case is disposed of; and people come to the conclusion either that the man is a disorderly character or that an injustice has been done him, because, being more or less familiar with the evidence, they are capable of forming an opinion. If misconduct in the conduct of an election takes place, the culprit should be brought- up in court for conspiring with others against the public weal, by giving or accepting a bribe, and on evidence being given, the magistrate should dispose of the case. That would not of itself void any election, but it would have a tremendous effect upon the election; and if, in the course

of time, some of these people were brought into the police court, and it were found that this sort of thing was going on, by the finding of the magistrate, the effect on thg public would be so tremendous- assuming that the public care about it at all-that the candidate whose agents were acting in that way would stop it all, or else the candidate would certainly be defeated at the polls. I am thoroughly convinced, from hitter experience, that the colossal undertaking of an election petition is so serious and expensive a business, and so likely to go off, that it is almost impossible to proceed with a protest. At the trial of the election petition your expenses are about $300 or possibly $500 a day, putting it mildly. You say bo-and-so is to be called as a witness at two o'clock, and two o'clock comes and he is not there. It is said, "Oh, he is ill,'' and a doctor gives a certificate to the effect that he cannot appear. What are you going to do? You stop the trial. The next day the same thing occurs-he cannot appear. There is an important witness gone, perhaps important witnesses gone. The bottom is knocked out of the whole case; whereas if you could arrest the culprits 'during the course of an election, if you could watch them and take them by the scruff of the neck to the police court and say: "Here is a man corrupting the people," and you prove it, you can have him fined a dollar or sent down for ten days, if you like. As long as the people know that corrupt practices are going on, they will hold that candidate more or less responsible. It is quite possible that the candidate is not the man really liable for the conduct of his agent; but the general tenor of the whole election contest is made quite plain. The people know the history of these men quite well, because men are not picked up at a moment's notice for the purpose of carrying out all sorts of wrong-doing at an election. They are well known; they are usually experienced ; and if they are properly watched and the opportunity is given, you can break up any system of corruption in a very few days; but if such men can sail around and have their headquarters at hotels and live like prize-fighters, and enjoy themselves thoroughly and be absolutely free while they are perpetrating all sorts of wrongs of this description, all they need to do is to clear out immediately after the election is over; and where they are no one knows: the deed is done, the public is defied. In the other case, that is not so. If they had the opportunity, policemen would simply say to these men: "You [Mr. Burnham. 1
are wanted in here; give an account of yourself; what are you doing?" You do that with *afll sorts of fakirs; you do it with people who cannot give an account of themselves; you do it with drunkards and people who commit misdemeanours of various sorts; but in the conduct of an election, which concerns the public weal more than anything else, you omit it; you do not allow it. Surely some simple device of this description might be added to the other machinery which would enable people desirous of breaking corrupt practices to do it in time, and not have to spend thousands and tens of thousands of dollars on a trial which consists partly of a contest between lawyers to defeat the ends of justice and of witnesses who desire to escape giving testimony.

There are no
doubt many crudities, apparent or real, in the Bill now before the committee. The truth is that no committee can within a limited period of time draft amendments to the Dominion Controverted Elections Act which will not be found imperfect. It should be the work of capable men for many months, perhaps a year or more, to revise this Act successfully. As a matter of fact, the committee engaged in revising the Dominion Controverted Elections Act practically gets no assistance whatever from the officers of the Crown or the Department of Justice. We have the assistance of parliamentary counsel, but their time is divided up on account of their being engaged in other duties, and the result is that any drafting is very liable to be imperfect. I am very much impressed with the objection made to this section by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German). I do not think that any member of the committee ever expected that this section would not meet with some very substantial opposition from members of the House when placed before it for consideration and review.
Section 45 of the Bill was intended to enable the examination of a witness upon notice, where it was abundantly clear that he intended to leave Canada, and that either the respondent or the petitioner were desirous of having his evidence taken. It may be remembered that in section 3 of the Bill, which defines the form of the petition, it is provided that the complaint shall be set out with some particularity. Just how far that should go, we are not at all clear, and we are agreed

that that section of the Bill should remain over for the present.
Section 10, which we are now considering, was inserted just because there was an amendment provided by section 4 in respect to the form of the petition. Some of the members of the committee thought that, inasmuch as the petitioner was compelled to set forth in his petition with some particularity the details of his complaint, he ought to have some opportunity in some way or other of examining the witnesses before the trial so as to circumvent the very usual practice of having witnesses leave the jurisdiction of the court. Inasmuch as we have passed over section 4 for consideration, I would suggest that we let this section stand, because if section 4 is changed we may find it quite easy to remove the objections which have been urged against this section. I must admit the objections are fairly substantial, and I am not sure that they have been well answered so far.

The great difficulty in proceeding with an election trial is to get the material witnesses. They are spirited away by some means or other, and the ends of justice are thwarted. How to prevent that is a matter for the lawyers to decide, but tnere is worse than that. At election times there are brought in from other countries, for example from the United States, men who have been Canadian citizens or who are perhaps still Canadian citizens, but who are employed in the United States and who' can leave conveniently a day or two after the election is over. They come to Canada for the purpose of doing an illegal or highly improper act. How can such men be detained in the country and brought to trial? I cannot suggest any method; that will be for judicial minds to decide. If an application could be made under oath to a judge by some responsible, reputable citizen or by one of the candidates who is aware of conduct of that kind being done, whereby those men could be detained in the country or their evidence got in some way much good would result. That in my judgment would add very materially to having justice done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As regards what the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., says, this section possibly does not goi very far to detain such a witness; but it would give some assistance in so far as it would at least make it possible for any person to make a petition at as early a date as he pleased, and thereupon to obtain an order to make such witness appear on some day, so that if the witness did not do so, he could be punished for contempt of court. But unless the proposition itself will meet with the approval of the House, there would be no useful purpose in our pressing for more effective means to enforce it.
With regard to the observation of my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), I would point out that he is under a false impression if he supposes that there is at present no method of punishing unlawful practices at elections other than by election petition. If he refers to the Dominion Elections Act, he will find quite a number of. provisions providing penalties either by actions instituted to recover them, by indictment before the criminal court or by summary prosecution. I have not all these before me, but I might refer to some of them. For instance, power is conferred upon the deputy returning officer to constitute constables with authority to arrest people who are guilty of unlawful practices. I admit that in these matters our law is susceptible of improvement, but it is not correct to say that there is no provision for prosecution before the criminal courts for unlawful practices at elections. The committee dealing with these two items were strongly impressed with the view that what was a lacking in the Dominion Elections Act was not so much the creation of offences and the imposing of penalties, but rather an effective instrument of enforcement. What we are trying now to deal with is a measure providing a method by which you can rectify the wrong done in the return of the wrong man. But in the Dominion Elections Act there are provisions for the punishment in the manner I have indicated of those guilty of unlawful acts at elections.
Is there anything other than by indictment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is provision for
action for penalties and also for trial for summary conviction. It would take a long time to read all these provisions, but I might give my hon. friend some references. Under the heading " Corrupt practices and other illegal acts," sections 265 and following define the corrupt practices and prescribe penalties; and under 284 and following are provisions for the enforcement of these penalties. These are in addition to the provision respecting indictable offences and offences made punishable on summary conviction. The particular sections dealing with indictable offences, I have not under

my hand, but I know that there are such provisions. As to the suggestion of the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), there is no doubt that this section is affected very much by what is done with regard to sections 4 and 5. We of the committee regarded this Bill as one whose sections completed each other and provided a more effective method of trying election petitions. No doubt most of the sections are so interdependent that one can hardly be considered apart from the rest. Yet there is more immediate connection between this section and sections 4 and 5 than between the others. Therefore, I have no objection to adopt the hon. member's suggestion and allow this section to stand until we come to deal finally with sections 4 and 5.
On section XI-place of trial; trial to proceed until all evidence taken:
The suggestion was made before lunch: if the respondent admits liability and the petitioner is content with that, who will supply the witnesses to go on with other cases?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The section does not purport to provide a method by which they can supply them. But it does provide:
The trial judges shall proceed with the trial until all the evidence relevant to the particulars filed in the case has been heard, notwithstanding any admission on the part of the respondent of corrupt or illegal practices sufficient to void the election, and notwithstanding that in the opinion of the court enough evidence has been heard to void the election.
This is another provision inserted to meet the possible suggestion that the court is without power to go on after enough has been established by admission or evidence to void the election.
Why not say that the court "may" proceed, instead of "shall" proceed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We make it the court's duty. If, notwithstanding the admission of the respondent, notwithstanding there being enough proof to void the election, the petitioner wants to go on to ventilate other cases of bribery, we want it to be made the duty of the judge to go on and deal with these matters, if they are covered by the petition.
Suppose he does not want to go on?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All we have said is that the judge shall proceed with the trial until all the evidence relative to the particulars filed in the case has been heard. If everybody stopped bringing in evidence, the court
	,
would not be able to hear any more; we have said that they shall go on until all the evidence is heard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I had a good deal of experience in the trial of election petitions many years ago, and the course usually adopted was this: after the petitioner had put in his evidence and the judges had come to the conclusion, upon that evidence and upon any that the respondent had adduced in regard to the several charges made, that enough evidence had been submitted to justify the voidance of the election, he usually asked the petitioner whether or not he desired to proceed with the personal charges. The petitioner had to answer yes or no, the judges usually intimating that if the petitioner proceeded with the personal charges against the respondent and did not succeed, he would be visited with the costs of his unsuccessful attempt.

In recent years the practice in Nova Scotia has been that even if the respondent admitted sufficient corrupt and illegal practices to void the election, the court nevertheless proceeded with the case. This proposed provision is putting into statutory form the effect of the practice of the courts in recent years.

The opinion expressed in the newspapers of Ontario is that the trial of a petition should not be dropped simply because the respondent admits his guilt. This section provides that the court shall go on with the case, but if the petitioner does not wish to go on, he cannot be compelled to bring witnesses to the court and to produce evidence. How, then, will the court proceed? There is no procedure under this Act, so far as I can see, which will secure the attendance of witnesses in such cases to establish personal charges against the respondent. The object of the trial of election petitions, aside from the proving of charges which would disqualify the person elected, is to ascertain whether or not corruption existed in the constituency during the election.
In all our provinces, the consent of the court or judge must be obtained before an action can be discontinued.

In Ontario a party may
discontinue the suit by filing discontinuance papers and paying costs.

The English precedent
is that you have to have the consent of the court or judge. But if judgment against the defendant is obtained by the plaintiff on consent, the judge may say:	I am not
satisfied that the matter shall be settled merely by consent; I am going to examine *witnesses.

I think 1
understand the motive of this section. In the trial of an election petition, one hundred witnesses having been heard, or one witness having been heard whose evidence proves one charge sufficient to void the election, the respondent may say:	I confess judgment; I am willing that the seat shall be declared vacant. In this case, the objection is that the taking of further evidence might establish that a general system of bribery and corruption had been in operation throughout the district. I believe it is wise, therefore, that under such circumstances the court shall be directed to proceed with the case and to make a report to Parliament as to whether or not there was in the district concerned a general system of bribery and corruption. I think the section is a wise one.

My observation of election trials during the last ten years has been that the solicitor really makes little effort to secure the disqualification of the respondent. The purpose of an election trial to-day is to ascertain whether or not a general system of bribery has prevailed. No solicitor conducting an election case will accept an admission of corrupt and illegal practices on the part of the respondent and a final order unseating the candidate. What I mean is that if a trial is conducted on that basis, the Solicitor does not perform his whole duty, because the whole purpose of an election trial is, as I have said, to disclose any system of bribery and corruption which may have prevailed. It should be remembered also that the hearing of an election petition is really not a trial, in the ordinary sense of the word; it is an inquiry. Parliament, having delegated to the courts the duty of inquiring into alleged illegal practices in connection with elections, must give to the courts power to go beyond the desires and requests of counsel engaged in the case. 1 think the distinction must be held clearly in mind that the hearing of an election petition is not a trial, but an inquiry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I entirely agree with the view that the court should have
power to proceed in such cases, if the circumstances of the case make it, in their judgment, desirable that they should do so. But if witnesses have not been subpoenaed, is the petitioner to be directed to subpoena them? What means will the judge have of proceeding with the trial if the petitioner does not desire to take the responsibility of doing so? I do not object to the purpose of the section at all; I think it is a very good one, and I think that the judge should have the power which is assigned to him under its provisions, but I am not desirous of putting something on the statute book which may appear to fulfil certain objects, and which will not, in the end, fulfil them at all.
If counsel do not wish to put witnesses in the box, can the judge force them to do so, or hold them guilty of contempt of court if they do not do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Three conditions may arise. In the first place, in the case where the defendant has admitted enough to void the election or where there is proof enough to void the election, and the petitioner wants to proceed with the case, we say to the judge: You shall go on. We do not say: You may if you want to; we say: You shall, because we want to have brought out whatever can be brought out that is in the public interest.
The judge may say: Prove all these charges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I may be quite mistaken, but if that is already the law perhaps the hon. gentleman would show me the text. If that is the law but if there is no express text, what harm can be done by saying perfectly clearly in this statute what the hon. gentleman believes to be the law now?
To me there are three combinations of circumstances that may arise. That is the first. Under these circumstances, in my judgment, the law ought to be imperative; it should not be in the power of the judge to say: no, I have enough evidence and I am going to render judgment. Then, there is, secondly, the case suggested by the right hon leader of the Opposition, where both parties say that they have enough evidence; perhaps the respondent has got in the box and has said: "I admit that by an agent or without my knowledge enough corruption was perpetrated to void this election," and there are sitting there a whole host of witnesses, and the petitioner says, "under these circumstances I am willing to accept that." Surely that

will be quite a clear case of duty to the judge to examine the people who are there. They have been brought there to prove allegations which we presume are specific and which upon their face are allegations of corruption and bribery that ought to be exposed. It seems to me in that case we should make iit imperative for the judge to continue ithe inquiry. That is the second case.
Then, there is the case where it may be impossible for the judges to go any further. I do not understand that our imperative section would alter the fact that if neither party would adduce evidence and there were no available witnesses there, then the court would be in the position of having heard all the evidence. We might use the word "available" in that case, because the court would not be able to go on, but would be in the position of having heard all the available evidence. What I think the committee had in mind was that he could go ahead as far as there was available evidence. If there is no evidence there to be heard, the judge cannot hear it, and he may take it that that is a condition where he has heard all the evidence. I do not think we would meet the purpose of the committee by saying that the judge may do that. We want to create a situation where, as far as possible, it would be the judge's duty, within the limit of the charges made, to hear all available evidence upon them, even although it might go beyond what was necessary to void the election. Wlnb was necessary to void the election may have been established by admissions.

My hon. friend perhaps misunderstood what I had in mind. I do not think the Controverted Elections Act in express terms says that a judge shall go on and hear all the evidence the petitioner chooses to present to the court. My belief is that the judge is morally bound, perhaps not by express terms, to hear all the evidence which the petitioner will adduce to establish the charges which were alleged in the petition; because it is not one issue of fact as to whether or not this man is entitled to the seat. A petition comprises several issues of fact; in fact, every section of the petition raises an issue of facts in itself. So that the one fact that the man is not entitled to hold the seat by reason of bribery and corruption proved voids the seat, but that does not dispose of all the issues raised by the
5 p.m. petition or pleadings. I understand that a court would simply

say: We are bound to hear all the evidence which the petitioner brings before us to establish the case as alleged in the pleadings which are before the court. To that extent I think the trial judges are bound to hear all the evidence the petitioner presents. When the petitioner is satisfied, saying, "I do not care to go any further," the seat is voided. Then you say by this section that the judge shall go on and further investigate. So far as my observations have shown, the practice is that the witnesses are not all subpoenaed for the first day; probably only one or two will be subpoenaed for the first day. Generally the strongest case the petitioner can make is taken up first. When you say here that the trial judge shall further investigate, you do not provide any means for having him do so unless you say that the witnesses shall be subpoenaed, and then you do not provide any means for furnishing them or say who is to pay the costs. If you say that he "may" go on, he may do so now. If you use the word "shall," it makes it compulsory on the trial judge to go on and subpoena witnesses of his own volition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The objection would be met if you put in the word "available" before the words "and relevant." Then we would not place any obligation on the judge to go out on the highways and byways and look for witnesses. We would simply say to him: It shall be your duty to go on with the available and relevant witnesses."
Would it do to add the word "then" and make it then available as applicable to the witnesses then present at the trial?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That might be very well where neither party wants to go on; but if the petitioner wants to go on, we should make it the judges' duty to hear the evidence he will adduce, and he should be entitled to make evidence available by subpoenaing more people for the next day if they are not there that day.

Would it not be better to use the word "may," because we know that in actual practice if the parties agree that there has been enough evidence, that the admission is sufficient, that the election is going to be voided, they will take care to have the witnesses beyond the control of the judges. What is the use of putting it in if it is to become a mere farce? If you gave permission to the judges to continue the hearing, it would be very much

better. In ordinary practice no judge would go on unless one or other of the parties wanted him to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The intention of this legislation is that the judge shall go on. I have heard it said repeatedly in civil courts by judges that they had heard all the evidence they required, that the case was proved, and they were prepared to give judgment and would not waste time hearing more evidence. It is by no means clear to me that a judge in an election case is not, under our statute as it now stands, free to say the same thing.
Most of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken seem to think that under the law at the present time the judge would be bound to go on.	I do not
think we would disagree as to the desirability of his being bound to go on if the petitioner desired it. I have not been able to find any provision in the statutes under which the judge Would not be at liberty if he thought proper, to say that for the purposes of the petition he did not propose to go on even if the petitioner wanted to go on. I think that we should have the word " shall " in the section. I do not see what harm would come from requiring the judge to go on with the case where there is available evidence to substantiate the charge. The public interest demands that where there is available evidence the matter should be gone into. Of course, as the hon. member for St. John says, the parties could put themselves in a position where there would not be available evidence. No great injury will come to anybody from requiring the judge to proceed with the available evidence.

The Minister of Justice is very familiar with everything that has taken place in the province of Quebec. Without referring to the legal side of this question, the minister knows that in the last thirty years in the province of Quebec the two parties have agreed as to whether or not the evidence is to be produced, the case allowed to go to court and an attempt made to have the election voided. There are not half a dozen cases in the last thirty years where the issue was pressed and disqualification asked for. The belief is present in the minds of those who have discussed the question that we will never be able to get at the bottom of these political cases unless they are taken out of the hands of the political parties and it is suggested that the only way to sift the matter to the bottom is to have a public prosecutor appointed for that purpose. Has the committee given this phase of the question any consideration at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We did consider the question, but we did not hope to be able to devise a plan for the appointment of such an official which would be satisfactory and which would pass this House. We are trying to do it in a more modest way than the procedure which the hon. gentleman suggests. I quite welcome the criticism we have had, but I think it shows that we cannot hope to do everything at once in the direction of improvement, and more particularly in the direction of securing an inquiry when the parties to the proceedings may not be over anxious to have the matter probed. I think, however, that what we did is a considerable step in advance if the House accepts it. Something in the direction of what the hon. gentleman suggests, if- it met with general acceptance, would also he desirable but the committee have no proposition of that kind to present on that subject.

Has the minister added
the word " available"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think that the section would be altered by putting in the word " available." Nobody, not even a judge, is bound by law to do the impossible. If he is told that he shall hear all the relevant evidence it must mean all the relevant evidence within his hearing.
On section 12-after thirty days clerk of court to apply, and court to fix day for trial:

Section 12 having been
adopted, I wish to suggest for the consideration of the committee an amendment which would come in very properly at this point because it would be in addition to section 57 which is the last dealing with trials for corrupt practices. I think the committee will agree with me that the law relating to elections is to-day very strict indeed. As the Minister of Justice has remarked, we have plenty of law on the subject, ample, one would suppose, to secure purity of elections, but unfortunately it has not had that result. There is more corruption at elections to-day notwithstanding the stricter provisions of the law than there ever was in the history of our country. Everybody will admit that the corruption which takes place at elections is only limited by the means of the representatives of the parties, and their ability to spend it.
No, their ability to get it.

Well, ability to get it. Unfortunately, that is the case. The agents of the two parties vie with each other in getting the greatest number of votes and they dd not seem to have any fear of the law or any fear of election petitions. They do not fear anything, either on earth below or in heaven above, and they all do their very best to win the election. Then they have in their minds that in the majority of cases there will be saw-offs in connection with these petitions, and they will get rid of any difficulty in that way. They have the expectation that no election will be voided for corrupt practices, perhaps by common consent, and therefore one side can rely upon the other to either abandon proceedings or not to take any proceedings.
Every person who has had to do with controverted election petitions will admit that the law has been an absolute failure. We have provisions now that any person taking a bribe Shall be subject to imprisonment and shall be disqualified for a term of years from voting, but that does not deter people from taking bribes. We have a provision in the law now that if a person bribes an elector he is liable to imprisonment for a term of years and is disqualified from voting at an election or sitting in Parliament, and that law has proved to be entirely ineffective. This Bill is a very good one because it facilitates the trial of election petitions, but in my opinion it will be just as ineffective as the present law for the prevention of electoral corruption.
I suppose that cannot, by any possible chance, be called an expert opinion.

My own view is that it is better to be frank about the matter than to pretend that a state of affairs exists which does not exist. Every one will admit that, either with or without the knowledge or approval of candidates, the agents, the workers, the party friends of the candidates do all they can to win. If a man is of a high moral tone he justifies his spending money with the statement that you must fight the devil with his own weapons. I have heard very excellent men say that, as an excuse for their going behind the barn arid paying something to an elector to vote for their candidate. My own judgment is that this Bill is not going to be any more effective than the present law, and the question is, what can be done? I have always had the idea that if you could hold out to a candidate the expecta-

tion that if he and his friends run an abso-. lutely pure election, so that they would be able to satisfy the judges that the election was pure, and that if a sitting member has by himself or his agent been guilty of corrupt acts so that his seat Shall become null and void, that the defeated candidate should get the seat. I believe in that way you will accomplish the object we all have in view. I would suggest for the consideration of the Minister of Justice and the committee a section like this:
57. On the trial of a petition under this Act complaining- of an undue return, and claiming the seat for any candidate, if the trial judges decide that the election of the sitting member is void, by reason of the commission of corrupt practices on the part of such sitting member or his agent or agents, and the judges are also satisfied that no offence was committed at such election by the candidate on whose behalf the seat is claimed, or by his agent or agents, which would have been sufficient to render his election void in case he had been declared elected, the trial judges shall declare the election of the sitting member null and void and shall declare such candidate, on behalf of whom the seat is claimed, to have been duly elected.
In case the seat is claimed for more than one candidate, two or more of whom the trial judges find have not, either by themlselves or their agents, committed an offence which would have been sufficient to render their election void in case they had been declared elected, the trial judges shall, in declaring the election of of the sitting member null and void, also declare such one of the candidates on behalf of whom the seat is claimed, having the majority of the votes cast for such two or more of the candidates on behalf of whom the seat is claimed to have been duly elected.
I would ask the Minister of Justice to look this over and to consider it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Do I understand that
the hon. gentleman puts this forward as supplying something which does not exist at all in the present Act?
Yes, there is a provision in the present law that you may have certain ballots struck off from the successful candidate.
That is a scrutiny of the votes?

Yes, but that is not
like my amendment. This suggested amendment holds out to the man an opportunity of being given the seat by the judges, who says:	I am going to run an absolutely
pure election, there is no money to be spent, there is to be no violation of the law permitted which would unseat me if I had been returned, and who being able to prove the purity of his own election can prove

that the sitting member by himself or his agents; has violated the law.
Regardless of what majority the elected candidate may have had?
Regardless of the majority.
It would be a reward for merit to the candidate and penalty on the constituency.

Not necessarily. It may be said that this might be hard upon the constituency, and to a certain extent that is true, but it surely is better to secure purity of elections, even though the constituency might be deprived of the services of the man who violated the law, by himself or his agents.
' Mr. BOYCE:	Would that be regardless
of the finding on a cross-petition against the defeated candidate?

Oh, no. On cross-petition, the defeated candidate's conduct may be inquired into, and the burden would be cast upon him of satisfying the judges that he had run an absolutely pure election, before he could obtain the seat. We have been trying for forty years in this country to secure purity of elections. We have passed most stringent laws providing for putting people in the penitentiary, and providing heavy penalties and disqualifications, but all these laws in the past have been wholly ineffective until to-day electoral corruption prevails to a greater extent than ever, and there is more money spent in elections than ever before in the history of Canada, which perhaps is owing to the country being wealthier than it was in former years. Unless there is some great injustice which would be done to a constituency, I believe that this plan which I venture to suggest would prove most effective in securing electoral purity. Whether it is worth while to subject constituencies to what might be some disadvantage or some injury by not getting the candidate they would prefer, is, of course, another question. But it does seem to me that it is worthy of consideration, because the object aimed at will commend itself to this House and to the people of this country. I believe there would be no more effective mode of securing purity of elections than a law like this, which would give to the man who runs an absolutely pure election an opportunity of getting the seat, and which would deprive the
man, who by himself and his agents violated the law, from sitting in Parliament.

Would my hon. friend
from St. John make it apply to the candidate, when corruption had been committed without his knowledge?
Yes.

Would it not be a great hardship to make him die victim of acts committed by agents, when he had not countenanced such acts at all? I would favour the hon. member's amendment if it applied only to candidates who had been themselves guilty of corrupt acts, or who had knowledge of such acts being committed by their agents; but in cases where they were the victims of zealous friends, it would be a great hardship on such candidates to make the amendment apply.

My hon. friend knows
that the law now compels a member elect to lose his seat by reason of corrupt acts on the part of his agents. It may be a hardship, but the question is: Is the securing of purity of an election of so great importance that the advantage will overcome the disadvantage of a man being held responsible for the actions of his agents? In the running of elections, candidates do have their agents; that is, as a rule the candidates are put up by the parties, and the parties have their agents to manage the elections, and there is no great difficulty in a party securing an absolutely pure election if they make up their minds to do so. The difficulty is to get them to make up their minds to have a pure election. If there were a provision that, if there should be a violation of the law on the part of the candidate or his friends, his opponent might get the seat, it would be veTy effective in securing purity of elections.

The candidate might be
the victim of conspiracy. A man might pose as an agent of the candidate and commit corrupt acts, and then go to court and admit that he had committed corrupt acts for that candidate. In that way he would secure the election for his friend, the other candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The law as it stands at present seems to contemplate upon the petition that the seat may be claimed for uie other candidate. "While I cannot find any special provision for that-

That is provided for
in the present law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 22 provides for tile examination of a candidate, although he is not a party to the petition. It says:
Whenever a petition has been filed claiming the seat for a candidate, such candidate, although not a party to the petition, may be orally examined as if he was a petitioner.
Section 49 provides that:
On the trial of a petition under this Act complaining of an undue return and claiming the seat for any person, the respondent may give evidence to show that the election of such person was undue in the same manner as if he h>d presented a petition complaining of such election.
Section 50 provides f r striking off names.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 50 says:
If, on the trial of an election petition, claiming the seat for any person, a candidate is proved to have been guilty, by himself or by any person on his behalf of bribery, treating, or undue influence with respect to any person who voted at such election, or if any person retained or employed for reward by or on behalf of such candidate, for all or any or the purposes of such election, as agent, clerk, or messenger, or in any other employment, is proved on such trial to have voted at such election, there shall, on the trial of such election petition, be struck off from the number of votes appearing to have been given to such candidate, one vote for every person who voted at such election, and who is proved to have been so bribed, treated or unduly influenced or so retained or employed for reward as aforesaid.
Then there is also the admission as to what may be done or proved in that particular case, and then tne judges are to report.
Section 58 provides that:
At the conclusion of the trial, the trial judges shall determine whether the member whose election or return is complained of or any and what other person was duly returned or elected, or whether the election was void, and other matters arising out of the petition, and requiring their determination.
And so on. I was under the impression [DOT]-it may be quite a mistake-that there was some form of petition for the claiming of a seat for the respondent. There are certainly provisions under which the seat may be claimed for a candidate. I felt, however, it would be wise, before saying anything as to the desirability of this amendment, to consider the matter more fully.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is perfectly true that the petition very often claims the seat for the respondent. The seat may be so claimed on various grounds:	for
example, the petition might set up the

contention that the person who is declared elected was not a person competent to be declared elected; that he did not fulfil the requisites of the statutes; that he was not a British subject, that he was not of the age of twenty-one years, or something of that kind.
There is no requirement that he should be 21 years of age.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then there is the result of the contest, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for St. John. For example, if the majority is not a very large one, it may be possible for the respondent to show that a certain number of persons have been bribed or unduly influenced-and for every person so shown to have been bribed or unduly influenced a vote is struck off from the votes of the successful candidate, and that may so reduce his vote that the respondent will have the majority. In that case he is, of course, entitled to claim the seat, and the provisions of the statute with regard to claiming the seat have in contemplation such a condition.
The first difficulty about the proposal of the hon. member for St. John strikes one is this, -that as pointed out by the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx), it might contain within it the inducement for a definite -and very insidious form of bribery, that is to say, the bribing of persons acting as agents for the successful candidate to commit some improper acts, which will void the seat and thus give it to the other candidate, who cannot be proved guilty of any such offence.
The suggestion put forward by the hon. member for -Calgary (Mr. Bennett)- is also a very important one. Suppose, for example, that a candidate has polled 4,000 votes, and that the candidate opposed to him has polled only 1,000 votes, and that upon a very careful and full inquiry it may be proved that half a dozen or eight men have been bribed or unduly influenced to vote for the candidate who has received the great majority of votes. The question under these circumstances is whether justice would be done to the constituency by pursuing the course which the hon. member for iSt. John suggests. According to the premise which he has laid down, the candidate who has been elected may have earnestly determined to conduct the election without offending in any way against the election law, yet through the misdeeds of his agents for which he is not morally

although legally responsible, the election is declared void.
The hon. gentleman proposes that for the action of some one person committed without the knowledge or consent of the candidate, and without any desire or intention on the part of the great majority of the electors thait those acts should have been committed, the choice of the constituency in the selection of the candidate is put to one side and the man who represents only one-fifth or one-sixth of the people of that constituency is declared elected.
That would seem to be a very anomalous and very incongruous result. While one is inclined to sympathize with every reasonable effort to bring about reformation in the conditions undeT which elections are held, I think it would require a great deal of consideration before any such proposal as that could be adopted.
So far as elections are concerned, it seems to me, a great deal depends, in every constituency, upon the condition of pubMc opinion. I have seen elections conducted, within very fecent years and in large constituencies in this country, where, I am absolutely sure, the provisions of the election law were well observed on both sides. I believe that was the case in the election held in Halifax in 1908. Public opinion had been aroused very much by some events to which I need not do more than allude, and I think that both sides were resolved that there should be- and at all events, public opinion compelled -a very strict observance of the election law. And there was a strict observance of the election law, I am very sure of that. Very strict measures were taken on one side, and I have no doubt on both sides, to see that the law should be observed.
Did the same thing continue in 1911?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So far as I know. I have no doubt it did. I did not speak of 1911, because I was not in the constituency except for a very short time in that election. In reference to what my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) has said, the provisions to which attention is called by the Minister of Justice were in the minds of the people on that occasion as they should be on all occasions. Very great precautions were taken to put these provisions in effect in case any attempt should be made to violate any provision of the Election
Act, and with very good results. And I think where public opinion is aroused, as it ought to be aroused in regard to these matters, in any constituency, similar good results wili be obtained. The hon. member for St. John city has made a very true statement, that we have plenty of law in this country if it is only properly used. And it seems to me that, in the absence of some such provision as that suggested here to-day-which I myself have spoken of in the past and have advocated-the appointment of a public prosecutor to see that election petitions are prosecuted to the end, it depends largely upon the condition of public opinion in the constituency how strictly the election law is observed. I would have been very glad if the committee had brought forward some feasible measure to provide for the appointment of a public officer who would discharge in the matter of election petitions such duties as are discharged by the public prosecutor in Great Britain. But I have not been insensible to the fact that in a country like this, with our population spread over so enormous an area, it would be a much more difficult task to make provision of that kind than in the case of Great Britain. The committee has made an attempt, a very earnest and I think a somewhat successful attempt, to provide otherwise for the bringing about of such results as have been had, at least in Great Britain, by the functions discharged by the public prosecutor, and I am certainly disposed to support their efforts in that regard to the utmost possible extent.

The amendment suggested by my hon. friend from St. John City (Mr. Pugsley) seems to be a drastic one, but it does not involve a new principle; it is simply carrying further the principle which is already in the law. Suppose the case of an election petition. The sitting member-taking the comparison just made by my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden)-has 4,000 votes and his opponent only 1,000 votes, showing that the overwhelming sentiment of the constituency is in favour of the successful candidate. If a single agent of that candidate has committed one single act of corruption, the election is voided and so the will of the people is set aside. This was enacted in order to promote purity of election. But is it straining the spirit of the Act, or proposing anything new, or extravagant, ot that will not be accepted, to provide that

i
the defeated candidate who has done his best to have a pure election should be given the seat? As the hon. member for St. John city has stated, very truly, we have been trying for more than forty years to promote purity of elections by laws such as this: If my memory serves me, our first Controverted Elections Act was passed in 1874. We have been trying ever since by these means to promote purity of elections. The present Bill! is -a testimonial of the fact that our efforts have not been successful. Is it not, then, right and proper that we should try a further remedy? The punishment we have inflicted against bribery in elections-not necessarily bribery committed by the member, but by any person on his behalf, is to have the election voided. That remedy has signally failed. My hon. friend suggests that in view of our experience we should give the seat to the man who has attempted to have a pure election.
Under the law as'it is at present, there are two parties to consider, the successful candidate and the constituency itself-the people. If a man is guilty of an act of corruption his seat is voided. He may have been the overwhelming choice of the people, yet because of one act of imprudence-we will call it merely an act of imprudence- the law steps in and says that his election shall be voided, and not only that but he may be debased from sitting and disqualified for years. So far as that is -concerned the will of the people is defeated, but defeated to a great extent by his own imprudence. But if the candidate is not guilty of personal corruption, but if the corruption has been committed by one of his friends, it seemis rather hard that he should have to suffer the penalty of having his elections voided and lose his seat for an act for which certainly, he could not be responsible. Still, the law has not hesitated, either here or in Great Britain, to inflict that injustice upon a candidate, with the single object that we may have, at any cost, purity of elections. We have tried this for forty years, with the very indifferent result we see at the present time. Therefore, I think the hon. gentleman is right in spirit when he goes so far as to say that when there is a contest between two men, if upon the side of the successful one there has been corruption either by the candidate or by his friends, and if on the other side there has been a pure election, then the seat ought to go by favour of the law to the other candidate. I would direct the attention of my hon. friend to the case of John Wilkes, whose

election as representative of the electoral district of Westminster was set aside three or four times by the British Parliament. At last, after Mr. Wilkes had been repeatedly elected and after his election had been repeatedly set aside, Parliament declared his opponent to be the representative for the constituency, although he was the minority candidate. It thus happened that the representative of the district was not the man who was the choice of the people, but the minority candidate. I give this instance to show to the committee that the suggestion of my hon. friend is not without precedent. As to the suggestion of the hon. member for Prescott that there may be conspiracy on the part of friends of one of the candidates to establish bribery in order that his adversary may loose his seat, this objection applies to the law as it exists to-day with just as much force as it may apply to the provisions suggested by my hon. friend. There is every reason why serious consideration should be given to the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I wish to point out that the law as it stands at present is not precisely as my right hon. friend suggests. In 1882 the dleoticn law was amended by a provision which is now embodied in section 56 of the Act, and which provides that if no corrupt practice was committed at the election by the candidate personally; if the candidate took all reasonable means for preventing the commission of corrupt practices; if the offences were of a trivial, unimportant and limited character, and if in other respects the election seemed to have been fairly conducted in accordance with the provisions of the law, then the seat shall not be vacated. I should like to point out also that it is in the interests of the purity of elections that an election may be declared void by reason of offences committed without the candidate's knowledge by agents of the candidate. But in all these cases the rights of the people are regarded, and it is permitted to them again to make a choice, by another election, of the man who shall represent them in Parliament. Probably at the time to which my hon. friend referred-the occasion on which the seat was given to the opponent of Mr. Wilkes- the rights of the people in that regard to their representation in Parliament were not. so strictly regarded as they are at the present time.

It is true that section 56 provides that the elected candidate shall

not he unseated for the commission of trivial or slight offences for which he was not personally responsible, or if he took all reasonable means to prevent the commission of corrupt practices. But it is also true, as my right hon. friend haq said, that while the sitting member may have a majority of votes which cannot be challenged, yet, by reason of the commission of corrupt acts by agents, he may be unseated, and in that respect an injustice may be done. That result, however, has been brought about by the operation of the law in the interests of the purity of elections.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I said, however, the people in that case are given the right to choose another representative.

If a provision such as this is to be put into the law, I think that the candidate for election should toe responsible only for the actions of the men whom he himself appoints as his agents. If in a constituency of 30,000 or 40,000 people, who perhaps become highly excited around election time, the candidate is to be responsible for everything that is done on his behalf, he will toe hellpless. Does the minister, in this proposed legislation, describe what constitutes an agent, or is everybody who supports the candidate an agent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The courts have devoted a good deal of time and attention to the question of what constitutes agency under the Election Act, and I think that they have arrived at a fairly settled jurisprudence. I must say that I would not venture myself to give an adequate definition, which could be so compressed as to be inserted in the statute, to cover all the conditions under which a man may be held to toe the agent of another. It has been pointed out that there is this very substantial objection to the amendment suggested:	It
is true that we have gone very far, in the interests of the purity of elections, in depriving the candidate elected of the honour and the right of retaining the seat in the operation of electing him to which there has been any material degree of corruption. So far, we deprive him of the seat and set aside the choice of the people to that extent. What the hon. member for St. John suggests is that we should now go a step further and foist upon the people for the future, as their representative, a man whom, as by their votes they have made perfectly clear, they do not want. The effect of the amendment
would be to penalize the people of the constituency because by some accident the election of the man for whom they voted in preponderating majority is declared void. The people, as a whole, are not responsible for that. As I understand it, in the cases where a man is entitled to claim the seat because his adversary was not qualified to be a candidate, so careful are the courts of the right of the people not to have somebody put upon them whom they have declared that they do not want, that they require that it shall be shown that the voters, when they went to vote for the unqualified man, knew that they were voting for an unqualified man, and were intentionally and deliberately throwing their votes away. If I am not mistaken, where you claim a seat because your adversary was not qualified to be nominated, you are not entitled to get more than an annulment of election, unless in addition to showing that he was not qualified to be a candidate, you establish that the people generally knew, or ought to have known, that you had called it to their attention so that it may be said that they ought to have known and must have known that they were voting for an unqualified person, and then you get the seat because the court says the people of the constituency, with their [DOT]eyes open, chose to throw away their votes. But I am not aware of a case under our Dominion Elections Act of this kind. I do know a case, not by virtue of specific statutes but in the contestation of a municipal election, of something of this kind. I had occasion to deal with one myself in the course of my judicial experience, and there I decided, and the judgment was confirmed, that though it was perfectly apparent that the candidate for whom the majority voted was not qualified to be a candidate for the office at all, and though the seat was claimed by his adversary, the minority candidate, who was perfectly qualified, the court, before it would be entitled to adjudge the seat to the minority candidate, should be able to say something more than that the elected man was not qualified-should be able to say that the electors, with their eyes open, threw their votes away when they voted for him.

I would call the minister's attention to the case of Baird and King in Queens county, in which the returning officer declared that the receipt for the $200 deposit required from the candidate was not in proper form. The election was

run, the people were perfectly innocent of any irregularity; there was a majority for Mr. King; yet the returning officer declared Mr. Baird elected and this House sustained the election of Mr. Baird, because, rightly or wrongly, they decided that there never was any other candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It was not a question of whether the candidate was qualified or wheather two men had or had not been nominated. I am not called upon to discuss that, as I understand the decision of the House went on the ground that only one man was legally nominated, who could be voted for. The case I was dealing with was the case of an unqualified person, and I only refer to it as showing the care with which the law proceeds before undertaking to say not only that the people shall not have a man for whom a majority voted, unless they choose him again, but also that they shall have a man with regard to whom it is absolutely manifest that they did not want him, that they had voted by an overwhelming majority that they did not want him. Are we going to impose such a man on the people because it happens that the other candidate or some agent or some other person who by a forced construction may be held to be the agent of the other candidate, was guilty of corrupt practice? While there is much to be said in favour of the view that an election is a fight between two candidates, we must bear in mind always the paramount right of the people to have in the first place the man they choose, and above all not to have forced on them a man whom they have repudiated. For these reasons it would be impossible to accept the amendment.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Sevigny in the chair.

I was going to say one or two words in reply to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and also in reply to the remarks made by the right hon. the Prime Minister, and in doing so I want to admit fully that I realize the force of the objection that is made from the standpoint of the constituency. But the question is whether the evil that is sought to be remedied is such as to warrant Parliament in making the provision I propose. As I said before, we must all admit that no remedy has been found so far for electoral corruption. Notwithstanding all the severe measures which have been passed during the

last forty years there has been no change in that practice. Corruption in elections prevails to an extent as great as, if not greater, than ever before. If we think that this amendment would have the effect of inducing purity of elections, then the question fairly arises as to whether or not the benefits that would result would more than counteract.any evil which might ensue with regard to the representation of the constituency in Parliament. The objection is made, with a great deal of force in it, that there may not be very extensive corruption by the friends and supporters of the elected candidate. If that is a real, substantial objection it might be got over by providing that the result which my amendment aims to accomplish would only be achieved in case of the judges finding that there had been a pretty general system of corruption, using the language contained in another part of the statute, in the interest of the elected candidate. I think everybody would admit that if the finding was to that extent it would not be a very great evil to return a man who had run a pure election free from all corrupt practices whatever.

I wish to say a word
in approval of the amendment brought in by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). It is not quite as drastic a measure as I would like to see adopted by this Parliament. I would rather accept the suggestion of the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) that the agent of corruption should be brought into court immediately and punished, if found guilty on the evidence of a few honest witnesses. Meanwhile the amendment of my hon. friend from St. John will certainly have a tendency to raise the political morals of our people and to create a certain terror in the minds of those men who so flagrantly violate the law at election times. It is not only on election day or at the polls that unlawful acts are committed, but they are committed, particularly in the rural districts, as everybody knows, the night and day before election. These men will ride in automobiles during the night in the back settlements, and strangers will go in to interview the voter while the local man who has taken them remains in the automobile. He is not a witness of what takes place between the strangers and the voters. When the voters who have been subjected to _this influence come down to the polls next morning it is found that they have

changed their political views. I think that this amendment will have a great effect upon the morals of our people, and that these political agents will not he as presumptious as they have been in the past.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the observations of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) this afternoon. Assuming, as we will, that we are all desirous of doing something to counteract the evils that are so prevalent, it does not appear to me that the amendment proposed will accomplish that object. We in Western Canada are situated in a very peculiar way. We have no lists in Alberta and in addition to that we propose to swear votes in on election day. That has been done for the last fifteen years. If we are going to lessen corruption we must start at the beginning and ask first: What is the object of an election? The whole idea of an election is to ascertain the will of democracy. To ascertain the will of the democracy the electors must not be fettered, corrupted or restrained. There must be a free expression of the opinion of the electors. How can that be accomplished? We know there is corruption, we know that the electors are corrupted, we know it, we believe it. Two plans were proposed in days gone by; one was compulsory voting and the other was the disfranchisement of the constituency. In addition to that wa have had punishment of the individual by the unseating of the successful candidate if the election has been won by fraudulent means. My old preceptor, than whom no abler man ever sat in this Parliament, I venture to say, Dean Weldon, of Dalhousie University, introduced legislation looking to a solution of the same problems as those which have been referred to by the hon. member for St. John. His Bill was finally passed and incorporated into the statutes. We have made certain provisions for disfranchising individuals who have been guilty of corrupt acts. I do not think that at the present time we are prepared for the . disfranchisement of constituencies. Compulsory voting has not been adopted in this country and we have never been sue- / cessful in enforcing the statute as it is.
I think we might do something in the way of disfranchising constituencies. If the judges were to report to Parliament tha,t a general system of corruption pervaded an election and prevailed through a constituency I do believe that the best way IK
for you to deal with it would be by disfranchising that constituency for the rest of th'e term of Parliament and holding it up to the people of Canada as an example of what corruption might accomplish. That would do something. Many years ago I entertained the idea, and I think I entertain it now more strongly than ever, that we must have a public prosecutor if we are going to accomplish any great amount of good under the present election law. In the 'different provinces there must be some such officers as a supervisor of elections and a public prosecutor. Electoral corruption is practised on such a scale that an individual cannot accomplish any good. I remember a general election in the West in which they were paying half-breed scrip. There was only one candidate for the whole province of Alberta, and the entire machinery of the Federal Government was at work paying scrip to thousands of individuals on election day. I remember that a telegraphic message was sent out something like this: "Majority large enough; stop the voting." That sort of thing cannot be overcome by single individuals. You require to have something more. You must have a public prosecutor who will make it his business, untrammelled by any consideration other than the public weal and the public good, to see that the laws are enforced. We do not need any new laws. The laws now in some respects are too drastic. Take the horse-hiring provision.
