That feature of the election law has become ridiculous because every one knows that horses are hired in every constituency from one end of Canada to the other. These trivial things are magnified into important things that have the effect of minimizing the advantages of the law as a whole. The amendment proposes what? Take the constituency of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), which that hon. gentleman represents here by a majority of something like 2,500 votes. Let us assume that the election was not run as an absolutely clean election and that three or four, half a 'dozen or a dozen of his agents, had been guilty of wrong doing and had violated the provisions of the election law; do you mean to say that it would be an advantage to this democracy to have that seat given to Col. Griesbach rather than a fresh appeal to the electors?
Will that make for any improvement? Is it not a very thwarting of the will of the people? One-half the electors and twenty-five hundred more decided that they desired to support the principles of the



Liberal party, and that one-half the electors and twenty-five hundred more are to be represented in Parliament by an opponent of the Liberal party and their principles because twenty-five men were guilty of corruption. Would that be right, or just, or fair? Is it not doing the very thing you should not do, namely, thwarting the very will of democracy? Is it not interposing against the will of democracy the corrupt views of twenty-five men? That is what it gets down to in the ultimate analysis. Why should twenty-five or one hundred corrupt men send to this Parliament a representative opposed to the wishes of the majority of the democracy in that constituency? I am certain that the proposal of the hon. member (Mr. Pug^ley) is not going to accomplish any good, and I think my hon. friend, with his large experience, will admit that. It is, as a [DOT] gentleman in the Press Gallery said to me this evening, an endeavour to utilize the political machinery rather than the legal machinery to accomplish good, and there is a good deal to be said for that. What you cannot accomplish by the enforcement of law, sometimes you can accomplish by political considerations, and that is what this amendment would mean. In other words, as I apprehend the amendment, you would say to the people of the constituency of St. John, for example: If you are corrupt and take bribes for the purpose of electing the hon. gentleman who now represents that constituency, you will find yourselves represented in the next Parliament by an opponent of the Liberal Government-the constituency will be represented by an opponent of the Liberal Government in any event-and that is what it would mean. That cannot be a sound principle.
The endeavour of the committee was not to make new larv, but to make effective the provisions of the law as they stand. The subject was too large to be dealt with in a week, or a month, or in several months. It would involve going over the old well-marked path, dealing with the question of compulsory voting, supervision of elections, public prosecutors, proper franchise, and matters of that kind. We simply had to deal with the situation as best we could, and the chairman of the committee outlined what the committee should undertake, and the committee has undertaken to suggest legislation that will make the existing laws more effective. Every hon. gentleman who has spoken on the other side of the House has admitted

that probably to some extent the committee has succeeded in that. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) were strongly in favour of certain changes which they conceived would bring about certain well-desired results, and these are incorporated in the Bill. The committee has decided that if you will remove preliminary objections, and if you will make it impossible to tie up proceedings for a length of time by technical objections and delays in the courts, you will have accomplished much good. That, this legislation will do.
I very much fear that the hon. gentleman from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) is desiring to make light of this whole endeavour of the committee to improve conditions, and that he really does not seriously believe in his amendment, because he must sea that its effect would be to nullify and destroy such good as we are endeavouring to accomplish by the Bill submitted. I think it will be found that simplicity, effectiveness, and efficiency, will be secured by the proposal now submitted to the House, and which has met with very general approval. It will, we believe, be a distinct improvement on existing conditions, and in addition, it will be found that instead of endeavouring to make new laws and create new offences we have simply taken advantage of existing conditions in the law as it now stands, to introduce simpler machinery into the statute-book for the purpose of making it more effective. I think we have succeeded in doing that.
If one were to generalize and philosophize on the question of corruption in the broader sense, how corruption is brought about and why, and whether the publication of contributions to election funds might not accomplish much good, one could do so, but these questions have engaged the attention of the House on former occasions, and we could not accomplish much good by discussing them now. We in the province of Alberta must first of all have a Franchise Act, and we must have some finality to our lists. We must endeavour in that new country to pass laws which will charge some one individual with responsibility for the enforcement of the law regardless of cost and regardless of consequences. I would point out that in my province, forty men who cannot speak the English or the French languages, who are foreign in every sense to our traditions and who know nothing of our history and nothing of the subjects under consideration,.

absolutely controlled the representation of at least one constituency, and that a similar number of such men controlled the representation of two or three other constituencies in the local legislature in the two new provinces. I think that our new Naturalization Act will do something to prevent that evil, but corruption can only be killed by making those who practise it pay the penalty of it. I do think that the legislation which is submitted in this Bill will do a little towards that end.
We all know that some corruption is practised in the election of the very best of men. As my hon. friend was speaking this afternoon, I was thinking of what John Morley tells of Gladstone's first election in Newark, that when he found the enormous expense of that election he was so disconcerted about it that he, for a time, contemplated the possibility of giving up his seat. Times have changed in England, and I doubt not that the right hon. gentleman opposite, who has seen so many parliaments come and go, and who spoke this afternoon about the changes wrought in the law about the time he came into this House would be able to tell us, were he in a philosophic frame of mind, that theTe has been at least an improvement in public opinion, as reflected in this House in its attitude towards corruption. The body politic may not have made as much improvement, for the simple reason that on account of large operations being carried , on in this new country there is a tendency on the part, not of the people themselves, but on the part of those who have benefits to derive from governments-to bring about corruption. Were this the proper time I might a tale unfold, by discussing that. I do not think that the amendment proposed by the hon. gentleman, anxious though he may be to see some improvement, will bring about good;
I do not think that any such measure as will thwart the will of the majority, and place the well-being of the people as a whole in the several constituencies in the hands of twenty-five or thirty corrupt electors, by sending to Parliament a man who is not the choice of the electors, can, in any^sense, be said to be a remedy for something for Which we must find a remedy, and which can only be found in clean, decent franchise, well-settled lists, a public prosecutor, and supervision of elections by some responsible authority, so that no financial considerations will prevent the law, as it now stands, from being rigorously and vigorously enforced. Beyond 128*
that I think we must look to the future and go slowly, being willing to make a little progress from day to day, realizing that such improvements as they have made in England, and in the republic to the south of us, have come slowly but have come surely gnd inevitably.

I would like to believe that the proposed amendments or any otheT amendments to the election law would result in iany very great change in the conduct of elections and in the purifying of the public life of this country. Twenty-five or thirty years ago election petitions used to be fought out. They are not fought out to-day; they are traded away, the reason for that being that there has come a feeling of complacency over the public. The public feel that it is an even fight; that the chances of election are as good on the one side as on the other; that when an election is over at five o'clock on election night, they had better get the result and go home, and that it is unsportsmanlike to challenge the other fellow's seat and try to get one's own candidate in. I think I am expressing a view that is very generally held.
Especially in the West.
The West is not an exception to the rule.

I have lived in the East and I have noticed that view quite as much in the East as in the West; in fact, I have seen more evidences of. tampering with the voter in the East than I have in the West. My experience of elections in the West is that the voter, as a rule, is not corrupt, although immense sums of money are expended. We have a provision that a candidate for Parliament shall publish an account of his election expenses within a certain time after the diate of the poll, and we all publish those statements. Those statements are asked for with a view of obtaining the amount expended by each candidate and of curtailing the amount, it being felt that by ttm public knowledge which is gained there may be less corruption* carried on. I am quite safe, however, in saying that the statement published by a candidate, either successful or unsuccessful, contains no information of the character which is intended; that it gives a person who reads the statement no idea whatsoever of the moneys used in the conduct of the election, and that for any purposes

of that kind we might abolish the statement altogether and realize at once that by that means at any rate no .information can be arrived at.
My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) spoke of the desirability of having a public prosecutor, and he has gone along the right line. The law as it stands is good enough if it is enforced. I am not objecting to having amendments; I am only saying that the same practice will continue whether you amend the law or not. When I was living in eastern Canada, I resided in the comity of my hon. friend the member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). In the provincial election of 1898, Mr. John R. Barber was the .successful candidate against Mr. William Kerns. An election petition was filed and the protest came for trial. Before the trial it was decided by Mr. Barber's friends that he should give up the seat, and that sufficient admissions should be made to void his election. There were two judges as the election trial judges; and when the attempt was mad'e to throw the seat open in that way by admissions, the judges said: " No, we will not let you do it in that way; you are bound to prove that there was general corruption throughout the constituency; we are not going to throw open the constituency by consent; you must bring your evidence." Therefore evidence was put in on behalf of the petitioners showing that in many polling divisions corruption had been carried on; in fact I recall that the information in some cases was supplied by the respondent, because it was a consent arrangement, but it had to be gone through with and the election was voided. On the report of the judges, the late Mr. William Lount, who was afterwards one of the High Court judges of Ontario, was appointed public prosecutor. The fact that Mr. Lount's political sympathies were those of the respondent made no difference whatever. He came to the county of Halton; he made his investigations; he made his prosecutions, and quite a number of those who were reported by the election trial judges were subsequently prosecuted by Mr. Lount and fined. Whoever paid the fines I do not know; but the prosecutions carried on at that time by Mr. Lount as public prosecutor under the direction of the Attorney General had a very salutary effect	in the	county
of Halton, and I	think if such
a suggestion as that made by my hon. friend from Calgary were carried out and in each province some counsel were

appointed-he would have to have very high standing so as to command public confidence-there would be such a shaking-up that perhaps corruption might be limited in some degree. I am not disposed to think that all the corruption is amongst the foreign element or the poorer classes of the people; very often it is high up. One of the reasons that we have corruption in our public life is the penalty which we put upon the man who is a candidate for Parliament or who is a member of Parliament or a member of the Cabinet, if he loses his seat. In the Old Country if a man loses his seat, he can get another seat; but he cannot do that here; if he loses his seat, he is down and out. There are very strong temptations in this country for a man who *wishes to remain in public life to let those things be done which will ensure his success.
Amendment (Mr. Pugsley) negatived
On .section 13-right to appeal on preliminary objections, etc., omitted:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only change effected by this amendment is eliminating from the provisions of the law as they now stand references to appeal on preliminary objections.

Section agreed to.
On section 14-substitution of new peti-titioner:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The change under this section is that instead of its being necessary for the applicant for substitution as petitioner to make his application to the court for leave to be substituted in the case of the withdrawal of the petitioner, provision is now made simply for the publication of an advertisement, and that a new petitioner may be substituted by filing in the court within one month from the last publication of the advertisement, or within such longer period as the court may prescribe, a notice of substitution in the form C in the schedule of this Act. Whereas under the old law it was provided that such party coming in to be substituted should give security as the original one did, and that in cases where there was reason to suspect any fraudulent connivance in connection with the withdrawal, the original deposit should remain as security, the provision here is that in all cases the original deposit shall remain as security.

In cases where an elected member had reason to believe

that his election would be protested, it has been known to happen that the elected member got a friend to issue the petition, and, the matter then being practically in the hands of the elected member, the petition was not proceeded with and the matter became a dead letteT at once. I do not-1 know whether there is in the law as it is to-day a provision under which any elector may interfere in such cases by asking to be made a party to the Suit in order that the petition may be brought to trial.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 37 of the Act is as follows:
When, under this Act, more petitions than one are presented relating to the same election or return, all such petitions shall, in the election list, be bracketed together, and shall be dealt with, as far as may be, as one petition; but such petitions shall stand in the election list in the place where the last presented of them would have stood if it had been the only one presented, as to such election or return, unless the court otherwise orders.
So that all petitions filed are combined and tried together as though they were one, coming in the order of the last one on the list.
Is it not possible, because of the fact that no time is fixed within which the clerk shall advertise, that there may be some delay in the proceedings?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The provision is that
upon any petitioner dying, becoming incompetent or being authorized to withdraw, notice shall be given by the clerk of the court. Immediately upon any of these things taking place, notice shall be given.

Has the minister made
any estimate of how long it will take under this procedure to bring an election petition to trial?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The respondent has 15
days within v'hich to file his answer to the petition, and, if he does not file that answer, he is taken to have denied- everything. Then, within 15 days after that, either party may apply to the court to fix a date for the trial. If at the expiry of the thirty days neither party has done so, it will be the duty of the clerk to call the attention of the court to that fact, and it will be the duty of the-court, after giving notice to the parties, to fix a proper time and place for the trial. I should say, therefore, that within six weeks after the forty days-two months, at all events-the petition ought to be brought to trial.
Is there an appeal on the merits of the case from the decision of the judges?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, there is provision for an appeal from the final judgment.

Section agreed to.
On section 16-witnesses to be summoned, and by whom:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This provision has relation to the summary trial of corrupt practices at elections. The officer charged with the prosecution is, under the present law, bound to summon such witnesses as gave material evidence at the trial, and, in addition such witnesses as he' deems requisite. Under this present provision there is imposed upon the prosecuting officer the obligation to summon such witnesses who deposed to any fact material to the charge as the trial judges may deem necessary or desirable to have -subpoenaed, and -such other witnesses as he thinks requisite to prove the charges. The only change, therefore, is that the prosecuting officer, in addition to his obligation to subpoena such witnesses as he may deem necessary, is bound to subpoena any witnesses that the judge at the trial may indicate as being desirable witnesses.

Section agreed to.
On section 17-punishment of convicted offenders:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The only change is a
provision making it clear that the penalty provided in this section is in addition to the disqualification provided for by section 282 of the Dominion Elections Act.
Is there anything in this law or in the proposed amendment to prevent a railway company from carrying liquor at election time into a county where its sale is entirely prohibited?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is not in this Bill any special provision with regard to their carrying liquor at election time.

For a distance of 500
miles along the shore of the St. Lawrence, from Levis to Gaspe basin, there are no licensed saloons. What I want to know is whether the Government railway or any other railway may carry any quantity of liquor into these districts, to be distributed and used for election purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It seems to me that a
railway company distributing liquor in a.

prohibition county would be violating the law just as anybody else would. Of course, the Government railway would not do this; in any case, I do not see that there is any difference between the man travelling on the railway and distributing liquor in a prohibition town, and any other man doing the same thing.
Mr. MARCH,:	In ten or twelve counties in the district which I have mentioned there_ are no licensed saloons, and if there is no provision to prevent a railway company from carrying liquor into these districts as ordinary freight at election times, and distributing it to be used by either political party for election purposes, I suggest that the minister give the matter consideration. There is a law now to prohibit the carrying of liquor in Scott Act counties, and I know that prosecutions under that law have taken place in the province of New' Brunswick.
But the law is not enforced.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Any law may be evaded, but the penalty is there.
These are not Scott Act counties'. The people simply refuse to have licenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are counties
where an individual would be free to give away liquor. The question is whether a railway company should be subject to some special prohibition that would not apply to an individual.
But do you not think it *would be wise to prohibit the carrying of liquor to these constituencies for a month before and a fortnight after the election?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That would be a subject for amendment of the Dominion Elections Act rather than the Controverted Elections Act.
I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Why should we rise and report progress without some statement of when we are to meet again?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought it was desired that further consideration should be given to sections 4, 5 and 10.

I wanted that explanation.
Progress reported,

Bill No. 112, to amend the Canada Grain Act-Sir George Foster-was Tead the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 1:
Section 27 of the Canada Grain Act, chapter 27 of the statute of 1912, is amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
"2. Such certicate shall be in all cases prima facie evidence of the facts therein contained."
I understood from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George' Foster) that the Bill coming from the Senate was not to be proceeded with.

The minister intends to proceed with the Bill; I am aware of that. He waited all afternoon with the hope of being able to proceed. It is his desire that it should go through to-night. The section read so far is in the form in which the minister wishes it to pass.

There is a misunderstanding somewhere. I understood from the minister that he was not going to proceed with this Bill, and to-day he handed me a typewritten copy which I understood him to say was to be substituted fo-r the Bill coming from the Senate.

The hon. gentleman
misunderstood. The Bill coming from the Senate is to be proceeded with. What he has is a typewritten copy of two clauses which are to be added by way of amendment to the Bill as it comes from the Senate.

Would the
Solicitor General say what is the effect of this clause?

The certificate referred to in this clause is the inspecting officer's certificate as, to grade. Hitherto, the Act has stood in this form, that the way- >
master's certificate as to weight is prima facie evidence, but there has been no clause giving evidential value to the certificate of the grade. This gives it evidential value-makes it prima facie evidence as to grade.
On section 2-official	certificate of
weight:

The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has a typewritten copy of the proposed amendment. I move that section 2 be amended so as to read:
No grain shall leave a terminal elevator without being officialy weighed, and the official

certificate of weight shall be final, subject to the provisions of section 120 of this Act.
The effect will be to make the official weight certificate-not the certificate as to grade, but that as to weight-final, subject to re-investigation, which re-investigation is provided for by section 120 of the Grain Act. This will make the weigh-9 p.m. master's certificate conclusive evidence of the weight of the grain, but it may be reviewed by the Grain Commissioner, hut not by any other tribunal.
Does this apply to harbour elevators in Montreal?

If the hon. member will look at section 118-1 speak from memory- he will see that it provides that Part II of the Act shall apply only to elevators in the western division and to public elevators in the eastern division in so- far as they carry western grain. By a subsequent clause public elevators include terminal elevators. Consequently, strictly speak;ng, this would apply to eastern elevators in so far as they carry western grain. But as a matter of practice it has never been made so to apply, because it has not been the practice to have weighmasters under the Grain Commission in these eastern elevators as in the others. Consequently it cannot take effect unless weighmasters are appointed.

The point I want to make is that the weighmaster appointed by the Harbour Commission of Montreal would, under the section proposed, naturally come under the supervision- of the Grain Commission, who have nothing to do with engaging him.

But the weighmaster appointed by the Harbour Commission of Montreal would not be such a " weighmaster " as is contemplated in the section. The " weighmasters " herein referred to are appointed by the Grain Commission; and until the Grain Commission appoints " weighmasters " for the eastern elevators, which I understand is not intended, this section can have no application.
Section as amended agreed to.

I beg to move the following amendment on section 3:
Section 118 of the said Act is amended by adding thereto the following words: " and to all water-carriers other than ocean carriers."
Section 118 is the section which I quoted to the -hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb); it is the definition section. The effect of adding those words to it is to make clear that part 2 is applicable to carriers between the western elevators and the eastern elevators, in so far as they carry western grain only.
That would cover United States ships going from Port Arthur to Buffalo?
No; the vessels to which the hon. gentleman refers do not carry grain from the western division to the eastern elevators.
Section agreed to.

I beg to move that the following he added as section 4:
The said Act is further amended by adding-after section 120, the following sections:
120a. The board shall also receive and investigate all complaints in writing under oath, of any shortage in grain upon the delivery of same from an elevator to a vessel or from a vessel'to an elevator, and shall have power to assess or apportion the loss arising from such shortage, amongst the elevator operators, water-carriers, and shippers, having to do with the said grain, and the finding of the board and such assessment or apportionment certified over the hand of a majority of the board, shall be delivered or sent to all persons concerned in such finding, assessment or apportionment, and shall be.final and shall be enforceable in any court of competent jurisdiction.
120b. The board may make regulations governing the responsibility for and the disposition of shortages and overages of grain upon delivery of same from an elevator to a vessel or from a vessel to an elevator, and may assess in .such manner and in such amount as it may deem just and proper, contributions from elevator operators, water-carriers and shippers, or from any of them, in favour of the board or otherwise, for the purpose of providing against such responsibility.
Provided that nothing contained in this section shall limit the powers of the board under the preceding section.
This is undoubtedly important legislation.
I believe the minister has already reviewed in the House the circumstances that have' given rise to it. A conflict has arisen between the lake carriers and the western shippers the lake carriers endeavouring to put into effect a form of bill of lading which would have turned back upon the shippers the entire responsibility for any shortages that might occur during transit from the western elevators to the eastern elevators. Heretofore there has been no special regulation governing it. Some of the companies have found themselves at the end of the year loaded with considerable loss by reason of shortages, the shortage arising by virtue of lesser weight being
20S-2

given to the carrier when he went to deliver this grain to the eastern elevator for transhipment to ocean steamers or to elevators at Kingston for transference to barges and thence to ocean steamers, than the weight given him by the Government certificate out of the western elevator. Similarly other carriers had what are called overages by the reverse process, that is the eastern weight was greater than the western weight. The result has been that a very determined effort has been made to get from under this responsibility and a conflict of interests has arisen. An effort has been made to bring the parties together, but I understand without final success. The intention of this legislation is to enable the board to provide against two classes of cases, the only cases that can arise. The first one is the class of cases where it is possible for the board, by investigation of the facts, to fix the responsibility for the shortage, to say to the western elevator operator: You have made an error, we have power under section 120a to investigate particularly questions of shortages and overages and we find that the error is on your part and therefore we say to you you must be responsible for the error, you must pay. Similarly they would have power to fix the responsibiliy on the lake carrier wherever the evidence was on hand which convinced them that the lake carrier was at fault; and likewise they would have power to fix the responsibility on the eastern, elevator. Another class of cases also arises, that is where there is no evidence available to enable the tribunal, which will' be the Grain Commission, to fix responsibility anywhere. That, I understand, is a very frequent occurrence. Cases arise very often where it is a matter of utter impossibility to bring home responsibility to the western weighmaster or to the eastern weighmaster or to the lake carrier. What is to be done with such cases as that? Obviously a solution can be found only along the line of a permanent regulation which may fix the responsibility always upon one party and fix a scale of contributions by which the other two parties also interested in the same grain, and who perhaps may be responsible, shall in every case contribute to a fund that shall be used by way of assurance against the loss which the class who are fixed w'th permanent responsibility in such, cases will have to bear. It will be observed that 120a provides that they may and must investigate the facts upon any complaint of shortage or overage. They have the power, if the facts 
brought before the commission are sufficient to justify its exercise, to determine who shall stand the loss of the shortage and who shall get the benefit of the overage. But they have also power under 120b to make .such regulations as may be required for governing the disposition of these shortages and overages. They may make regulations assessing against any one of the three, or indeed the four parties, for the shippers are the fourth parties, any scale of contribution, that scale of contribution being made to the board or to any one of the parties. The words used are: " Being, made to the board or otherwise," and that scale is fixed as against the party by whom the contribution is to be made and against the party who is to be held to consistent responsibility for the loss.

While the Solicitor General says that the board will have' power to investigate under oath all complaints in writing of shortages in grain, will he t<dl us what is to be done about overages? I will give him a case. Early in October last there was a vessel loaded at three different elevators at Fort William. When the ship reached port at the Georgian Bay end of the route there was an overage of 10,000 bushels reported. Word was sent back to Fort William, and immediately one of the men said':	That is my
grain; 1 made the mistake. But as they traced it along a little farther it was found that the overage was not in the hold loaded at that particular elevator, but in another hold. How will they trace that?

I do not see how an
overage could occur at one point unless there was a shortage at another. It seems that it will be necessary to complain as to a shortage.
The shortage would perhaps only be discovered in the elevator at the end of the season.

Yes, but before it is
discovered there has to be a complaint as to the shortage. No man is going to complain of an overage. The man to whom the overage accrues is the man who benefits. Unless somebody complains of a shortage there could scarcely ~be any call upon the board to interfere. The case that my hon. friend referred to would arise and come before the board only if a shortage had existed causing the ultimate overage and was complained of. If the word "overage" were to be inserted, it would mean the recasting

of the whole clause, and I do not see that the clause would be improved thereby, or that it would cover any real case that is not covered by the clause as it is.

I am not a lawyer, and 1
do not know anything about that. What I want to find out is how they are going to take evidence under oath. That case actually happened last fall, and there were three different elevators interested.

They might take evidence under oath on any complaint, but they cannot assess as for overage because there is no loss. Somebody will have to lose before there will be a complaint. This empowers them to assess against loss. They cannot do that unless there is a loss.
I think if my hon. friend would agree to leave the clause as it is, he will find that there is no case that can arise that will not be covered by it.

Would section 120b make provision for the case mentioned by my hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Robb)? It says that:
The board may make regulations governing the responsibility for and the disposition of shortage and overages of grain upon the delivery of grain from an elevator to a vessel or from a vessel to an elevator.
Could they take evidence under oath?
The hon. member asks could the evidence under section 120b be taken under oath.

Section 120 provides,
subclause 2, that "for the purpose of such investigation the board shall have power to summon witnesses." It strikes me that to make certain they can summon witnesses and investigate under oath for the purposes of these two clauses, which certainly they must have power to do, it might be well to add after the words "such investigation" in subclause 2 of section 120, the words, "or any investigation authorized under this Act." It may be that they have a general power, but if they had there would be no reason for putting in subclause 2 of section 120. Subclause 2 has stood in that way since the Act was passed.

Do I understand the
Solicitor General to make the suggestion that there should be such a provision added?
Yes, I think it should be added to subsection 2 of section 120.
That would cover the point raised by my hon. friend from Huntingdon?

Yes, I think the point is covered by section 120b. In an investigation under both clauses they could take the evidence under oath. They have power to investigate overages under section 120b. They cannot investigate complaints of overages, because there could be no complaints; consequently it would not do to include overages in 120a.
New sections 120a and 120b agreed to.

I beg to move that a clause be added reading as follows:
Subsection 2 of section 120 of the said Act is amended by adding, after the word " investigation," in the first line thereof, the words,
" or of any investigation authorized under this Act."

While I do not offer objection to these amendments, because I have no doubt they are the best that can be put forward at the present time, I would like to point out that in their nature they are very indefinite as to where the responsibility is to rest amongst the different parties who handle the grain. The authority and the responsibility is placed upon the Board of Grain Commissioners to find out the particulars if a certain occurrence takes place, and probably that is the best that can be done at the moment, but my opinion is that there should have been a more thorough examination into the conditions surrounding the shipment of grain, and that the amendment to the Act should be so framed as to, so far as possible, place the responsibility directly upon the parties to the transaction. It seems to me that the tendency of his declaration is to say to the shipper, the carrier, the receiver, and the dealer: if you can get by with a shortage you are welcome to do so, it is up to the Board to adjust the matter amongst all the parties concerned. statement which my hon. friend makes, especially in view of the fact that-1 myself had the pleasure of visiting Saskatoon, of meeting a large number of people there, and of examining this site, together with others suggested at that time. In my humble judgment, the site selected is one of the very best in the city for the purposes of a post office, and, so far as I have ever heard, is satisfactory to practically the entire population of Saskatoon. In regard to the excavation, we were pressed this year to find employment for many unemployed persons, and we undertook to excavate for the foundation of the proposed building. I am sorry that my hon. friend is opposed to our putting up a public building of this magnitude in an important centre like Saskatoon, but we believe it to be in the public interest, and will, therefore, proceed with the work as rapidly as possible.

The hon. minister is
not justified in suggesting that I am opposed to the erection of a public building in Saskatoon. I want to see a public building in Saskatoon, but in the place where a building of the kind proposed ought to be.

Why is a new building necessary? I confess that when I was there a year ago I was very much surprised at this old building, I regarded it as a very poor building and I thought it was not in keeping with the importance of a city such as Vancouver.

From that time on, as my hon. friend is well aware, we have not been pressing, as we previously did, the construction of public buildings g'enerally. The minister might also call our attention to the fact that instead of bringing his Estimates on earlier so that they could be passed and, if it suited the convenience of, His Royal Highness assent-to, he could get on with the work, the minister,. with his usual adroitness, waits until we are wearied out at the last of the session-

Mr. PUGSLElT:	-when we have not

If I remember aright, when my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) was minister he always brought down his Estimates at the end of the session.
No. Does not the Minister of Customs remember how he used to fight me from the beginning to end of the session, day after day, and night after night.
We will take advantage of an early session next year to bring down the Estimates.

The total amount asked for public works in 1912-13 was $7,601,800, and the total number asked for this year is $14,891,300, so that the increase in the past few years is alarming. The erection of public buildings is not a productive expenditure, and with a decreasing revenue it shows gross extravagance to ask close on fifteen million dollars, in a year like this when the Government finds it necessary to increase the postage, and to tax patent medicines, 'and to levy unusual taxes on
the people. I venture to say that the erection of buildings represented by three-fourths of this fifteen million dollars could be delayed, without any loss to the country. It is a nice thing to have public buildings when you can afford it, and the total amount asked for this year is to have them, but I do not think we can afford these public buildings just now. The minister will find it difficult to defend his policy.

The principal expenditure has been on the harbours and rivers.
Experimental Farms-new buildings and improvements; tobacco-curing station, renewals and repairs, etc., in connection with existing buildings, fences, etc., $150,000.

How much of this is to be expended on the so-called experimental farm near Fredericton?
JJr. ROGERS: $5,858.

Ottawa public buildings-repairs, including ventilation and lighting, furniture, etc., $415,000.

I hope that no more furniture will be bought for the ministers' offices, because, judging by tbe Auditor General's Report, enough was bought last year. I referred to this question last Saturday night.
You only spoke of two last Saturday night.
I referred particularly to two, but there was new furniture for all the ministers' offices, and I hope there will not he any more purchased.
There was none purchased for my office.

How much is being paid by the Government for rental in the city of Ottawa?
I shall be glad to get that information for the hon. gentleman.

It has been stated by the minister, in reply to a question, that $44,000 per annum is paid by the Govern-

ment for the rental of a portion of the Rea building. Is that entirely for the accommodation of the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Naval Service?
Yes.
So that the very large sum of |44,000 per annum is paid as rental for the. accommodation simply of one department.

There are really two
departments.

There are two departments, but under the one minister. That $44,000 per year amounts to 4-4 per cent on a capitalization of $1,000,000, and does not the minister think it is an enormous rental to pay?
The space rented in the Rea building for the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Department of Naval Service is rented at the lowest price we have paid in the city of Ottawa for years.

In considering whether rent is low or not, one must have regard to the part of a building which is occupied. I understand these are three flats which are above the store of the A. E. Rea Company, Limited, so that whether the rent is cheaper than the rent paid in other places depends somewhat upon the relative value of the upper stories as compared with the low'er stories of the building.
My deputy minister informs me that all the space is used on the three flats.

When I was minister, there seemed to be plenty of accommodation for the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Department of Naval Service in The western block. I realized, of course, that some additional accommodation may be needed in the near future; but we were all looking forward to the erection of new public buildings. I was astonished that it was found necessary to go outside and pay such large rents in order to give that accommodation which only three years ago was found in the western block for the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Department of the Naval Service. I do not understand why the demand should grow so suddenly that it is found necessary to go to this large additional expenditure.

My hon. friend appears to have overlooked the fact that, while the Marine and Fisheries Department was in

the western block, it had four or five other offices, in other parts of the city of Ottawa, in the Corry building on Sussex street, the Birks building and the Canadian building, all of which have been vacated by that department.
Has the Canadian building been vacated?
The tidal service is still there.
The Canadian building is still being occupied by the Government and the rent is still being paid by the Government?
We assembled the whole department under the one roof.

What department is
occupying the buildings vacated by the Department of Marine and Fisheries?
The Customs Department in the western block; the Printing Bureau took the Sussex street block, and the Department of the Interior took the Canadian building. The Corry building has been given up.
Then, with the exception of the Corry building, all the other buildings rented three years ago are still occupied by departments of the Government?
Yes.

Take the Customs Department. There seemed to be plenty of room in the western block for that department. I never heard there was any overcrowding, and there has not been any large increase in the number of clerks to cause . them to want one more room. I really find it difficult to believe that it has become necessary to rent all these additional buildings during the last three years.

Some of the branches of the Customs Department were in outside buildings. I think the cheque branch and part of the statistics branch - were moved into the western block when the Department of Marine and Fisheries vacated it. It is more convenient to have the cheque branch and the statistics branch, in fact that Department of Customs generally altogether. The statistics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce also took part of the offices vacated by the Department of Marine and Fisheries in the western block.

I understand it is more convenient to have larger accommodation so

that the clerks can move around without being too near each other, but the expenditure to which the Public Works Department has gone during the last three years is simply appalling.
You mean with regard to rent; you do not mean our department.

I mean the general expenditure. One expenditure is in harmony with another. It is a case of increasing expenditure all around. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has drawn attention to it. I would like the Minister of Customs to take for a moment the figures of the last three years. It was he who told the people of St. John that if they wanted larger accommodation the expenditure of more millions of dollars, all they had to do was to come to the Customs Department and get all the money they wanted. H is such .extravagance as that, which he has been holding out to -his colleague the Minister of Public Works, that has led him -astray and kept him from keeping a tight rein on expenditure. In the three years ended the 31st of March, 1912, the total expenditure -on account of -both capital and income, of the Department of Public Works, amounted to $36,000,000, whereas in the three years ended the 31-st of March, 1915, taking the Estimates of last year as the basis of expenditure, the total expenditure amounted to $86,000,000, a difference very close to $50,000,000.

How many millions
vould a fleet have cost?

If we had had -a fleet to-day of light cruisers iand d-estroyers, no doubt they would have been able _ten times over to- have paid what they would have cost, in capturing ships of the enemy while this war was on, and those vessels sailing upon the Atlantic.
They would have been -a floating liability.

Does not -the Minister of Customs think those figures -are calculated to startle the public of this country? Yet, with all this enormous expenditure the Minister of Customs rejoices that he h-as been able to get more accommodation. The Minister of Marine -and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) is not here to-night; but it , certainly 'seems astonishing that to give accommodation to one department alone the enormous -rent of $44,000 i-s being paid for three upper stories of a building, the lower stories of which are occupied as a
departmental stor-e. Those upper ^ stories, of course, would not be -necessary for the business of -a departmental store, and it must be very profitable to the owners of this building to have them rented. I should think $1,000,000 or $1,100,000 would be a very good price for the whole building. As a matter of fact, three or four years ago $900,000 was regarded as a good price for that building, and I believe -the owners of the building said that they would be willing to sell it to the Government at that price.
That was before they put the other three stories on top.
There w-eTe not three new stories.
Two or three.
I think only one.
The deputy minister informs me that two new stories were built.
Two extra -stories on a building of that size would not -cost a very large amount of money. I venture to say th-a-t they would not cost over $50,000 or $100,000.
Did the A. E. Rea Company, Limited, no-t. build an -addition to the building as well as build the two new stories?
If they did, that would be for the benefit of the business as well.
They have built the north end from the ground up.
That would materially affect your calculations.
It would to that extent; but you can put up -a very good addition to a building -at from $50,000 to $100,000. It does strike me as a very large rental.

Do officials of the Canadian
Navy occupy this building?
Yes.
How many officers employed in the Canadian Navy are in -this building?
The hon. member will have to get that information from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

The Minister of Customs (Mt. J. D. Reid), I notice, is in his place. About three weeks ago he promised to bring down information about the rental of a building for his department in North Syd-

ney. I called attention to the factt that he had refused to do business directly with the owner of the building who would have rented it for $15 a month, and thought it necessary to bring in a middleman and give him twice the money. The minister said he could not believe that such a transaction had taken place. But I put a question on the Order Paper since, and the answer confirms what I said. The middleman's name is given and double the amount of the rent at which the owner would have rented the building. Perhaps the minister has looked into my statement and found it to be correct.
Mr. J.D.REID: The rental of the building in North Sydney was arranged by officials of the department. I inquired of thenr, and they tell me that the rental is fair. If I remember rightly, part of he building is occupied by the person from whom we have rented it, and we have only part of it.
That is what I said.

We could not deal with the owner if another person had the whole building under rental. I do not know about the matter, but I have confidence in the officials that they would secure, the place at a reasonable rental.. If there is any further information in the department I will bring it down.

This is a small matter but the minister is not going to slide out of it a second time. There is no question about the facts. The owner of the building told me personally that he would have been glad to rent the building to the Customs Department at $15 a month and tried to do so, but they would not do business with him-that is the straight talk. But a stranger who had nothing to do with the building came and said: I will rent the building from you for three years. The owner rented it to him at $15 a month, and he immediately turned it over to the department at $30 a month. Pure graft on a small scale.

It is a strange thing, if he wanted to rent the building to the Department of Customs, that he would not write to the department or to myself as minister. It is all very well for a man to make a statement after the building is rented; he can make any kind of a statement then, when it is too late. The Commissioner of Customs tells me that the building was rented at a fair and reasonable rate.

The party who rented it from the owner had no use for the building except to rent it again, The owner tried

to do business with the department before the third man came in, but they would not do business with him, but did rent it from the other party at double the price.
To what officer did he want to rent it?

I understand it was
Mr. Cameron, the appraiser, who wanted a room.

The appraiser would have nothing to do with renting a building. The collector is the one to be seen in such a matter. Why did not he go to the collector, who is an appointee of the hon. member himself.
It does not make any difference; there are the facts. There is no mistake about it.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman says he has the facts. Will he let us know who is the officer of the Government who could have rented this place at $15? If the hon. gentleman will let us know, we will make inquiries.

The building is owned by Mr. Charles Millar, who told me himself what I have stated. I did not solicit the information, and know nothing about it of my owrn knowledge. He told me that he wanted to rent the building to the Government, but they would not do business with him.

The same
thing happened in Montreal, in the case of a building in Maisonneuve occupied as a post office. It is No. 116 Letourneau street. speechtext: The only reason I made the inquiry was that the hon. gentleman said that he was seized of the facts. He made the statement, as I understood him, that some officer of the Government had declined to do business in respect of this building at $15 a month and had afterwards done business at $30 a month under different conditions. If that is true, very strict inquiry should be made into it. I asked the name of the officer because I understood the hon. gentleman knew it.

I do not. I am perfectly honest in the matter. I would give the name of the party who negotiated the business, but I do not know it. I am relying on the statement made to me by the owner of thp building; and I am supported by the statement which the minister himself brought down showing that the Government is paying $30 a month for the building, while the owner says he is receiving $15.

This is a sort of breakwater, I understand, to afford shelter to boats. Has anything been done in connection with it, or is it the intention of the minister to go on with it during the coming summer?
Nothing has been done so far. The estimated cost of the whole work is about $8,000.
I was rather surprised to find that such a small amount had been put in for this work.

It is a revote from last year.
Cole harbour-wharf, $8,300.

This work was first projected by the late Government in 1911, and it has appeared in the Estimates each year ever since. I should like to know what the minister intends to do with regard to it. Does he intend to go ahead with the work, or is it put in the Estimates to tantalize the people? This is the only item of expenditure in my constituency, which has a seacoast of 150 miles. A good jmany small improvements, along the coast, were asked for by the fishermen, and were all refused by the minister. Some of the most important items were struck out of the Estimates as provided in 1911, including an extension to the New Harbour breakwater, which was a very important local work. . New Harbour is an exposed harbour on the Atlantic coast. It was with great difficulty that the fishing population in that vicinity carried on their business at all, and when the breakwater was built about ten years ago it was so useful that a village grew up there and the place became a flourishing fishing station. The boats became so numerous that the shelter constructed at that time was not ' sufficient, and the late Government, acting upon the advice of the chief engineer, decided to extend the breakwater so as to give shelter to the increasing number of boats operating in that vicinity. The present minister, for some reason which I do not understand, took this $10,000 out of the Estimates, and it has not been put in since. This is an important matter to the people of that vicinity.

I am not acquainted with all the details of the matters to which my hon. friend has referred, but so far as this vote is concerned, it is the intention of the department to go on with the work as soon

as possible. There has been some difficulty in the way of securing a proper title, by reason of the fact that it has to be obtained from certain heirs of an estate. It is largely owing to this condition that the delay has occurred.

Fur a survey.
Have any proceedings been taken to settle the title?

We have been hoping from time to time to succeed in getting it, and if we do not get it in the near future, we propose to expropriate.

I could not say; I have only the record here that it was revoted last year.

It will depend on our being able to get to it. My hon. friend is anxious that we should cut down the expenditure and we are anxious to please him as far as we can.

That is in Pictou?
Yes, that is under contract and this is to complete it.

They are at work there now.

that?

river is new. Is it the intention of the minister to extend it and make it longer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:

Section 1 a's it left the House made it an indictable offence to incite or assist any subject of any foreign state or country at war with His Majesty fo leave Canada, and section 1 contained these words:
If the circumstances of the case do not exclude the possibility that assistance to the enemy is an intended object in his so leaving Canada, and-if such inciting or assisting do not amount to treason.	-

Without the consent of the Crown, unless the person accused shall prove that assistance to the enemy was not intended, and providing, that such inciting or assisting does not amount to treason.

On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), Bill No. 121, to amend the Supreme Court Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 1-appeal in election cases, where appeal is given by local legislature:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill is introduced in view of the fact that the province of Manitoba, by its Controverted Elections Act of 1913, has provided that there shall he an appeal in controverted election cases to the Supreme Court of Canada. The Provincial Legislature, of course, has no

power to confer jurisdiction on the Supreme Court of Canada, which is a Dominion court; but, inasmuch as by its legislation the legislature of that province has in effect declared that it is desirable that there should be an appeal, and so far as is in its power has created that appeal, it would seem that this Parliament, which alone has power to confer jurisdiction on the Supreme Court to hear and determine such an appeal, should give that jurisdiction. This legislation creates no appeal of itself; it merely confers upon the Supreme Court of Canada jurisdiction to hear and determine such appeals, wherever a Provincial Legislature determines that such an appeal is desirable and ought to be had.

I have no intention of opposing this legislation; but in my opinion it is rather dangerous. It was only yesterday that we had a long discussion upon the difficulty of getting a final decision in controverted election cases, and we are this session in this Parliament passing new legislation to expedite as much as possible the bearing and determining of such cases under the Dominion Controverted Elections Act. If I have a fault to find with our judicial system, it is that in the province to which my hon. friend and I belong there is an appeal in such cases to the Supreme Court or Canada. In Manitoba there is an appeal from the trial judge to the Court of King's Bench sitting as a court of review, and another appeal from that court to the Court of Appeal. Under this legislation there would be still another appeal; so that I think we are not conferring a favour upon the province of Manitoba by passing this legislation. I understand that it is the wish of- the legislature of Manitoba; but, even so, I would not be disposed to mix up federal matters with provincial matters. If I had an amendment to move to this legislation, I would move that provincial laws should be administered by provincial courts, and federal laws by federal courts. My hon. friend has, however, thought differently, and I merely wish to call his attention to the point I have mentioned, which I believe he will find worthy of consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In so far as the desirability of creating such an .appeal is concerned, I share in very large measure, if not entirely, the views which the right hon. gentleman has just expressed. If it -were a matter of considering the legislation of the legislature of the province of Manitoba in this regard, I would probably concur in

the view that he has expressed, and I think there is also very much to be said for the view that we should have these matters speedily settled. The reason which leads me to propose this legislation is that it seems to me that questions concerning the composition of the legislature of a province are in a peculiar manner questions which that legislature itself should determine, and it is therefore a fair thing that, when the legislature of a province has itself determined that it is desirable that upon questions concerning controverted elections there should be an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, we should make it possible for that to be carried out. In fact, the motive that leads me to move this legislation is the recognition which I think ought to be given to the absolute right of the legislature of a province itseslf to determine the, best process or means by which elections to that legislature should be determined.
Have any of the provinces asked for this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The province of Manitoba has legislated providing for such an appeal, and has, following upon that, asked that we make it possible for such an appeal to be entertained. As I said at the outset, this legislation does not give an appeal; it merely provides that, where the legislature of a province sees proper to create such a right# of appeal, then the Supreme Court of Canada shall have jurisdiction to hear that appeal.

I concur entirely in the observations of the right hon. gentleman opposite in regard to this matter. I do not believe in an appeal from the supreme court of a province to the Supreme Court of Canada regarding controverted elections in that province, and I never have done so. From a logical standpoint, such an * appeal should not be entertained, because the legislature itself should determine who should sit in the legislature. It has delegated that power to the supreme court of the province, and I believe no power beyond the territorial limits of that province should in reason have a right to determine or consider who shall sit in its legislature. In the province of Alberta, *where we have legislation by which an election petition is regarded as a suit in a court, an attempt was made two years ago to bring an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada; but that court rejected

it, saying it was outside of its jurisdiction. This will enable provincial appeals to be entertained, with the resultant delay in having an appeal heard so many miles away from the place where the case arose; but other provinces have this right and provide for it in their Controverted Election Acts, so that if we desire to have the law uniform I suppose we must pass this legislation, but I am very strongly opposed to the principle of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. member thinks that this legislation would give the right to appeal a case such as is referred to from the province of Alberta, I venture to think his idea is unfounded, because we have carefully provided that the jurisdiction to hlear and determine shall exist only where the legislature has given an appeal from the provincial courts in a proceeding under any provincial Controverted Elections Act.
I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Unless the Legislature of Alberta has expressly provided that there should be an appeal in election cases, this legislation will not give an appeal.

But in the province they say an election case shall be treated as a case in the Supreme Court, and so, inferentially, this legislation may be construed to authorize an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.

We are simply giving effect to the desire of the Legislature of Manitoba, which is a very respectable reason. I do not know the circumstances which have led the Legislature of Manitoba to enact this legislation, but I should be very much surprised if that reason were not that they were dissatisfied with some decision of the court. That is always the case; a certain law is passed to affect a certain case, and we violate the principle which should be inviolate-that provincial laws shall be interpreted by provincial courts and federal laws by federal courts. This section reads:
The Supreme Court of Canada shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine any appeal from the judgment of any provincial court in any proceeding under any provincial controverted election Act, whereby such an appeal is given.
Are these words sufficient to restrict the appeal to those cases in which appeal is allowed under provincial legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think so. That was the intention in adopting that wording. I may say that the wording of the original draft did not make reference to a Controverted Elections Act in express terms. For the purpose of making it quite clear that we were merely conferring power to hear and determine where thle Controverted Election Act of the province allows an appeal, I adopted this wording. If there is any wording that will make it clearer I shall be glad to adopt it.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

There is one point in connection with experimental farms which I wish to impress upon the minister. The largest development of immigration that there has been in western Canada has been into southwestern Saskatchewan, I do not 'say that the immigration there has been larger than all the rest put together, but the greatest manifestation of immigration has been in the country south of Moosejaw, Gull Lake, Maple Creek, etc. The reason that that country has been the geographical scene of that activity is that for so many years it was considered to be a dry belt, and was for that reason disregarded and 130
rejected by the homesteaders. I think that a district that has been the centre of immigration activity should receive a great deal of the minister's attention at the same time. The very fact that the land in this so-called dry belt was left to the very last must be evidence that it is a [DOT]different kind of land from the larger part of Saskatchewan and, of course, those of us who know the West know that that is true. It requires a different kind of farming. If the experimental farms are for anything it is to teach the people a kind of farming that is not the ordinary farming in the province or in the whole country. In that whole district, into which have gone tens of thousands of people, there has not been the slightest attention paid by the present Government to the question of establishing an experimental farm. I cannot impress this on the minister too emphatically. The country is one that requires teaching. The same kind of farming will not do there as is employed around Regina or Calgary or Lethbridge or Edmonton, It is a country all by itself. In years when we have lots of rain and the crops turn out favourably the people are well off, but they need to be taught how to farm under other conditions. In southwest Saskatchewan, for twenty years, while the rest of Saskatchewan was being settled, that country was looked on as a purely ranching district. But now the railways have gone in there, towns have sprung up and it is becoming thickly settled. The minister may say that he has established a farm in Alberta. That does not fill the bill. In the first place I do not think the establishment of that farm is a serious attempt to solve the problem. The Lethbridge country, where that farm is situated, is largely an irrigation district, in fact the experimental farm there is partly an irrigation farm. True, at that farm there is some kind of lecturing on dry farming, but, in the first place, it is too far away from us; it is altogether out of our line of travel; our homesteaders have no chance or purpose to take them into south Alberta; and, apart from that, it is a different kind of farming from what is required in southern Saskatchewan.
Is it not a demonstration farm that you want?

I am not familiar with the technical terms used in the department. What I want is a demonstration farm all



right. We want a farm that will demonstrate how to farm under the circumstances.
Like the one at Indian Head.

That would be splendid; even a smaller one would do. The late Government when it went out was on the point of purchasing a farm in the district I speak of. Perhaps the minister does not even know that the establishment of an experimental farm 75 miles southwest of Moosejaw was authorized by the late minister.
I am not aware of that.

The money was not voted and the arrangement did not go through. If the minister had taken enough interest to investigate he would have found out that the late Government had even arranged to secure a farm southwest of Moosejaw to demonstrate, as well as the Government could demonstrate, the method of farming which would be most profitable in that country. I feel that I need offer no apology for taking up time to discuss this subject, which is of tremendous importance not only to that province but to the whole of Canada. If the new homesteaders do not learn a successful method of farming they will be in a terrible state. With the markets closed against them and the taxes piled on them that this Government has put on, why I feel sorry for them.
Oh, oh.

It is all right to laugh. There was not a foot of that country surveyed when I became a member, and it was on my recommendation that it was surveyed. So I feel that I have a special interest in those settlers, every one of whom has gone in there while I was the representative of that district, and I would feel a small representative if I did nothing but sit here and laugh when their wants are mentioned in this House. With markets closed against them, with the taxes piled on them, with the banks and implement firms grinding them under their heels, it is a terrible condition and the least I can do is to ask that the minister should establish without any delay a good demonstration farm in that new country to the southwest of Moosejaw and, if possible, show the most profitable use to which that land can be put and the most favourable method of farming in that district. I make this suggestion in all friendliness to my hon. friend
[Mr. Knowles. 1
the minister and would be glad to have him to take it up.

I think the great difficulty was that the land should never have been opened for homesteading at all, , and that the fault lies entirely with the late Government. There is a section of country there that formerly was occupied by ranchers, 'and I think experience will prove that the land should not have been opened for homesteading.
You might say that all of Saskatchewan, Moosejaw and Souris, and all that country, was formerly occupied by Indians and should be kept by them.

I understood the hon. member to say that there was a difference in the conditions in southwestern Saskatchewan and that that was why an experimental farm was needed to demonstrate how that section of country should be farmed. Everybody knows why settlers did not go into that country. Why was it necessary to give a purchased homestead or an extra pre-emption? Because it was clearly manifest that they considered the land was not like the other land in the three western provinces. There is no question, about that, and it is being proven to-day that that section of country should never have been opened for homesteaders.
SIt WILFRID LAURIER: I remember the diay when there were pamphlets circulated by high authority stating that wheat could not be grown in the valley of the Red river above Fort Garry. All these theories 'have been proved to be untrue. The same may be true also of the section of country referred to by my hon. friend.

I do not think the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) need apologize for bringing this matter to the attention.of the House or to my own notice.
I may say that all of these things are being attended to. Although I am not a representative of a constituency on the western prairie, I am fairly familiar with the conditions aJll thiough that district, *and I have as warm a sympathy as any man can have with the settlers there, as I have been closely identified with agriculture in a practical way for many years.
I am strongly desirous, as the Government is, of relieving the conditions as far as the Government can do so. There are now three experimental farms in Saskatchewan : one at Indian Head, which has rendered excellent service to the

country, under the direction of Mr. McKay, another at Scott, and a third at Rosthem. The last two have been extended in order to do more experimental work with'stock. I quite admit that they have not quite fulfilled the needs of the southern country to which my ihon. friend alludes. Every part of the country naturally would like to see a demonstration or experimental farm established in a particular county. We have hesitated for .some time because we have always had the feeling that with the Federal Government lies particularly the duty of carrying on experimental work for the whole country, whereas showing by object lesson, in a practical way, how to carry out the results of these experiments is more the part of the provinces. It is purely for that reason that we have hesitated from year to year about invading that field. Manitoba, British Columbia, Ontario, and I think some of the other provinces have done a certain amount of work in that direction. Last year I was asked by the Prime Minister to interview both the Alberta and the Saskatchewan governments, and to investigate as far as I could the conditions in the drouth-stricken area. That investigation brought home to my mind the fact that conditions there were extraordinary, and that something would have to be done. I am not going into the question raised by my hon. friend whether it was wise or not to open up that large district. That is a debatable point. But it has been opened up, and is now largely settled. They have schools and all kinds of municipal activities, and I hardly see how any government could abandon the country. We have, therefore, to do the best we can to develop it, and I think we were thoroughly justified in taking up this demonstration work. My hon. friend suggests that I have not given any attention to that kind of work, but I want to assure him that we have given it our most sympathetic and earnest attention. I went into the question very fully during the five or six weeks prior to going to California, and made up my mind to establish twenty or thirty demonstration stations all through that dry belt in southern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta. Our Director of Farms has been out there, together with two very capable young graduates of Manitoba College who are to assist him in the work. We expect these twenty or thirty stations to be thoroughly organized and in work this year, our object being simply to prove to the farmers of that coun-1301
try that if proper methods of rotation are followed they will, even in a dry season, be able to get at least some crop. In that connection, I may say that when I was looking over the drouth-stricken district, I saw right next to farms that had not a single spear of grain other farms, which having been properly summer-fallowed, had as much as fifteen or twenty bushels to the acre. I quite appreciate the fact that a great many of the farmers who have gone out there know little about the conditions of the country, and that it is up to us to do something; and I sincerely hope that the work which we have already started will be of some practical value to these people, and enable them to hold on to what they have got and make better use of it.
