This demonstration work is in one sense a new policy, but in another it is not. The experimental farm system, even under the late Government, has always included a certain amount of demonstration as well as experimental wo A; so that really it is not a new principle, but an extension of a principle that has always been recognized. We do not propose to buy any of these farms, but to select forty or fifty acres in a thoroughly typical section of each of these districts. We shall choose stations that will be get-at-able by all the farmers in the district, and put in charge the man who already owns that landi, and who will be a practical, sound farmer. He will have to carry out our instructions as regards the routine of crops, and we shall keep a complete record of the work. The expense will be small; about $400 or $500

for each plot. I am hopeful that this policy will benefit the people of the whole country, and that we shall get the work thoroughly started this year.
Will the land be rented, and' the Government own the crop; will the work be done by day labour, and will these college boys have charge of it ?

I said that we were
sending out two graduates of Manitoba College to assist in the work. The director, who knows the conditions out there pretty well, will of course he at the head of the work, and under him will be Mr. John Fixter, who is a thoroughly practical and reliable man, and who for the last few years has been with the Conservation Commission. He will be largely responsible for the work. I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend all the details, but I think my lion. friend from Calgary, who has been out there lately, may have more recent information than I have and may be able to enlighten my hon. friend.
Mr. R, B. BENNETT: With the observations made by the hon. member for Moose-jaw (Mr. Knowles) I think most of us who live in the West are very heartily in accord. We realize that in order to get successful results we must have two things: first, good seed; and, second, proper cultivation. Dr. Rutherford, who is in charge of the agricultural work in connection with the Canadian Pacific's undertaking near Calgary, pointed out only recently that while those farmers in the drouth-stricken area who had not properly cultivated their soil had failed with their crops twice, other farmers in that same district who had properly cultivated their soil and done the necessary summer-fallowing, had been able to obtain a crop under the most adverse conditions. Many of us have pointed out to the Minister of Agriculture and the Government the necessity of establishing some demonstration plots throughout the territory; not experimental farms, as the hon. gentleman has just suggested, not a utilization in the first instance of what the hon. member for Kings has described as college and academic men, but rather the utilization of th'e good farmer in every district. For there is always in every district a good farmer, some man who is a better husbandman than his neighbour, who cultivates his soil more properly, who selects his seed with care, who estimates weeds, and whose crop gives better results. We all know this kind of farmer; and the idea of the department, so far as I understand it, is to use

the farm of such a man for the demonstration station. Mr. Grisdale, who is well known to us all, and Mr. Fixter, who was with the Conservation Commission, have been sent out to look over the drouth-stricken area, and select 40 acres at points that will be visible to every person passing along the main travelled highway. They will pay the farmer who owns that 40 acres a small sum, for he has to plant the seed and cultivate the ground in the manner that is indicated as best by the men who are supervising the work for the Department of Agriculture. The Government will buy the seed, under certain conditions, and the crop will belong to the farmer. The idea is to show what good seed and good cultivation will do. It is to be an ocular demonstration, which, after all, is the best kind of demonstration, of what good seed and good farming will accomplish in any locality. I was out West only a few days ago, and I understand that Mr. Grisdale has been going over the territory and selecting twenty-five or thirty points at which to establish these demonstration plots. These plots will be in charge, not of college men, as has been suggested, but of the farmers who have been getting the best results in their own particular locality. This kind of farmer is to be asked to permit the use of 40 acres of his land for a visible demonstration of what good farming will do. That is how I understand the matter from my discussions with the director, who is now out West.
Of course, there would be none of them in my particular locality. They are all south of that in the drouth-stricken area because it was decided by the Government that in the area east of Calgary the Canadian Pacific railway was carrying on that class of work, and that the Government need not duplicate it in these places. Neither will this work be carried on at points 'wh'ere the local government has small demonstration plots, such as that at" Medicine Hat. In the territory of my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) there are two or three such plots, and I think the director told me that he was arranging to establish one or two in the locality to wnich the hon. member from Moosejaw has referred, but the difficulty was, having started the plans last fall, to find a particular piece of land that was in such a state of cultivation that it might be used to afford an accurate demonstration to the rest of the community, of what may be done by proper cultivation and good seed.
I think the real value of these demonstration plots cannot be overestimated. If

I had my way in western Canada, I would gee a thousand of them established in the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan within a very short tim'e. That sounds very extreme, but when you come to think of the enormous area of these two provinces and when you come to think of the kind of settlers we are bringing in, my idea is not far wrong. We are bringing men to our land who are not used to cultivation of that particular kind of soil; men who have not been able to understand the true value of good se'ed and who are not themselves able to make those experiments which are necessary to get the best results. The Government has placed at the disposal of the settlers a seed-germinating laboratory, and they have given that supervision and instruction which is essential for the purpose of obtaining the best results. We provide for these settlers small demonstration plots-as I have said, I hope there will be a thousand of them in the two western provinces before many years- which afford visible evidence, which is the best evidence, to the farmers of the locality of what may be acco,mplished by good husbandry, proper cultivation, and good seed, and this will cost the country little or nothing.
The arrangement is only for one year at a time.
That was what was originally proposed, but I understand it is to be extended for a period of three years.
Yes, for three years.

Three years was the period mentioned for the purpose of establishing what would be the best system of rotation of crops, it being felt that if you merely took a piece of land for one year and took a crop off it, you would not be able to indicate to the settlers of that locality what would be the best rotation of crops to secure the best results in the cultivation of the land there. I feel very sanguine as' to the results which will come from this. I am very hopeful that in northern Alberta, where there are very large numbers of Galician settlers, the establishment of such demonstration plots will do the very greatest amount of good, because these men are really ambitious to make good farmers. I have observed that a large proportion of our foreign population shows perhaps the greatest ambition to become good farmers, but the difficulty they experience is to understand exactly what is the best rotation of crops, how best
to summer fallow, and how to get the best results from proper cultivation. I think this experiment will teach them that. This experiment, small though it is, and only involving twenty-five or thirty demonstration plots, is in my judgment a move in the right direction and one that will do incalculable benefit to our western country.
I am satisfied that if we are to continue a wild system of settlement in - the West we will not obtain any commensurate results for the money we expend. The day of people settling far remote from railways where neighbours are ten miles apart, must pass, and the only hope we have is to bring about a system of settlement in the West which will be based upon a scientific principle, whereby townships will be settled with proper settlers and demonstration plots will be established throughout those townships, so that there will be a real incentive to men to do the very best that is in them, and to obtain the very best possible results from the cultivation of the soil. It will also, in my judgment, lead to the establishment of a sort of social centre in these townships whereby the loneliness incident to the system of settlement followed up to the present time will pass away, and so that there will be happiness and comfort to those who are homesteading in these townships. Without some broad, comprehensive, and far-reaching settlement scneme in western Canada. I look for no great progress along the line of increase of population of a permanent and staple nature. I welcome this experiment, and I think everybody in the West does, as being a move that must inevitably result in a better and more comprehensive scheme of settlement, the introduction of a better system of husbandry, and, more content, more happiness, and what perhaps is of more value still, greater wealth to the state.

I thank the hon. gentleman (Mr, Bennett) for giving us this information, but I think the minister should be possessed of the details of this a little better, because he has been back from California quite a while and he has his deputy beside him to give him the information. I think the minister shows a little absence of that tense interest he should have in such a serious problem, but no doubt he has been busy with other things. I am not going to say I am against this scheme; in fact I would like to see the minister do a great deal more than this. I was sorry to hear the minister say: I do not see how we could abandon that country

and these people. The very suggestion of abandoning that country is a joke. It is a grand country; there is no need of the minister saying: We would ..think of abandoning it but we do not dare to.

I cannot allow that statement of the hon. member to go unchallenged. I hlave made no suggestion about abandoning that country. What I stated was that the Prime Minister asked me to interview the people in the West when the suggestion was made here and there that the country might better not have been settled, and when it was an open question with some-as to whether it would pay to go on developing it. My view was that such an idea could not be entertained for one moment, and that we should go on with our work in that district. I never thought of suggesting that it should be abandoned.
I took the minister's words down and he certainly referred to a suggestion about abandoning the country.
I am sure my hon. friend does not want to do me an injustice.

Absolutely no, and I do not think the minister ever thought of abandoning it, but he should not speak as if he thought of such a thing because it will give a wrong impression. As for the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) saying that the country should not have been settled, I say it is as good a district as the average district in the West, and it will do itself credit in a few years when the people really get on their feet. They went in there poor people, they have met with great hardships and reverses, they have been away from railways, they have had to haul their flax and wheat seventy or eighty miles, but in spite of it all they have stood up foursquare to every wind that blew, and to-day they are doing well there, despite everything else except the drouth which came on this year, when they expected to pay off their debts. The idea of saying it is a debatable point whether the country ever should have been opened up is too absurd to be mentioned in this House. It is a splendid country. South of Moosejaw fifty miles and southwest of Gravelbourg they had this year very good crops and there is no relief work there. But further west the rains did not come this year, and if you are going to lay that down as a reason for abandoning them or saying that the country should never have been opened up, then there is an enormous part of Canada which has 
towns, and railways, and churches, and everything else that the people may well clear out of. Surely we are not going to say, because we have had the worst year for fifteen or sixteen years, that a district so stricken is to be deserted.
I do not understand the scheme well enough to be able to approve of it or to criticise it. It seems a kind of buckshot proposition, a little scattering here and there. I do not think many of my constituents will go to see how another farmer twenty or thirty miles away, is going to cultivate a small plot, and I think the Government would have been better advised had they established real experimental farms situated near a railway, which the people would think it worth while to visit.
That would be too academic. They want to have the farmer himself do this work under proper supervision.

I do not think it would be too academic. The minister was once a very fine lecturer on agriculture, and see what a fine robust man he is to-day-a typical farmer, every inch of him. I do not think that, because a man has been through an agricultural college, he is any worse a farmer.

The fact that a
man has been through a university does not make him a lawyer.
Mr. -KNOWLES: I do not think it keeps him from being a lawyer either; and if it does not help him, it certainly does not hurt him. These demonstration plots will be such little, picayune affairs-I hope they will not be, but if you are going to scatter about twenty of them over the prairies, you are going to have something which perhaps one or. two neighbours will look at, but which it will not be worth any one leaving his work and going far to see.

A farmer will have to pass one of these plots every day he goes to market. It is going to be situated on a highway and usually at a corner, so that as he goes to market, even if he does not want to see it, he will have to see it willy-nilly.
I understand the whole matter. In my district, which is about 200 miles long by 200 miles wide, there will be two of these plots.
I was speaking only from very hazy knowledge.

Well, suppose there are half-a-dozen stuck in my district. The number of people, who will pass a certain corner and see the plot there willy-nilly will be a very small proportion of the people in my large constituency.
A still smaller proportion would see.the thoroughly-equipped experimental farms that my hon. friend advocates.

My hon. friend has a
right to his own opinions, but I do not entertain that view. Thousands of people go to our Indian Head experimental farm every year.
My hon. friend is begging the question. I do not think it follows, that because money is spent on a farm on a large scale, the education derived from that farm is any the less.
That is what the farmer sometimes thinks.

I must take exception
to that. As regards my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), I think people will go to experimental farms. In my district we have special excursions to the Indian Head experimental farm from all parts of the compass. Husbands and their wives and children come to the experimental farm in large numbers; and the women look at the things that interest them, such as shade trees, poultry, dairy produce, etc., and the men at anything that interests them, until it is time to return. It is idle to say that men will not go to experimental farms. If that is the custom in Ontario, perhaps the people there are so dashed wise that they will not learn anything; but while the people in my district
are willing to go to experimental farms, I am sure they will not go very much out of their way to see this little bit of a plot which the hon. member for Calgary says they must see willy or nilly when they go to market.
Not willy, nor nillywilly-nilly.

I am sorry I had not
the gentleman's name right, but the Hansard man will get it correct.

It seems to me the hon. member has concerned himself more with the question whether the Department of Agricu.ture of the Government is going to do something that will be a credit to the Government than he has about the farmers.
I did not catch that.

You will see it in Han

ard to-morrow.
I thank the hon. gentleman for Ms courtesy. I will not be bothered looking, because I know it is no good anyway.

It will, of course, be in the judgment of the House whether it is or not. I was referring to something It'at the hon. member said, and of course it is quite possible it was not of much value.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition, in advocating a farm for the clay-belt, touched a very important point in connection with this whole question; that is, he referred to the climate and the general conditions in that part of the country as being so different, for instance, from what they are at Ottawa or at Guelph, that an experimental farm at Guelph or at Ottawa is really of very little use to that part of the country. We have a very large country with a comparatively small population, and we are far behind other countries in regard to experimental work along agricultural lines; perhaps not so far behind them when you compare this country with-others on the basis of population; but we have to consider the vast areas and the differences of climate and of soil. I am entirely in sympathy with this move on the part of the Minister of Agriculture. I suggested something along the same line, I think, two or three years ago, in speaking of this very subject. It seems to me that our whole agricultural education should be systematized in something the same way as our general education is; that is to say, that as the primary school is a step to the high
20&4

school or the collegiate institute., and the high school a step ito the university, so our education along agricultural lines should work out in the same manner; that is, the fully-equipped experimental farm should be the university for agriculture. If you are going to reach the mass of the people with information that will be of benefit to them, you are not going to do it by sending	out
agricultural bulletins, no matter how valuable the information in them may be, because hardly one out of five hundred farmers reads those bulletins. It is also absolutely true beyond a shadow of a doubt that the general farmer looks upon an experimental farm as something beyond him. He says: " Lots of money is spent on that farm, and I cannot hope with my limited means to do as the experimental farm is doing." In the province of Ontario ill recent years the Government has done a great deal of good by sending men out to do experimental work,, such as demonstrating in this neighbourhood and that neighbourhood, fifteen or twenty or thirty miles apart, how to preserve their orchards by [DOT] spraying, how to get rid of certain weeds by spraying at certain seasons, and so on. Such things are educating the pepole; the farmers have an opportunity of seeing them, and they feel that they can imitate them. The general farmer does not feel that he has the means at his disposal to imitate the work carried on at experimental farms. It is true that occasionally, say once or twice a year, an excursion may be got up to visit an experimental farm, and some of the farmers, who perhaps have the means and want a holiday, will take in that excursion. They see a great many things in a few hours, and they go away confirmed in the idea that it is impossible for them to imitate what tney have seen at that farm. I would like to see this work carried on in the manner the minister has indicated that he intends to carry it on in the West. He wants to have some twenty or thirty stations; lut I would like to see that system spread throughout the Dominion of Canada. I would not stop at
1,000	or at 2,000 of those small 'experimental plots. If you had 10,000 of them scattered turoughout this country, in every constituency, you would get splendid value for every dollar that was spent.
In various European countries they have carried their work on agricultural lines very much further than we have in this country. The result is shown in the statistics of crop returns, not only in grain

but in roots as well. It seems to me we acted wisely in establishing experimental farms here and there in the country to carry on experiments and give the people the benefit of the knowledge they gained. But the people ought also to have the benefit of these little demonstration stations, and these stations should be as numerous as possible. I think the money would bring a big return in the form of a larger yield and in the encouragement it would give to the agricultural population. And that is another element that should be considered. If the minister can succeed in demonstrating in the West that crops can be raised in that drouth district by proper cultivation, it will not be merely one or two or a dozen men going by who will learn and benefit. It is not going to stop there, because, say what you will of the farmer, he is always ready to impart his information to his neighbour. If he has made a success in cultivating his fields in a certain way, he will tell his neighbour; he does not try to keep the information to himself. So, if at these demonstration farms a hundred farmers see and learn the proper course to follow, the information will not benefit these people alone, but they will carry it to hundreds of others. I am heartily in sympathy with this plan, and I hope the minister will carry it out and will establish these smaller demonstration stations throughout the East as well as throughout the West.

I do not wish to take up much of the time of the committee, but as this is a subject on which I have had something to say in other sessions, I desire to say a few words now. The late Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Fisher, and I used to have a friendly combat every time his Estimates came up as to the utility of experimental farms and the best way of getting to the people the benefits those experimental farms could give.
The plan outlined by my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) is not exactly an experiment. I have not a word to say against the general and large experimental farms that have been established in various parts of this country; I believe they have been of great service to the agriculturists of Canada. But we have had these great experimental farms for many years^at Ottawa, at Brandon, at Indian Head, and elsewhere. It did not seem to me that we were getting value, at any rate in western Canada-I say nothing about eastern Canada-for the money expended on these experimental farms. One

suggestion has been made to which we have referred before. The experimental farm in Manitoba is situated on the bajik of a river, on soil different from any other in the province except, perhaps, in one locality.
Now, I am not taking any credit to myself for the adoption of the plan outlined this morning; nevertheless, in justice to myself-and the proof of what I say will be found in Hansard-this plan is identical with or very similar to a plan which I outlined and tried to influence the late Minister of Agriculture to adopt. Soil varies, as my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) has said. And that gentleman may say what he likes, he may be as flippant as he pleases about that country to which we have been referring, but the fact is that climatic conditions and soil conditions there are different, perhaps from those of any other place in western Canada. That being so, a different system of farming must be adopted in order to attain success. And that is exactly why we should have these demonstration farms. One experimental farm in the province of Manitoba, situated on a peculiar soil-a splendid soil, none better in the world-would not give to the farmers who live on a different soil, one with more gravel, if you like, or different in some other way, the example and information that they should have in working their land. I used to say to Mr. Fisher, in the kind way in which I always speak, that I thought he should establish demonstration farms.
It has been said here this morning that you can have excursions to your experimental farms. So you can; and it is a good thing and is being adopted more and more. But, nevertheless, here is the experience- and experience is what you can depend upon -both at Brandon and at Indian Head, that very few farmers avail themselves of the excursions to the experimental farms. I have had conversations with Mr. Grisdale about it. I said: "If you cannot get the farmers to come to the experimental farm, you must take the experimental or demonstration farm to the farmers." They are doing that in Manitoba. But who is doing it? The local government. The provincial Minister of Agriculture, the Hon. George Lawrence, has established within the last year or two something like twenty-five of these demonstration farms. They are exactly as outlined by the hon. member for Calgary. Each farm is forty acres in extent. The land is not bought, but is leased by one of the best farmers within a mile or two of the town.
The Government fences it and also supplies the seed in order to be assured that that seed is the very best; and the Government has supervision. The farmer who operates the farm gets no pay, but I think is permitted to have the crop raised on the forty-acre plot.
Now, the farmers in our country, of whatever political party, recognize the importance of that demonstration plot. I have never heard one adveT&e criticism of it. They think it is the best policy that has yet been launched in the interest of the farmer. But it comes from that progressive province in which I have the honour to live, and which has given so many progressive ideas and policies to the western provinces. Take the railway policy, and the telephone policy, and now the demonstration farm policy-they all originated in the province of Manitoba; and I am glad to say, in the interests of western Canada, that they have all been successful.
We have another idea which, I dare say, has been adopted in Alberta and Saskatche-wian, and which with us has proven very successful. We have an agricultural college in Winnipeg, just as you have an agricultural college in Guelph, of whose work we hear glowing accounts. But there was the same difficulty that I have been speaking about in the other case: you could not get the people to this agricultural college, it was too expensive. But in Manitoba- and I do not know but what the same is done in Ontario-they take the agricultural college to the farmers. A train is supplied free by the different railways, and is fitted up practically like the college at Winnipeg or Guelph. That train goes from town to town, its arrival being advertised ahead. So far as, my town of Boissevain is concerned, I never knew that train to come in but there were from two hundred to four hundred people, men, women and children, who came to Boissevain to see the results attained by the agricultural college in Winnipeg, and these people have always gone away well pleased with what they saw and convinced that this policy of the touring agricultural college was one eminently in the interest of the people at large.
If a municipality in Manitoba wants to establish one of these agricultural plots -and our municipalities are, , on the average, about 18 miles square- they have only to make application to the provincial Minister of Agriculture. I believe that this plan is identical with the plan outlined by the hon. member for Calgary. I am glad that the Minister of Agriculture

has seen fit to adopt this plan, and I believe it will prove entirely successful.

So far as the northern part of the province of Manitoba is concerned, experimental farms are of very little use, but demonstration farms are of the utmost importance. I believe that if we could induce this Government to clear dozens of tracts of landdn the northern part of Manitoba and to Start demonstration farms there, the work would prove of very great value to the people in that district. Some of the land in that part of the province is very difficult of cultivation. Much of it is covered with scrub timber. The settlers who have gone in there, while they are first-class men, are not always in good financial circumstances, and, without encouragement, it is almost impossible for them to make headway. I have advocated time after time that some comprehensive scheme should b.e adopted by tire Goyemment with a view to assisting these people to acquire and settle these lands. It has been said that I have advocated a paternal government, but I think the time is coming when the Government of Canada should be more paternal than it has been in respect of the farmers. The land in the northern part of Manitoba is, I believe, destined to become the most valuable land in the northwest country, but, owing to the nature of the soil, it cannot be successfully worked unless the Government comes to the assistance of the people. I would not advocate the 40-acre plots in my own district, but I would advocate the Government's taking up 10-acre plots in different parts of the northern portion of the province, clearing them and putting them under cultivation in order to show these people the possibilities of the land. If this were done, I *am sure that the Government would be amply repaid in a very short time, and that the settlers in that part of the country would very soon become a thoroughly independent and prosperous community. I would call the attention of the minister also to the fact that the northern portion of the province is well adapted to dairying, but the people in the district being poor, they require some assistance in order that their efforts along this line may become productive. I have advocated, and I 'advocate now, that the Government of the country should make it possible for these men to secure sufficient stock to start them in the dairying business. If this were done, in a short time these non-productive districts would become productive, and 
every dollar of the money expended by the Government in the way of stock and the clearing of the land would be repaid. I would strongly urge upon the Minister of Agriculture the advisability of his devoting some little attention to assisting the farmers in this part of the province. I agree with what the hon. member for Souris lias said with regard to the efforts of the Manitoba Government in establishing these demonstration farms. Some of them have been established in my own county, and in every case they have proved to be of great value. But the finances of tile provincial government are limited, and I believe that the Dominion Government ought to come to the assistance of the people and do some of the work that the provincial government is not able to do. In my own county we have brought in some 30,000 or 40,000 foreigners. These people deserve encouragement and assistance in order that they may become selfsustaining and prosperous. I wisli to impress upon the committee the fact that these people are industrious and "thrifty; they are doing all that men can do to become good citizens and prosperous farmers, and this they will do if they receive encouragement and assistance from the Government.

We have discussed this session many matters concerning the district known as the drouth district in Saskatchewan and Alberta, but I question whether any matter that we have taken up in that connection is of as much importance as the question which we have under consideration at the present time. Personally I am in favour of experimental farms, but I am also inclined to believe in the demonstration plot idea which the min' ister has in view. As to the experimental farm at Lethbridge I would not say that the conditions which exist at Lethbridge are exactly similar to those which exist from that point to the Saskatchewan boundary and thence on towards Moosejaw. I have had this complaint from the farmers about the experimental farms. You may tell the farmer that the experimental farm had a good crop while in his own district there was a failure. His argument is that at the experimental farm they have all the facilities for practising farming on a proper scale, they can afford the labour and can put in the crops at the proper seasons and test them all the way through, and so are bound to get a crop of some kind. A a matter of fact, in that drouth district this year there were farmers who had crops because

they happened to get their land in shape, they had summeivfallowed it and got it seeded in the proper time and were able to have crops of 15 bushels to the acre in a district where farmers for miles around did not have a crop of any kind. The experimental plot idea is necessary in my particular district for the reason that the climatic and soil conditions are so varied all through that country, within 100 miles of Lethbridge. In the district of Macleod there were crops this year towards the foothills, in the Pineher Creek country and also along the Calgary and Edmonton line. They had not very large crops, but at the same time they had something. In my own district around Cardston, near Lethbridge, they had crops, and north and west along the Carmangay line of the Canadian Pacific railway they had crops which in some cases were very good. Yet there were instances in that district where farmers did not have anything whatever. I think that the experimental plot idea has a good deal to commend it. At the same time I believe in the experimental farm, I believe it is helpful in giving the farmers directions as to the proper method to follow in their particular district.
As to what has been said by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Sc'naffner), I can understand people losing hope about the future of that country owing to the crop failure this year. I have discussed that matter in the House this session and have instanced other sections of Canada and sections of the United States, where similar conditions was met in the early days and overcome. I have hope and I believe that much can be done by proper education of the farmer ; if the farmer, for instance, had had the proper idea about farming methods in that country when he went in there in the beginning he would not have required relief this year. I have been told that by farmers that if they had known how to farm properly when they went in they would have made enough out of'their operations during the time they had been there prior to last year to have put themselves in a safe position to carry them through such a crisis. I have known in that district good yields from seeding on stubble. For a few years farmers there thought they could raise a crop of grain by throwing seed belter skelter over the land because they had ideal conditions, and farmers in many cases seeded on stubble. I have even known volunteer crops of 12 to 15 bushels to the acre, and that made the farmers think
they could do anything with the land there and it would yield a crop. But they have met with adverse conditions and these adverse conditions are driving them to adopt a system of farming which I am satisfied will be successful in that district. -These very adverse conditions are going to be helpful to farmers, in southern Alberta at any rate. The summer-fallowing idea has only been adopted within the last year or two, and where it was adopted last year there were in a great many cases crops of some kind. I believe that that idea, properly practised and followed out, will result in a great deal of success in farming in that part of the country. As for the future of the district, I would mention that in Saskatchewan, in what is known as the Qu'Appelle valley, I have been told that people left the country in the early 80's and on towards the early 90's, because they had to face adverse conditions, thought the country.was not any good; and yet today that country is considered the most fertile district in Saskatchewan. In Manitoba exactly the same conditions were faced by the farmers in the early days of farming in that province. These conditions are being faced in southern Alberta and in southern Saskatchewan. I believe that history will prove that the opening of the country was warranted and that as soon as the farmers acquire the proper knowledge of how to farm in those sections of Alberta and Saskatchewan they will meet with success in their operations. I believe that we should have an experimental farm in the heart of the affected country, and also that the establishment of experimental plots throughout that particular country or for that matter in any part of Canada will be helpful to agriculture.

The minister referred to the fact that some additional land had been purchased for the farm at Ros-thern. Would he give the House the particulars of that purchase? He announced last summer that a quarter-section or a half-section had been bought.

I will give it at three
o'clock. I have not the exact details now.

Would the minister give
a brief summary of what is being done in the province of Quebec by his - department, especially with regard to Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere?

We are carrying on the work at Cap Rouge and at Ste. Anne de la

Pocatiere and at Lennoxville in the Eastern Townships, where we have recently established a farm. We are increasing the work at Ste. Anne de la Pocatihre. We are carrying on the work on the usual lines of experimental work at all these stations and are endeavouring to extend the work and help those sections of the country more than before.	[DOT]
Is the work at Ste. Anne de la Pocatibre confined to the farm itself or is it extended to the surrounding country?

A good deal of the work is confined, as always, to the experimental farm; but in so far as our officers can make known the results that they are achieving to the farmers of the neighbouring district it is their business to do so, and if hon. members say that this is not being done, that every effort is not being made to render that farm beneficial to the country, I will be only too glad to take the matter up.
Will the minister give an idea of the chief experiments being made at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere?

I think there as at the other farms, they have carried on the various branches of animal husbandry, livestock raising, soil fertilization, rotation of crops and everything that in common parlance is known as advanced agricultural methods. I do not know that we are carrying out any particular lines of work there that we are not carrying out at most of our experimental stations in other districts.
How are the results communicated to the farmers in the district?

The chief way we have of reaching the farmers generally who cannot visit the farm is by our farm report. This, in the case of Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, is a special repor' frcm the superintendent giving the result of all the experimental work, giving the exact conditions on the farm. That report every farmer who is at all interested is entitled to receive, he is .put on the mailing list and gets complete copies of the whole work. If he requires any special bulletins we are only too happy to put him on th!e list and give him every bulletin in which he is interested.
Have the farmers to apply to the farm?

Either to the farm
there or to the central farm here. The farmer can apply to be put on the list for

all reports or for any special reports in which lie is interested.

I have always contended that as there is a great difference in climate and geographical .situation between the two constituencies of Gaspe and Bonaven-ture and the place on the St. Lawrence where the experimental farm is, Bonaven-ture and Gaspe being much further south and nearer to the Maritime Provinces, there should be a demonstration farm of some kind either in Bonaventure or Gaspe. Some years ago New Carlisle was suggested as a suitable location for such a farm. Perhaps the minister may see his way clear to giving us such a farm. I must say a good word of the department for what it has done in my province in assisting the dairying industry, which is becoming quite an important one aown there. The department sent down the Dairy and Cold Storage Commissioner, and he has been of considerable assistance to the various butter factories that have recently been established in my constituency; and other butter factories are b'eing started this year. A number of lecturers have also been sent down to deliver lectures in the parishes of Gaspe and Bonaventure, and I should like to know wheth'er the minister intends to follow up the good seed that has been thus sown, or are the department's efforts to end with the lectures?

I know my hon. friend takes a very lively interest in uiat part of the country. But he understands that owing to the financial condition of this country at the present time we hesitate to plunge in large expenditures, even for agriculture; although I must cordiany acknowledge that the Minister of Finance and. my other colleagues have not held up their hands in regard to this department. But we felt that there was at this moment a special need for this kind of work in the West, that no matter how strained the finances might be the Government was absolutely warranted in doing something for those particular districts in the West. Later on I hope we may be able to do this sort of work in other parts of the country, including those * portions of Quebec where the settlers are in considerable need of more advanced methods. I can assure my hon. friend that the matter 'will not be forgotten. *
