Experimental farms-maintenance of Central Farm, and establishment and maintaining of additional branch stations, $785,000.

I doubt
if there is a single vote in all these Estimates that is of greater importance to the people of Canada than that which we are now discussing. While to-day there has been a good deal of discussion on this vote by the representatives from various provinces, very little has been said so far by hon. gentlemen who represent Ontario constituencies. I wish to emphasize what has already been said as to the importance of experimental and demonstration farms. I believe that the Minister of Agriculture has acted wisely in providing for the extension of agricultural instruction in this direction, and I feel quite sure that no expenditure of public money in Canada will give better results than will the expenditure of this $785,000. I may say that personally I would like to see a much larger appropriation for this purpose. We have heard a great deal in recent years about educating the farmer in the science of their industry, and I am satisfied that these small demonstration farms or plots will accomplish better results than possibly any other scheme, because through them you bring directly under the eyes of the farms what can be done by the study and practice of advanced agricultural methods.
I was amused at the remarks of the lion.
. member from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) to the effect that agricultural education of this kind was probably a custom in the province of Ontario, where the people were so " dashed " wise, as he said. I do not think the people of Ontario deserve that sneering remark from the hon. member. They have been the pioneers in agricultural education in this country, and shortly after Confederation, John Carling, afterwards Sir John Carling, then Commissioner of Agriculture in the Government of John Sanfield Macdonald, established the Ontario Agricultural College, the reputation of which has always stood high in Ontario, in Canada, and, I may -say, throughout the world. From the day of its establishment to the present hour, the province of Ontario has paid cheerfully all the expenses in connection with that institution, which has trained more men in the science of agriculture than probably any other institution in the world. And yet the hon. member for Moosejaw finds it not beneath him to sneer at the people of Ontario. When Sir John Carling was Minister of Agriculture in the
Government of Sir John Macdonald, he established the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa, and shortly afterwards there were established experimental farms at Nappan, for the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, it being situated near the boundary of these two provinces; at Indian Head, for the Northwest Territories; and at Agassiz, for British Columbia. For twenty-five years afterwards not an experimental or a demonstration farm was established in the whole of Canada, until in 1911, when several others were brought. into being. Let me call attention to the fact that from that time down to the past year not one experimental farm was established in the great province of Ontario. Session after session I have taken this matter up, and I have urged on the Government the necessity of doing justice to the province of Ontario in this respect. I am glad to see that since last session the Minister of Agriculture has made arrangements to establish a demonstration farm in Northern Ontario, along the line of the Transcontinental railway. That part of our province suffered severely through a report that was made by a man who was sent out by the Conservation Commission a few years ago, who went along the line of the Transcontinental railway in a motor car, and made a report which was most damaging to all that northern territory. I commend the minister for establishing this experimental farm in Northern Ontario. .
In view of all the circumstances, it is indeed ungrateful on the part of the hon. member for Moosejaw to sneer at the people of Ontario, forgetting the sacrifices made by them to develop the West. In past years the people of Ontario realized that we had a great heritage in our western country, which needed development and settlement, and to-day we do not complain that the Government is bearing the expense of these agricultural stations throughout the West. But the time has come when Ontario must look to herself to see that she also gets fair treatment. In the matter of immigration, for years past., Ontario has been discriminated against, and the flow of immigration has been diverted to the western provinces, with the result that by the Redistribution Bill, that wealthy province loses six of her representatives in this House. That may please some hon. gentlemen opposite, but :to me it is evidence of the fact that in the future these western provinces must look to themselves and depend on their own resources, without seeking the aid of the other provinces to help them out of their

difficulties. We are told by an hon.-gentleman on the other side of the House that the farmers of the West were not going to see these demonstration stations when they were driving their wheat to the market, thus implying that taking wheat to the market is the only thing that brings a western farmer from his home, which, of course, is an absurd view to take. In my opinion, the sooner demonstration farms are established throughout Canada, in order that our farmers may he taught to practise what is preached, the better it will be for the people of Canada. We have no mean province in Ontario; we have an energetic, an enterprising and an educated people, and they have learned to do for themselves what some of -the people in the western provinces think the Government ought to do tor them. The dairy products of Ontario last year represented a value of $125,000,000, t'hie live stock of Ontario had a value of $510,000,000; the, exports of Ontario last year were $186,000,000, and the imports of Ontario $290,000,000, the latter figures not including interprovincial trade. But that does not represent all the wealth developed by the people of Ontario.	'
So far as fruit growing is concerned, 80 per cent of the fruit of Canada is grown in the province of Ontario; yet there is not a fruit station nor an experimental station maintained in that province by the Dominion Government. Ninety-seven per cent of the grapes and peaches grown in Canada are grown in the province of Ontario; yet you find that, although stations are established in other provinces, such as British Columbia and the Maritime Provinces, the people of Ontario have to do all their experimental work for themselves. A number of experimental farms were established in 1911; but with the exception of a tobacco-growing farm of forty acres in the county of Essex, not one was established in the whole province of Ontario. This should not be a contentious matter; and I would not have made any reference to it, had it not been for the manner in which the hon. member for Moose-jaw (Mr. Knowles) referred to the people of the province of Ontario. The sooner the people of the western provinces depend upon their own resources and do not come to the Dominion Parliament looking for special favours, the better it will be for all concerned.
The hon. member referred to the necessity of supplying with wheat the farmers in a certain area who unfortunately lost 
their crops last year. In some of the older districts of Ontario where land is very valuable, if the people farmed in the manner in which the people farm in Western Canada, they would not grow very much. In my own county immense numbers of live stock are shipped from western Canada, and are fattened up and placed on the market. Pood is brought, in from western Canada and fed to live stock in the East; in fact, two dealers in foodstuffs for live stock, two feed stores at one shipping point in the county of Oxford during the present winter handled no less than nineteen carloads of cottonseed meal averaging about 22 tons to the car; and other feed in large quantities is being brought in. The Government of this country for many years past pursued one of the most reckless policies-yes, I will say a criminal policy-with regard to the importation of foodstuffs from western Canada. When a Government permits the screenings of grain from the elevators to be shipped out and distributed through some of the older provinces, such as the province of Ontario, it iis doing something for which it ought to be held accountable. Hon. gentlemen here h-avie stated that the western farmer who summer-fallows his land is practically assured of a crop. I 'remember in, the old days in Ontario, when nearly every farmer summer-fallowed his land, but afterwards with a better system of farming he fo-und that it was not necessary. To-day, however, he has to go back to the summerfallowing system -again by reason of the foul seeds that have been distributed over the province of Ontario and that came largely from western Canada. L-ater on in the Estimates the question will be brought up whether the Government of this country should see that all grain shipped to Government elevators is -screened and tiba-t the screenings from -that grain are destroyed and not distributed over the country.
I have taken longer than I intended in regard to this matter, but I want to emphasize the fact that Ontario is no mean province; that outside of the province of Quebec it is the largest province in Canada, and that not 15 per -cent of its area is under cultivation. I commend the minister for his action in establishing an experimental farm in northern Ontario, and I believe he h-as adopted -a splendid method in order to clear that by having interned prisoners do the work, because it ,will undoubtedly reflect gTeot credit on

the northern' country. Notwithstanding Professor Per now's report, in which he istated that that country is not fit for settlement, geographically it is not located as far north as the city of Winnipeg, and it is to-day rich and fertile, although mostly covered with timber; and I am satisfied that the experimental station established there by the hon. Minister of Agriculture will do work that will call the attention of the people of this country to the advantages of location and the capability of the soil of northern Ontario to raise as good crops as are grown in other parts of Canada.

I have no argument with my hon. friend in regard to the .importance of the province of Ontario in many ways, and I think he has rather misunderstood my remarks. Smely the hon. gentleman does not wish to put me in an unfair light, because I did not make any remarks derogatory to the province of Ontario, as I think he ought to have known if he had been in the chamber at the time. I was advocating that we should have -experimental farms to which the people would go in great numbers. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) stated, as I understood him, that men would not go t-o experimental farms, and I said that, if it be that the people of Ontario know so dashed much that they do not have to go, the people in the West are different: we do not think we are the whole shooting match; we do not think we know everything. True, we do not live in the delectable province of Ontario; but my hon. friend will have to account for having lived in such a godly place as Ontario, and inasmuch as the favours bestowed on him are so much greater, he will have to be so much more careful of the way he walks. My hon. friend has told us many times that Ontario is such a wonderful country, and he has scolded us because some weeds have gone from the West into that province. I do not want my hon. friend to run away with the idea that Ontario is altogether ready for the next world. I dr. not think we send our weeds to the East; 1 think large numbers of weeds, came to us from Ontario at the start, because I cannot imagine any other places that they came from than Bruce and Huron and Oxford, where we got our seed from originally-and some very bad, devilish weeds they were too. My hon. friend should not say the West is under any favour to Ontario, because that is a played-out statement. We are not under
any favours- far from it. True, the policy of the country at present is dictated largely by Ontario and the protectionist spirit. While Ontario has sent us some of its vile weeds, thank Heaven, it has not yet sent us its vile protectionist spirit. We have not the protectionist spirit brooding over us; we do not believe in it yet; but the protectionist spirit controls our politics and we are suffering. We are not, however, under any obligation to Ontario because we are under the heel of Ontario so far as the present Government is concerned. I say that to my hon. friend in all kindness.
My hon. friend speaks about the good land in Ontario. There is a great deal of good land in Ontario and it was here long before my hon. friend and I were born, and much of it was under cultivation; but my hon. friend should for a while take a whack at farming along the Canadian Pacific railway line between North Bay and Fort William and see how much Marquis wheat he can grow in that beautiful part of the province of Ontario. I am more pleased than I can tell my bon. friend to see that to-day, from his seat in the House-I will not say he has given the lie; I speak in all good humour, but he has repudiated the argument of his friends who said that the agricultural belt of the National Transcontinental was no good, because my hon. friend says it is a good country and is going to support a great population. We are pleased to have heard the truth from the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), that this district, through which the late Government built the National Transcontinental, is one of such fertile land that even the very good province of Ontario is proud to have it within its boundaries.

I would like to take up the time of the committee for a' few minutes in raising my voice in protest against this attempt once again to set the East against the West and the West against the East. It seems to me that the farmers of the Dominion of Canada do not require to be put in hostile camps of that- kind, nor will their best interests be served in that way. The West has its own peculiar problems and difficulties, and these have been looked upon with a great deal of consideration by the representatives from other parts of the country. Everything has been done that we could reasonably do-those of us who represent the East-to change conditions in favour of the farmer of the West. I trust that the best representatives from the West

look upon the farmers of the East with the same measure of consideration. Our problems are one, after all. Now, we have some difficulties in the East. I would ask the minister to take into consideration the ininterests of that large tract of the province of Ontario lying between the agricultural and fruit-growing portion of Ontario to the south and the great clay belt to the north. There is there a great stretch of country not quite so favourable for agricultural production, but admirably adapted for a great many things. Our people in the section of country from which I come do not know exactly what can be produced in that country, and we would like very much to see an experimental farm established there. The country of which I speak takes in such districts as Muskoka, Parry Sound, Nipiss-ing and Haliburton and other constituencies further to the east whose conditions are somewhat similar. We believe there are a great many kinds of fruit that can be grown in that country.. We believe it is admirably adapted for the production of a great many kinds of vegetables and roots. True, we produce great numbers of cattle and also no inconsiderable quantity of grain and vegetables. But we are not working under the best conditions. With a view to demonstrating the possibilities of that country, our people have approached the local Government at Toronto and pressed their claim time after time. But we have been met of late with the reply that the lack of funds has made it impossible for the local Government to take part in carrying out our wishes. So, I bring the subject before the Minister of Agriculture for the Dominion and ask his assistance so that we may have some kind of demonstration farm established in that country to show our farmers there what our particular part of this great Dominion is capable of producing. We have been able to come down to the city of Ottawa for two or three years and, at your great annual exhibition, carry off first prize with our display of potatoes. We have been able to do the same in the city of Toronto for eight or ten years handrunning. Our people were able to go to the town of Brockville and take some of the prizes in grain last winter. But our farmers are not educated in a general way to take advantage of the peculiar qualities of our soil. These cases that I mention are the result of individual effort. There is no general effort to demonstrate to our farmers the benefit of certain kinds of cultivation and to show them for what line of 
production our conditions are best suited. Therefore I ask the Minister of Agriculture to give to our section of the country the consideration to which we think it is entitled.

My hon. friend from
Saskatoon (Mr. McOraney) asked me what land had been bought in connection with the Rosthern farm. A strip of land lying between the station and the right of way of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway and Steamboat Company, containing approximately 15 acres, was bought at the price of $1,000. Another plot of 440 acres was bought from Jacob Janzen. It forms the NE. i and S. i of section 26, tp. 42, range 3, west of the 3rd meridian.
I desire to say just a word in answer to the remarks of my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) and the remarks of my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright). As to these farms and the work of the Agricultural Department generally, 1 hope that hon. members understand that there is no East and no West in what we are doing. I happen to be a western man myself, my home being much farther west than that of my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) or other hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken. I was also an Ontario man. I think that everybody in this House will agree that what is done for agriculture should be done, so far as possible, equitably throughout the country. It is true, we are making this initial step in demonstration work in southern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta. But that does not mean that northern Alberta, northern Saskatchewan, Ontario and other parts will be left out, as the work develops and the opportunities warrant. I shall be glad to keep in mind what my hon. friends have said.
M. H. ACHIM (Labelle) (Translation): Mr Chairman, it was not my intention to take much of the time of the minister to air my viewTs on this question, but the prolonged debate on this subject participated in by my hon. friends from the west and from Ontario does away with any hesitation I may have had. In view of that lengthy discussion, I cannot be accused of loquacity if I devote two or three minutes to the province of Quebec. It is not out of place to recall in this House, as elsewhere, that there still exists such a province, which has played an historic and important part in this country.

From the viewpoint of agriculture, it needs envy very little either of the western provinces or the province of Ontario. The complaints that I bring to the minister from my constituency are very much similar to those laid before him by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles). In his reply, the Minister of Agriculture freed me from certain misgivings which have been worrying me for the last two or three years. When I became a member of this House, I received numerous petitions from the district of Labelle, requesting from the Government the establishment of an experimental farm or rather of an agricultural station in that part of the province of Quebec. Heretofore, and more especially during the last few years, new districts such as the Abbitibi, the Temiskaming and New Ontario have engrossed public attention; but it has been too readily forgotten that for some fifty years past the region of Labelle has been opened to settlers by a distinguished and zealous priest, Mgr. Labelle, whom the federal and the provincial governments encouraged in his task and that the new district has helped to alleviate the congestion of some of our cities. And the fact must be kept in mind that in the district of Labelle the soil is not as fertile as in the valleys of the St. Lawrence and of the Ottawa. The settlers of Labelle have migrated for the most part from the valleys of those two rivers and are of course prone to apply the same methods of cultivation with which they had become familiar in those places where the rich clay is very different from the soil of the northern regions. Moreover I must add that many of the settlers had never been on a farm; most of them, are workmen who have been snatched away by this enthusiastic apostle from the dangers of cities and under his guidance have pitched their tents in that region and set themselves to the task of bringing up their children. To-day the influx of settlers has slackened and I must be within the truth when I say that colonization is best brought about by the family. When a father has settled upon a lot and has thrived, he seeks to settle his numerous children around him. Up to the present time, the almost exclusive means of livelihood in those parts was the lumber trade. The forest was the principal source of revenue. Now, unfortunately, lumber is beginning to get scarce; the land is clear and the settler must resort to its cultivation to find his living and the sustenance of his family.
The soil with the exception of a few more fertile localities, is generally poor, and requires for its cultivation appropriate methods. We have here at Ottawa, it is true, an experimental farm with a splendid equipment, but the settlers cannot be expected to take frequent trips of two or three hundred miles to Ottawa at a cost of twenty-five to thirty dollars each for the purpose of obtaining information on the best agricultural methods. My idea is that the settler should not have to come to the experimental farm, but the farm should go to the settler. In this connection, I take pleasure in congratulating the Minister of Agriculture upon his scheme by which those new farms will be made centres of distribution; over those centres, the Ottawa experimental farm will spread its sheltering branches as far as my constituency, to which it would certainly be beneficial.
As regards the measure under consideration, I fully agree with the minister. I heard him state in the course of his reply to the hon. member for Moosejaw that he intended to set up some twenty stations of that type in the West. ' Without the least thought of harming the West, I may, on behalf of my electors, ask the minister if he could not reduce to nineteen the number of western stations and give my county the twentieth. Those districts where 'a fertile soil yields hay, oats and other grain a-plenty are not those whose farmers have most need of scientific model farms. But in our country, where the soil being lighter is of course less fertile, and where climatic disturbances are more frequent and dangerous, I venture to say that agricultural stations are a necessity, because there the land is not made to produce as much as it could, that is, proportionately to the area under cultivation, it should yield one-third more than its present production. The farmers are not acquainted with the scientific methods of cultivation which are best adapted to the nature of the soil and its geological formation.
I may be allowed to express my thanks to the minister for inaugurating such a progressive system that will solve a problem of great importance and for a long time agitated. I hope he will not forget the settlers of the district of Labelle and that he will do as much for them as for the farmers of Ontario and of the Great West.

Mr. Chairman, the condition of my throat does not allow me to make a lengthy speech, but 1 deem it my duty to express my views in a few words



I listened with keen interest to the remarks that have-been made on this most important topic, agriculture, and my congratulations are due the hon. members from western constituencies for the convincing arguments they have brought to support their contentions. It was also a pleasure to hear the explanations given by the minister during the debate; his efficient work is praiseworthy and his initiative in the furtherance of agricultural interests commendable. The item now before us relates to experimental farms. I can see that the subject absorbs the attention of all members, but especially of those from the western prairies, and also that in the more northern districts, the farmers, through their representatives, attach much importance to this question, which, in fact, is for us of the most vital consequence. I realize that in the particular circumstances in which Canada is placed, the minister cannot easily satisfy the demands made upon him from all parts of the country. To get over the present difficulty it has been suggested that demonstration farms or stations be established on a much smaller - scale than the branches of the experimental farm. Doubtless the scheme is practical and under the circumstances will be very beneficial. But the minister's solicitude must not extend exclusively to the western provinces. Every session for the last few years, the Canadian Parliament has been called upon to provide aid for the settlers of the new provinces. This year we are asked to vote the large sum of ten millions to provide seed for those farmers who have settled on the Government lands_. That grant is not a gift but will have to be repaid by all those who have been helped. The Dominion Government had to take such a course because, at the time the new provinces were erected, it kept to itself the control of the public lands; but in view of the obligations which that reservation entails, had we not better amend the law and put those provinces on the same footing as the older provinces, transfer to them the full control of their own lands and let them shift for themselves. Does it not seem anomalous that next spring the farmers of the province of Quebec as well as those from the eastern provinces, will have, as. they have been doing, every year, to purchase large quantities of seed grain from the west itself. Is it not an oddity that we easterners are buying our -seed from the west while at the same time we are asked to advance millions of dollars'to the very people who supply us with what we want. On account 
of the nefarious war which shakes all Europe and even the whole world, Canada is placed in a peculiar position; its evident duty and interest lie in increasing to its limits its agricultural production, so as to enable Europe, by supplying it with the necessaries of life, to stave off starvation. With this in view, the Minister of Agriculture has organized throughout the country a series of patriotic lectures, as they are called, having for their object to awaken the farmers to -the necessities that have arisen and still more to those that will arise in the future; and also to point out to the farming community that now is the time to go to work and take the necessary steps to meet the needs I have jhist mentioned by an unprecedented excess of production. There has been generally a happy selection of lecturers. The farmers attended the meetings in large numbers and listened with deep interest to the important discussions carried on. The scheme is a patriotic one and its beginning as a means of theoretical education bodes well for its success; but as was pointed out in to-day's debate, it must necessarily be supplemented by object lessons, by an increase in the number of experimental farms and by the establishment of agricultural stations. I desire at this juncture to warn the minister that it is of the utmost importance that these lectures on agriculture should be kept free from all party politics. At one of the meetings wThich have been success-, ffilly carried out by Hon-. Mr. Burrell in the province of Quebec, after two officers of his department, Messrs. Fortier and Gingras had delivered their lectures, *which they always manage to render practical, a man by the name of Gareau, lecturer for the Quebec Government got up to speak. In an outburst of vituperation, he warned the audience against the movement organized by the Dominion Department of Agriculture to awaken the farmer t-o the necessity of improving his stock, and against their taking advantage of the offer of the department, who lends choice bulls to those farmers who wish to improve their methods and who apply to the minister at Ottawa. This man Gareau went so for as to denounce the Minister of Agriculture as the agent of certain cattle-breeders of Ontario and of the eastern townships, who desire to get rid of old worn-out animals. How can practical results be secured when such partisan wrangling is carried on before the farmers who have attended the lectures in good faith and are put at a loss to know what to do when the Minister of Agriculture

hands over to the Quebec Government a special subsidy of $190,000 a year as a help to agriculture in that province, it seems to me that the only proper thing to do for the Provincial Government is to employ none but men of judgment and discretion, and not mere election agents, who, disregarding all propriety, and callous to the public interest, drag the Dominion Minister in the mire for no purpose but to disparage the good work he is doing.
In past years, I spoke in this House of the question now before the House in so far as my constituency was concerned. I am aware that in this forum, our own separate local interests must not monopolize our attention, but the interest of every locality must, be considered as those of the one great Canadian family. But if I revert to the discussion that has taken place here to-day, the most serious complaints and the most forcible arguments that have been heard have come from the representatives of the most northern districts. It has been shown how, even in the West there is found, with a difference in latitude, great differences in geological formations and climatic influences, that create, in the more northern regions, even on the best farms, special difficulties of cultivation. If on the western plains, which are so fertile, the higher latitudes present special problems to the agriculturist, the same endures in the eastern provinces. In the East, there are localities favoured with mild winters; others where it is colder and others still are found, as my county, where a severe winter lasts for six or seven months and where climatic conditions differ radically from those of the province of Quebec, because the atmospheric currents are different and. so the chances of successful cultivation are lessened. The soil is fertile, the farmers live comfortably, and from the railway records we see that the agricultural population, which numbers
30,000	in the districts of Chicoutimi and Lake St. John, has secured from the cheese and live stock industries more than two million dollars of revenue. But such a revenue can be obtained under such special circumstances only by harder labour, and a better grasp of the underlying principles of good farming than what is required in other more favoured sections of the province, on account of the more strenuous efforts exacted from the tiller of the soil by a less bountiful Providence, so to speak, and the continued climatic disturbances.
To the north and south of the Lauren-tians, the Dominion Government has estab-131J
lished branches of the experimental farm at Compton, in the eastern townships, at Cap Rouge and at Sainte Anne de la Pocatiere. Moreover, a philanthrophic Canadian millionaire has erected in the vicinity at Ste. Anne de Bellevue, the famous Macdonald agricultural college, which is after all an experimental farm, perhaps the best equipped in this country. We also have in that part of the province agricultural schools at Oka and at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, which are in their way experimental farms on a smaller scale. Here then in the province of Quebec we find six very important practical institutions, of which two, under the control of the Dominion authorities, are situated in the same district and subject to absolutely the same climate.
Excursions of farmers to the experimental farms have been suggested. Of course, such trips have a certain educative value, but others have stated here before me that they cannot be of much help especially when the visitors come from a region subject to a different climate and having a different geological formation. I have myself at different times organized similar excursions to the central experimental farm at Ottawa. Coming from such a distance, the excursionists found little time to appreciate the methods used and so different were the nature of the soil and the climatic conditions, that, after their return home, they found they had brought back very little that could avail them on their farms.
We now hear on a sudden of a great agricultural movement along the Transcontinental railway, around Lake Abitibi, a new region about whose geology and climate nothing is known. Why such a leap in the dark, and why overlook the province of Quebec, especially those localities where settlement has already been shown to be possible, . where agriculture can .be carried on with success and where there - are still left, as in the Matapedia valley, especially in my constituency, lands of great fertility, on which numerous parishes could be established, but wherein farmers hesitate to settle through fear of unfavourable geographical conditions. It seems to me more rational to take all possible means to maintain and increase a country's population in well known districts rather than let those regions shift for themselves and confine our efforts to those localities in which success is quite uncertain. That policy explains why I take it to be my duty to state anew in this House the needs of my electors, and tr

insist on the minister and the Government doing immediately what is fair by us.
During the last few years, I have maintained with the department an active correspondence on this subject. I have forwarded numerous petitions, and our position has been put before the minister in a clear light. The answers were never unfavourable, but a definite asquiesc'ence is yet to come. Other places more favourably located have received attention while the department, without any ill-will, I know, has been neglecting that part of the province wherein the first experimental farm ought to have been established. The minister, I hope, accepts my remarks in the same spirit in which I make them. I advocate now the claims of justice and common sense, and of course common sense, as ever, is bound to triumph, and the long expected answer will come in due course.
On behalf of my electors, I must express publicly to the Minister of Agriculture our appreciation of all he has been doing to promote the welfare of the farming community of which I am a representative. He also deserves the thanks of that community for the practical assistance given to the improvement of cattle, especially of milch cows. The farmers greatly appreciate the help he has given them, and I deem it my duty to tell him so in this House.
As regards the educational work to be continued, I believe that the minister would do well to take advantage of the rights which accrue to him from the federal subsidies to the different provinces to be devoted to the promotion of agriculture, and introduce in this country the system followed in Germany, France, Sweden, Norway and Denmark, where experimental stations, agricultural colleges and lyceums have been established in large numbers in every section of their respective territories. To put the final touch to the education of farmers' sons and daughters, the Government, at its own expense sends them to visit the best colleges and the most practical farms, so that, by this comparative study, they may become better farmers and develop a greater love for the calling of their parents. That course will, better than all else, help to make agriculture more congenial to them and to keep on the soil the children who would forsake it for the cities.
We are now in the throes of a financial crisis; everybody must make sacrifices; economy is the watch-word. But an expenditure which cannot be cut down or delayed, is that which aims at stirring up

the farmers' apathy, awakening them to the needs and obligations of their profession, and making agriculture as prosperous as lies in the power of a Government. If there is on the surface of the earth an industry which more than another has not remained stationary, it is assuredly agriculture, so, whatever may be the actual stress, I respectfully submit that the Government cannot devote too much of our revenue to its upbuilding and prosperity, and it is the duty of public men who understand the true interests of the country to help the efforts of the Government in that direction.

Mr. Chairman, it was a pleasure for .me to be able to listen from the beginning to this debate participated in by both English and French speakers, and I must say that I fully concur in the remarks which have been made by the hon. members for Labelle (Mr. Achim) and for Chicoutimi (Mr. Girard):	I submit that
the climatic conditions which prevail in the county of Rimouski and the eastern portion of the province of Quebec, call for greater assistance from the Government than the old part of Ontario and even the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, which all enjoy the benefit of a most favourable climate. The farmers of the eastern districts of the province of Quebec have to cope with inclement weather conditions. Seeding cannot take place before the month of June; and very often early frosts blast the hopes of an abundant harvest ; to that the inhabitants of those regions, with a winter season lasting generally all of seven months, show greater courage and endurance that the farmers of Ontario and the other provinces in which winter lasts but three or four months. Those districts especially have a right to look to the paternal solicitude of the Government. In Ontario, fruits grow abundantly and grain ripens easily. Once the land is sowed; the farmer has only to wait for the crops to ripen; he has no fears of frost.
The representatives of the western provinces are anxious for the Government help that will enable them to purchase seed grain. They are indeed fortunate in having secured a law which favdurs them to the exclusion of certain other parts of this country who. need such assistance a good 'deal more than they. I fail to see, as also the hon. member for Chicoutimi, why we grant millions to the farmers of the west to help them in procuring seed grain, when,

in the eastern part of Quebec, where I have my residence, we .often have to purchase our own seed grain from the western farmers. It seems to me that those farmers could bear certain inconveniences and obtain their seed from their neighbours without continually appealing for assistance from the Government.

Will the hon. member allow me to call his attention to the fact that, after asking this explanation from the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche), I was made to understand that the seed thus furnished to the western farmer is not given but sold to him, and as security the Government takes a lien on his harvest. It is a mere loan.

I am thankful for the information, but I can say that the farmers of the province of Quebec would be glad to enjoy the same privilege. If the same course were followed for such districts as Temiscouata, Bonaventure, Chicoutimi, and Gaspe, which often find themselves in distress, I believe that the farmers would be glad to take advantage of such loans, because quite often at spring-time, they have not the money to buy their seed grain and they could easily in the fall repay out of their harvest the money that would have been advanced to them by the Government.
I have already pleaded' for an experimental farm in the county of Rimouski. There is one already in the county of Kamouraska, et Ste. Anne de la Poca-tiere, but on oooount of the distance, our farmers cannot easily visit it. The Gaspe peninsula, comprising the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure, is so to speak, a small province in itself, and there especially the farmers require to be helped along. If an experimental farm cannot be established in the county of Matane, for instance, the least that could be done would be the establishment of agricultural stations, which would be of great usefulness to the farmers. If an experimental farm were erected in the Matapedia valley, where the land is of the best to be found in that country for farming, it would render great services to Bonaventure an,d Rimouski, where good results could be expected at an early date. I entertain the fervent hope that the Minister of Agriculture will not henceforth overlook those districts which have a greater call on his attention than other parts of the country. Our farmers show such courage and struggle so bravely against an adverse climate that they should be given more encouragement than elsewhere. We would think ourselves fortunate if we lived in a country like the province of Ontario or even the western part of Quebec or New Brunswick, where the climate is a great deal milder than ours, but there we are and there we must stay, and the Government is in duty bound to extend to us its solicitude.
Now I may be allowed a slight criticism of the staff of the Department of Agriculture. I find that in that department, especially among the higher officers it is impossible for a French-speaking person who does not speak English to make himself understood. Those higher officers who are frequently in communication with the farmers of Quebec, ought to understand French. We go to their offices, and no matter how important the information we desire, it cannot be given us. These officers, moreover, go into the English speaking sections of the country and deliver lectures for the benefit of the English-speaking farmers, while the province of Quebec, whose population does not speak English cannot derive any advantage from such visits, because those officers do not speak French. I claim that all higher officers should speak French so as to be able to meet every elector and every farmer of Canada. For the most part, they are competent men and qualified for their position. It would be a great advantage for the province of Quebec to meet them and hear them expound the best agricultural methods; but we are deprived of that opportunity. When we call at the department, we have to pick up an interpreter among the young clerks or stenographers. I myself speak English with a certain fluency, but when I have to discuss technical questions I cannot express myself with as much freedom in English as I do in French. The other day I ventured into a room where nine employees were at work and not one of them could understand me. This state of things is- the same in all the departments and the Department of Agriculture is not an exception. The staff of the Department of Agriculture, according to the Civil Service List of 1913, comprises 31 French Canadians and 237 Englishspeaking employees. It seems to me that such a condition is unfair and that there should be a larger number of French Canadians, more in keeping with the importance of the French-speaking population of this country.

I
appreciate the remarks made by my hon. friends from the province of Quebec and I

take note of them. The requirements of the province of Quebec will be dealt with in the same spirit as those of the other provinces.
I understood my hon. friend to say that a great many of the officials of the department are unable to speak the French language. I may say that the director of th'e experimental farm speaks French fluently, and a great many of our other officers are familiar with the French language.

As I rise
for the first time to address this House, 1 take a great deal of pleasure in seconding the remarks made by the hon. member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay (Mr. Girard) in his denunciation of those officers of the provincial government who take advantage of their position to throw discredit on the officers of the Dominion Government.
I also agree with what was said by the member for Labelle (Mr. Achim), in his plea for equal justice for the beautiful district, through whibh, flow the rivers Gatineau, La Rouge, and Du Nord, a land which some years ago the late Father Labelle opened in the north and, with prophetic insight pointed out to the settler.
Arts and Agriculture-for the administration and enforcement of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act, $100,000.

I wish to direct the attention of the minister to the regulations regarding the shipment of potatoes from areas affected with powdery scab to foreign countries. In the case of Prince Edward Island, these shipments would be made to the islands of Newfoundland, St. Pierre and Miquelon. The regulations affecting the shipments of potatoes under these conditions are such that, if enforced, we could not ship at all. Shipments made from our province are made very largely by water, and it would be quite impossible to comply with the regulations as I find them in the Royal Gazette. I understand that the department permits shipments to be made without regard to these regulations, and I should like to have it definitely understood whether or not that is the case.

Regulation B, section 2, which has regard to shipments from infected areas, is in accord with the Destructive Insects and Pest Act. Our regulations say that within the infected area you can move the products concerned virtually without inspection, but when you come to ship to another province which is not infected, you would have to have an inspection.

There is nothing to stop you from shipping your potatoes to Newfoundland except any objection which might be made by those to whom you ship. We do not have any inspection of shipments of potatoes going to Newfoundland; if the Newfoundland people say to you that your potatoes are infected, the onus is on you.

There is a good deal of doubt as to whether the potatoes in our province are really affected by powdery scab. When the potatoes are loaded into the ship the shipper has no means of knowing whether they are affected with powdery scab or not, and if some fussy official comes along -who, perhaps, does not know a great deal about powdery scab, he can give the shipper a great deal of inconvenience under the present regulations. It is to provide against a condition of that kind that 1 should like to have the matters cleared up.

None of our inspectors are concerned with shipments to a foreign country; they would be concerned only with shipments to other provinces of Canada which are free from powdery scab. I quite admit that in all these things there is a good deal of inconvenience to potato growers, and I can only assure my hon. friend that the feeling which I have always held very strongly is that it is unfortunate that the United States should have taken the drastic action which they did take in this matter. The action that we have taken * in this country has been entirely owing to the stand taken by the United States authorities. I have always firmly believed that this disease is not anything like as injurious in its nature as potato canker, and perhaps not more serious than the ordinary scab. However, we were face to face with an embargo upon our potatoes on the part of the United States, and, in order to accede to the request of the shippers to give them as good a market as we could, these regulations were made. The people of the eastern provinces thought that it was better that these regulations should be put into effect and that they should get some kind of a market than that -they -Should have no market at all in the United States. A short while ago a shipment of potatoes was refused at Boston on the ground that they were infected with powdery scab, and the embargo was replaced on the whole country. I am informed by my inspectors, however, that the officials, after searching for seven hours, found but two

potatoes which were infected with powdeTy scab. I cannot speak with authority, but I am inclined to think that the United States authorities will gradually come to the conclusion that this disease is not. as serious as they at first thought it was, and that the whole embargo will be wiped out. It has done good, however, in calling the attention of the potato growers of the country to the necessity for wiping out any serious disease of potatoes. I can only tell my bbn. friend that so far as we are concerned we are simply- making these regulations to try and give shippers a market under the best possible conditions.	[DOT]

I am quite pleased to have the assurance of the minister that there will be no trouble so far as shipments from our province are concerned. I agree, too, that the United States was not justified in putting into force such drastic regulations. I think that we ourselves were somewhat to blame, because in the autumn of 1913 we sent a man to Washington who told the American authorities that our potatoes were diseased. We could hardly expect them to take any other course than to take us at our word, and so they imposed very stringent regulations against the exportation of our potatoes.

I know that my hon. friend would not wish to be misleading. We could not deny that we had powdery scab; and as for our officer saying that we had it, he was only stating what they already knew. They had their men in the country, and they knew absolutely, as we knew absolutely, that wre had powdery scab. I do not personally attach the importance to the disease that some people do; but you cannot conceal the fact that the disease is in the country. We have it to-day, but I do not believe that it is of the serious nature that many people believe.
In my province there is no doubt about that.
We have not any doubt; we know.

Some few years ago two officials of the department from Ottawa visited our province and visited the premises of one particular man who was a representative potato grower.* They informed this man that he had powdery scab, and told him he must not on any account use his potatoes for seed purposes, that he must get potatoes from some other person
where he would be sure that they would be free from disease. This particular person attached no importance to the instruction, and went on using his potatoes for seed purposes. He had two crops, and this autumn two other officials came along, visited his farm, and gave him a clean bill of health as having no powdery scab on his place, while some other farmers had it. A thing of that kind becomes well known in the surrounding neighbourhood, and it leaves everybody in doubt. I think the first officials must have been mistaken. The scab they saw must have been the old scab that was not at all dangerous.
Last autumn two gentlemen came to the province to lecture on this subject, Mr. Adams and Mr. Holmden. Mr. Adams, who was supposed to know a good deal about this disease, came from Ireland, where they have it very extensively. He lectured on the causes of the disease and the method of propagation. He told us that . a moist climate was favourable to its production, and also a soil in which lime naturally occurred. In the province of Prince Edward Island we have a moist climate; that would be against us; but our soil contains no lime. The other gentleman followed him the same night, and lectured on the prevention of the disease. He advised the farmers to spray their cellars or potato warehouses with a solution of formaldehyde or, in the absence of that, with a preparation of lime, which would kill the spores. We asked him to tell us why lime in the soil would propagate the spores and in the cellar would kill them-and we did not get an answer. I presume ther'e is an answer. These are the things that lead farmers to believe that these men do not know much about their subjects, after all. It would b'e better for the men sent out in that way to be thoroughly posted on their subjects before going to lecture people, becaus'e questions are sure to be asked. For my own information and for the information of others, I would be glad to know how lime in the soil will propagate that disease and lime in the cellar will cure it.

I could not attempt to answer all the expert or technical questions my hon. friend puts. I may say, however, that occasionally a good dose of whisky will save a man's life and perhaps if you give a dose of whisky to the next fellow it will kill him. It depends on the condition of the man.

And something on the
quality of the whisky, too.
Yes. I think that what my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) has said does not contradict anything I have advanced, and I hope that conditions will become more favourable very soon.

I notice that some of the members of the House are very anxious to have lecturers sent into their respective districts to instruct the farmers in the best methods of farming. I do not ask the minister to send any lecturers into our district. Our experience is that these gentlemen do not know much about farming. They may have spent a year or two perhaps in college and learned the names of vegetables and plants, but beyond that our experience is that those who come to our province know very little about practical farming. The consequence is that the farmers do not, in any number, go to hear them. The minister can save that expenditure so far as our province is concerned. Some few years ago a lecturer came to our province who advocated deep ploughing. He told the farmers that they had a second farm under the one they were using and that they could obtain access to it by deep ploughing and thus get virgin soil and much better crops. A year or two after that another man came along and condemned that absolutely. He opposed deep ploughing or much ploughing of any kind. He advocated surface cultivation.

What do you think about it?
.Mr. HUGHES: I am addressing my remarks to the chairman and the minister, who know what I am talking about. Another lecturer came to our province, I think last year, and a number of farmers went to listen to him. One man asked him what he would do to bring in a worn-out field, or worn-out land, and the prompt answer was: Sow clover on it. The minister knows well enough that that was no answer to give to a practical farmer, that the land would have to be well cultivated and in good condition before you could get a catch of clover. Yrou might as well sow the clover on the sea shore as on a worn-out field. Consequently practical farmers go away from meetings of that kind and doubt (everything they have hearu. I would therefore ask the minister to send a better class of men to our province, if he has any at all, and if he has not any of a better class, not to send any, and save that much expense. These are practical questions, and upon them I am sure the minister will agree with me.

Has the minister given up all hopes of having the embargo on our potatoes removed? This matter came up when the minister was away. The Minister of Customs stated in the House that the shipment came from New Brunswick, but the hon. member from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), who took part in the debate, was most positive that there was no powdery scab in that shipment at all; and what the minister now says confirms that statement. Have the American authorities extended that embargo to the whole of Canada?

Apparently they have, and apparently they are within their rights, because they explicitly stated that if any powdery scab was found they would restore the embargo. They find powdery scab undoubtedly, although in exceedingly small quantities, and after a great deal of trouble. I do not say that there is no hope of getting that embargo removed. On the contrary I am inclined to believe that in the course of not a very long time the attitude of the United States authorities, especially of the technical officers, will be entirely changed, and that they will come to the conclusion that the situation doss not warrant such drastic action.

Perhaps one of the officials could 'hand me the information, for members ame often asked these questions, even when going along on the train. Some of us who are interested in agricultural societies give special prizes to encourage the raising of various kinds of stock, milch cows, for instance, and dairy herds. Has the department any suggestion to make as to the best use that can be made of these prize distributions? For instance, I know of one member that gives [DOT]two prizes for the best dairy herd. The idea in giving a prize is to stimulate competition between the ordinary farmers as well as between the producers of the very finest stock, but we find that .the same people get the prizes every year, no matter how you change it around, and they are, of course, entitled to them because they exhibit the best herds. The only thing you
could do would be to Offer prizes to those who never got a prize before.

I thought of that, but
I had reference more to what we would exclude in a prize of that kind.
It is a pretty wide subject and I would be very glad to get suggestions with reference to it.
Dairying is becoming an important industry in my constituency, and I would like to know from the minister if he has had an application from Bonaventure for one of these cow-testing machines?

What we usually do is to try to find some district where the dairying industry is not quite up to the mark, where there are a sufficient number of cows, and where the people are anxious to bring their dairying up to the highest standard. We have now thirty or forty of these stations, and this year I do not think we can do any more than carry them on, although we hope to extend the work later. For the last year or two we have been reaching out to all districts possible, including many in Quebec, and in Ontario, and in the West. It does not follow that because there is an application for a dairy-record district that we establish one, because it means a great deal of expense and we have to cut our coat according to our cloth. A great many applications have come in with which we have not been able to deal.

The farmers in a county like that which I represent have a great many hardships to encounter which are not the lot of other farmers in Canada. The summer lasts for five months and the farmer has seven months of winter to face. In Bonaventure, ten or twelve butter factories have sprung up in recent years, and some are coming into existence in Gaspe county. The farmers are far removed from the markets; they have to depend on an out-of-date railway, the climatic conditions are severe in that part of the country, and the people are most certainly deserving of help from the Department of Agriculture.

I will bear that- in
mind.

I have before me a number of pamphlets issued by the Department of Agriculture, dealing with the dairying industry, cold storage, cow tests, ice on the farm, butter-making on the farm, and so on, and all these pamphlets contain most valuable information for the farmer. I find on inquiry at the department that the supply of this literature is very limited and that the system of distribution is, to my mind, inadequate. The members representing rural constituencies would, I believe, value most highly a generous supply of literature of this description. We do get a certain number of copies of the evidence taken before the Agricultural Committee of this House, but to my mind it is of little value from the educational point of view and only useful as an attestation of the fact that certain members attended that committee.
I should like to have 400 or 500 copies of each of the publications I have referred to for distribution throughout my constituency, but I have been informed by the department that some of them are out of print, and that the supply is not equal to the demand. Does not the minister think it would be in the interests of agriculture and of the country generally to spend a little more money in distributing a liberal supply of this literature, and possibly to economize on the printing and distribution of certain blue books which are worthless? *

I endorse the suggestion of my hon. friend t'hiat money spent by the Government in the publication and distribution of such pamphlets as he has mentioned would be far better spent than on a number of publications which are of no use whatever. Many of the blue books I receive go to the waste-paper basket; I

do not want to read them, and I have no place to put them, and the two copies of each being sent simply doubles the nuisance. The British Government print and distribute certain publications, such as the correspondence in connection with the war, which are issued at a mere nominal fee, and that is not a bad" idea. For example, t'be white papers of the French Government, which is quite a large volume, has been issued at the price of one penny. The members of this House receive a bound edition of the sessional papers. Since I have been a - member I have sent my copy to the University library where I can have access to it, and where the public can have access to it as well. I have let it be known in the public library and other places that these books are available there.
I believe that if some of our libraries were supplied with the sessional papers, and if the members of Parliament were not supplied with so many, it would be an improvement. The publications of the Department of Agriculture are, as a rule, very valuable, and I should like to see a wider distribution of them.

I believe that a great deal of public money is wasted in publishing and distributing Government reports that are not read by anybody. I and others have studied the matter, and I think it can be safely said that a saving of half a million dollars per annum could easily be made if more regard for economy were displayed in the distribution of these parliamentary publications. Only a few short days ago a report went through here, perhaps unnoticed, by which the usual allotment of the copies per member has been reduced to one. Henceforth for a year my hon. friend will not be burdened with more than one copy of each parliamentary publication. Apart from that a great saving can be effected, because there go to members of Parliament, newspaper offices and elsewhere a great many publications that they do not need and that are simply a burden to them. The Department of Trade and Commerce have a system by which they ascertain by means of return postcards whether their publications are desired or not, and the same rule could be applied to all parliamentary publications, so that no publications would go to those who did not desire them and had no use for them. I rose simply to tell my hon. friend that he will not be burdened as much as he was
before, although, even after this, he may be burdened more than he wants to be.

Some of the remarks
which have been made are absolutely true, although I think they apply more to the other departments than to the Department of Agriculture. The rule in the Department oi Agriculture is that every farmer in Canada, if he applies, can get all our literature; or if any member wants to give a list of the farmers to whom he would like to have it sent, they are put on our list and receive our publications. We find that is the only method to pursue, because if hon. members had to distribute our publications themselves, there would be a duplication and a lot of unnecessary work On our experimental farm list we have more than 80,000 names, and we issue more than 2,000,000 publications every year, and a lot of this matter is very highly appreciated and is doing a lot of good. If the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Dougilas) or the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Hugh Ol-ark) know of any people -to whom they want us to send thiis literature -we shall be only too glad to send it. We do not charge for doing so, because there is a feeling in Canada against paying for Government publications, and we have made a charge only in the case of some expensive publications, of which there is quite a limited issue.

My observations did not apply in any sense to the publications of the Department of Agriculture, because I have always found them excellent, and they are the class of publication for which I would like to see the -money provided.

Would the minister give me some information as to the scarcity of these pamphlets at present? I understand from one of the officers of the department that the supply has been practically exhausted, and that is why I wish the minister would have more of them published.

As a matter of fact, there is not a great call for many of the bulletins and they have been allowed to go out of print. This year, in consequence of the campaign we have been carrying on in connection with our agricultural work, there has been such an enormous demand for a number of the bulletins and pamphlets that the supply has been practically exhausted; but we are putting in fresh orders to have them issued again, so that, although in some cases there may be a -scarcity, we shall soon be able to remedy that.

One thing that should not be overlooked is that the same bulletin will not suit all sections of the country. Why not get those that will suit the different sections and publish more of them, and economize in that way? As far as blue books are concerned, the local newspapers which are supplied with all these documents, make very little use of them, and it would be better to have them sent by request. A great saving could be made in that way, and what was saved might be expended in increasing the issue of the agricultural bulletin which is so much desired by the people throughout the country.

I understand the hon. member has in the employment of his department a Mr. Giard, who is thoroughbred livestock commissioner. What are his duties and what is his remuneration? I understand that he has opened an office in Sherbrooke, and I would like to know the names of Ms employees, their salaries and their duties. I am asking for this not for the sake of criticism, but simply to know what has been done. My contention is that neither this Government nor any other Government has done what it should have done for the cause of agriculture; and any money legitimately and wisely spent for agricultural purposes will never have any criticism from me, because agriculture is one of the things that have been seriously neglected. If the minister cannot give me the information off-hand, if he will give it to me be-for the end of the session, I shall be satisfied.
I can give it to my hon. friend when we come to the live-stock vote. Mr. A. W. Giard is representative of the live-stock branch for Quebec.

Can the minister tell us if
any progress has been made in the manufacture of butter and cheese in the Eastern Townships, or is there an increased exportation of cream to the United States from the Eastern Townships?

1 am sorry I cannot
tell my hon. friend that off-hand, but I will try to get the information before I get through with my Estimates.

In the Montreal Gazette the statement is made that cream all the way from Stanstead through to Richmond was exported to the United States and that the farmers of that particular district proposed to ask the department to establish butter 
and cheese factories to off-set that exportation. The minister might also have that looked up.
Towards the encouragement of cold storage warehouses for the better preservation and handling of perishable food products, $200,000.
How is this work progressing?

This is exactly the same vote that we have always put in. It is paid in six instalments for the encouragement of cold storage industries under our control; that is, we have control of the rates and give for each warehouse a grant based on 30 per cent of the cost of construction, the plant having to conform to our specifications and the warehouse having to be a public utility. This work has been in operation for a great many years, and we are carrying it on along the same lines.
How many plants have you?

About twenty-six or
twenty-seven scattered throughout the country. The practice has been followed not to establish or encourage them in districts where they will conflict with cold storage plants that are serving a public purpose.
Is there one at Brockville?
Yes, it has had its fifth instalment. It was built at a total cost of $52,000.
What is the name of this company?
I have not the exact name. I will give my hon. friend the information this evening. I see that the fifth instalment is due in 1915, so they must have been established about five years ago.
What is the cost of the cold storage at Port Hawkesbury, and how many instalments are still due?
The cost is $200,000, and the third instalment is due in February, 1916.

I do not think there is any provision of that kind, for it is practically impossible to carry it out. Of course, we have control during the time the instalments are being paid, because we can refuse

to pay if they do not carry out the conditions on which the subsidy is paid. It' has had to be a question largely of good faith.
After the instalments are all paid, I fancy the Government has not much real control over the rates or operation of the plants.
I do not know that we have. Of course, we never had.
What is the position in regard to the cold storage establishment at Edmonton?
The third ',r'stalment is due in February, T916, so, apparently, two instalments have been paid.
Are there reports as to the operations of the establishment?
I presume that the cold storage commissioner would have that. We always send a man out before instalments are paid to see that everything is according to conditions.
What is the amount of subsidy paid to the cold storage plant at Port Hawkesbury?
It is 30 per cent on the cost, the cost being $200,000. It is at the same rate as the subsidy paid to others.

Will the payment of the balance depend on any inspection?
. Mr. BURRELL: Yes, we do not pay unless they conform to the requirements of the department.

I do not wish to take up more of the time of the committee than is necessary, but I am glad to speak a word on this subject, as it is one in which I am interested and I know that that interest is shared by all. The man in charge of this work is Colonel Hutchison, the commissioner, who has been in the service of the department for about fifteen years. The long experience he has had in connection with other exhibitions has served him splendidly in this case. Two years ago, when the subject of a Panama-Pacific exposition was first spoken of, we had two deputations, one from San Diego and one from San Francisco, asking Canada to take part. We came to the conclusion that it would be impossible to take part in more than one exhibition, and, after consideration, we decided that the San Francisco exposition would he the most important. At that time I suggested to the Prime Minister that if Canada took part in the exhibition there, especially in view of the colossal scale on which the exhibition was to be carried out, we must make a first-class exhibition or not exhibit at all. I got the consent of the Prime Minister and of my colleagues, and later on the support of the House, to a vote that amounts practically to twice what we have ever spent in an international exhibition before. I have just had the pleasure and responsibility of going to assist in the dedication of the Canadian building and have had the advantage of seeing what they were doing. I can only say that the exhibition is an extraordinarily important one. And, although the war is undoubtedly doing some injury to it in preventing attendance from Europe, they are getting a tremendous attendance from all over their own country and from South America and Canada; and perhaps on the whole, the attendance will justify the expectations of the promoters. The prime minister has just suggested to me that I should say something about the general character of the exposition. It is pretty hard to describe in a word an affair so big as this, for they have spent $18,000,000 to $20,000,000 in connection with the various buildings. Nearly every state of the Union has a separate building, some of them very expensive and very beautiful. Practically all the nations in the world, all the leading nations with the exception, I think, of Germany and. Austria, have buildings of their own and very large ex-

hibits. The French, the Italian and the Argentine exhibits are not quite ready; these nations are just completing their buildings. The other states and nations have their buildings practically completed and the exhibits installed.
So far as our own work is concerned, I have no hesitation in saying that not only has Canada the best exhibit it ever had at any exhibition, but it is quite evident we have been made the centre of attraction of the whole exhibition among the nations. We have the best exhibit and the best building, I think, of the whole exhibition.
Some hon members: Hear, hear.

If I felt justified in
taking up the time of the committee, I could give any amount of testimony to this, because Californians have been most generous in their praise, I do not think I can do better than read a couple of very short extracts from newspapers published in prominent counties in California devoted to fruit-growing. . . . I wish to read a portion of another article from the Fresno, California, Republican, as follows:
Every local booster in California ought to visit the Canadian building at the exposition, if for nothing but a visible demonstration that the best local advertising, is that which does not advertise the locality at all. Simply as an exploitation of the country and its resources, this Canadian building is incomparably the most skillfully presented exhibit on the grounds. I could give dozens of similar quotations, but I shall not weary the committee by reading them. Colonel Hutchison and the members of the permanent staff who have been doing this work for a great many years, deserve great credit for the work which they have accomplished in the face of tremendous competition. Colonel Hutchison has given the most loyal service. He has marked abilities for this special kind of work, and, to use a phrase that is understood by all men, he has made a killing, so far as >this particular undertaking goes-Tttie Canadian building was the only one in the grounds which was completed and ready on the very day the Fair opened. I should like to add my appreciation of the hospitality and kindness that was extended to me as a Canadian during my visit to the exposition and my attendance at the dedication ceremonies. Mr. D. C, ROSS (Middlesex West): I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a matter to which I referred this morning, and to which some weeks ago I called the attention of the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister. It is a matter of great importance to the province of Ontario, old Ontario particularly. The principle has been accepted by both parties that farmers and grazers whose animals must be slaughtered for the public good to prevent the spread of any contagious disease shall be compensated. The Act is, however, an old one, and the compensation that the Government is allowed to give by Order in Council under the Act is not at present in keeping with the prices of cattle and hogs. Insurance companies and railway companies have raised the maximum amounts that they will pay in case of the death of cattle, and I think the Government should not lag behind at this time, especially as we are to-day threatened in Ontario with a very terrible disease. At present all a farmer can get for a grade animal that has been slaughtered in the public interest is $40. The minister well knows that that is no compensation in that case. All he can get for the killing of a grade hog is $15, which is a wholly inadequate compensation. I made the suggestion to the Prime Minister some time ago that the Government might introduce an amendment to the Act, because I do not see that anything else can bring about the result I desire to attain. I do not think it is too late yet for the Minister of Agriculture to bring in such an amendment.

He could easily raise the limit of $60 to $110, and the limit of $15 to what he thinks proper. It may be that the Government will not have to pay these prices, because the foot and mouth disease may not get into the country; but at present there is alarm in regard to it, and I think the Government ought to take the necessary precautions before the disease reaches the country. I should judge from what the minister has said to me in conversation that his idea would be that if the disease should come into Ontario, compensation should be made to the farmers by a measure which would be made retroactive. If the session is so far advanced that it is impossible to amend the Act, the minister's statement to me is some solace; but I think that my suggestion would be a much better solution, and I would submit it to the consideration of the minister and the Government.
I wish to say a word also about the publications of the department. They are issuing some splendid publications. The only trouble I see about them is that the members are not able to get as many copies of those publications as they would like to distribute. On making application, I was told that I could get six. friend's conversation with me, while I did say that if the foot and mouth disease should unfortunately come into this country, necessitating the killing of cattle and the Act were altered, it would be made retroactive, I would not like to make any positive statement as to what alteration there might be. Of course, no man can say it is impossible, because there are at the present time, in spite of all efforts that have been made in the United States, 20 states under quarantine. The United States have killed about
100,000	animals, about 50,000 head of cattle and roughly about 50,000 hogs. Roughly speaking they have spent about $1,000,000 in compensation. Tiiat compensation is not fixed along the same line as ours because there the State bears one-half the

expense and the federal authorities the other half, and the State has usually fixed the appraisement of the value. I am not sure that it should not be raised on hogs as well.
