The time to take care of a situation is before it arises rather than afterwards. If we are in imminent danger, as we must be-
I do not think we are.

-as we must be in imminent danger of the spread of this terrible disease, it seems to me the minister and the House would do w ell to make such preparation as would seem to be necessary so that when it comes we will be in the very best position to deal with it. The principle of compensation to farmers for animals slaughtered in the public interest is, I fancy, something like this:	If the owner
of the diseased cattle is going to suffer the loss of his cattle because of the disease, he is impelled by the ordinary instincts of self-preservation to try to shove that loss off on to his neighbour, that is to say, he will try to dispose of the diseased animal. Compensation is granted so that he will not have that inducement; but, if the compensation is far below the valuation, the inducement still remains. As a matter of fact, the compensation has, measurably, if not actually, to be brought up to the valuation of the animal, or else the purpose of the compensation is in a large measure lost. But after all, the amount of the compensation is only a small part of the transaction. The great object is the prevention of the spread of the disease, and the tremendously greater losses that might follow because of it. I speak somewhat feelingly on this question of compensation, because in our part of the country tremendous losses have been suffered through diseased hogs; and I know whereof I speak when I say that the owner who suspects disease in his herd is inclined to escape from the loss by disposing of the animals to other parties. I am not prepared to say what should be done as to valuation in the case of hogs or cattle. But I am prepared to say this:	that in view of the imminent
danger to Canada of this terrible foot and mouth disease, this Parliament could not better spend its time than in making whatever preparations are adequate and possible to meet that contingency.

I do not regard the danger as imminent because, since the outbreak of the disease last October, the United States authorities have been working at it practically all the time, and every month has seen them in a much stronger position to prevent the spread of the disease. Our 132
restrictions are not relaxed at all: we are watching the matter very closely. I am glad to have heard my hon. friend speak as he has, because some people do not hold these views on compensation. It is a very big subject, and very debatable. For the administration and enforcement of the Meat and Canned Foods Act, $275,000.
What work is done under this vote?

This is to pay for the inspection and control of all the abattoirs in the country. As my hon. friend knows, under the Meat and Canned Foods Act no one in Canada can ship meat from one province to another or out of the country unless from an establishment which is under Government control an'd inspection. We maintain a staff of inspectors who see the animals killed and the distribution of the carcase, who f& fact watch the meat at every stage. Every diseased animal is condemned, and sometimes certain diseased parts only are condemned. This system 'of inspection ensures that nothing can be shipped from one province to another or out of the country unless it has been pronounced by the Government inspectors absolutely free from disease.
That does not apply to animals slaughtered for local sale?
No.
Even in the abattoirs?

At the abattoirs it would include everything. The legislation was enacted principally to protect our export trade, and it was then concluded that within its own boundaries a province might very well look after its own health and the inspection of meat. Some of the provinces have done so and some have not. If a firm like the Matthews Company or the Davies Company were killing and selling even in their own province, . nothing could come out of their establishments -that was not inspected.
Then there is nothing to prohibit any person else from killing and selling without inspection?
No.

There is one difficulty in connection with this inspection which I wish to bring before the attention of the minister. Recently, I understand, the

Militia Department has advertised for a supply of meat for the barracks and military college at Kingston, and it is stipulated that the meat to be supplied requires Government inspection. It seems to me that this is another way of saying that the only meat that can be supplied will be meat from Toronto or Montreal or places where these large abattoirs are, and, as a result, the people of the locality surrounding Kingston are excluded from tendering, unless, of course, they get their supplies from these large firms. In that way this inspection has a tendency towards creating a monopoly or centralization, which I do not think is fair. Government inspection was designed to protect our export trade, but if Government inspection is required for the supply of meat to Government institutions then there would appear to be no alternative but to get that meat from the large meat packers whose products are inspected. I think the Government should carry this inspection system further, and that inspectors should be appointed in different centres. In Kingston is located the Royal Military College, the barracks, the Kingston penitentiary, the Rockwood Asylum, and it seems to me that in all fairness to the people of the district they should have an equal show with the big companies to tender to supply meat to these institutions. Why could not the Government appoint competent men to inspect the meat in these centres, so that the farmers of the district might be able to sell to Government institutions.

In the province of Alberta the question of monopoly comes up in another way. Under the provincial Act all meat killed at the abattoirs of the Swift Packing Company or P. Burns & Company has to bear the Government inspection stamp, and the city of Edmonton has made a regulation that no farmer is permitted to sell slaughtered meat unless it is killed at these abattoirs where, of course, it necessarily must bear the Government stamp. The farmers claim that this has a tendency to create a monopoly and to prevent competition in the sale of meat. The provincial Act requires that the animal shall be slaughtered in these abattoirs and inspected by the officers of the Agriculture Department.
You will have to get after your provincial Minister of Agriculture.

The point is whether it is wise to have the regulations in connection 1321
with the sale of meat so stringent as to create a monopoly. The complaint of the hon. member for F-rontenac (Mr. Edwards) is that there are not enough meat inspectors and that a monopoly is in consequence created, but in Alberta the monopoly is created by having-too many inspectors.

The way out of it is to follow the example of the city of Toronto, which owns a municipal abattoir, from which the meat is supplied to all the local butchers. The city of Toronto has absolutely the best abattoir in Canada, and it has been a great success. There is no reason why the smaller towns sfiould not follow that example and have all the local cattle killed in a well-regulated local abattoir. The people are entitled to protection even more than trade is entitled to protection, and while I agree with the member foT Frontenac that there ought to be local inspectors, I see no means of remedying the difficulty other than by establishing municipal abattoirs.

It seems most peculiar that all the meats for export are inspected by Government inspectors, while a large proportion of the meats which are consumed by the people at, home are no-t inspected at all. As I understand it, the meats that are supplied to the soldiers in the London camp are not Government inspected, and I do not think that is right. I contend that it is an absolute impossibility for an inspector, no matter how efficient he may be, to detect from the dressed carcase whether the animal was diseased or not. When you come to look into the matter and find how many ani-

mals are really diseased and how many parts of these animals are diseased, it is quite a revelation., The percentage of meat killed in an abattoir that finds its way into the fertilizing plant is astonishingly large. I believe that Canadian^live stock are becoming more subject to disease from year to year, and I think the day is not far 'distant, when in order to protect the health of our people the Government will find it necessary to adopt still more stringent regulations.

I do not like the idea of our own people being supplied with uninspected meats, whereas we have to have government inspection of all meats exported from Canada. The quicker this matter is remedied the better it will be for all concerned.

They were told to leave the Canadian horse market alone until the Canadian Government had secured all the horses they required, so that the price should not be advanced against this Government. I do not know how far this statement is true, but I know that the purchasing agent of the British Government, stated to a member of . this House that that was the condition of affairs. If there is any truth in the statement, then this Government is guilty of malicious, almost criminal, injury to the horse breeders of this country. What is the use of spending money for the purpose of improving the live stock business of this country if the Government do not assist our stock breeders to secure a market when that market is available? There was an opportunity for our stock breeders to get rid of a surplus of animals, many of which were unfitted for farm work, but the Government. did not help them to secure that opportunity. So far from helping them, according to this statement they put obstacles in the way of our stock breeders availing themselves of a market which was brought to their door. The opportunity was turned away by the action of this Government. I want to be fair, but I want to tell the Minister of Agriculture and the Government that that is the feeling throughout a large part of this country both in the East and in the West. For some reason or other, while French and English buyers are plentiful in the United States and down as far as Texas, in Canada there is a woeful dearth in the demand for cavalry and artillery horses. If there is such an embargo placed on purchases from outside by this Government, it is up to this Government to take that embargo off at once; it is the duty of the Minister of Agriculture on whose shoulders rests responsibility to protect the interests of the agriculturist, the stock-breeder, and the farmer, to see that the embargo is lifted. The number of horses purchased or likely to be purchased by the Canadian Government is only a very small percentage of the number of horses which are for sale at present. Surely the stock-breeder and the farmer are not to be deprived of this' opportunity to get a good price for thair surplus stock, simply because the Canadian Government wishes to monopolize this market for themselves, so that they may purchase horses cheaper than they otherwise could. We all believe that our agricultural industry

is the most important in Canada; we believe that Canada is playing to-day its greatest part in the world's drama by the food supplies which it is able to furnish to the allied armies in Europe. If it be important, as it is important, and as the members of the Government tell us, it is important, that production should be stimulated in every possible way, then we must carry that proposition one step further and we must see that the necessary markets are found for this increased production. If this suspicion of which I have spoken is not well founded, then it is only fair and just to the Government that they should have an opportunity to make a full denial. We would like to know the truth about this.
We in the West have no fault to find with the price we have received for our -grain, but we know that up to date the horses we have sold have been sold at a very moderate and reasonable price. I believe that in Western Canada we have furnished horses for military purposes at a lower price than they have been secured for anywhere else in Canada or anywhere else in the United States. I know that the minister has been absent on foreign soil from his department for some weeks, and it is possible this has not been brought to his attention, but I tell him now that if he wishes to assist the live stock industry in this country-and he evidently is trying to do it under this vote for the improvement and development of the live stock industry-he must take the responsibility of seeing to it that iany farmer in Canada, who has a horse suitable for military purposes which he wants to place on the market, be not deprived of the opportunity to do so. I trust the minister will see to it that the Government will encourage foreign horse buyers to come to Canada even though it means that when the Canadian Government comes to buy the horses they require they may have to pay a few dollars more to the farmer who is entitled to this extra profit if he raises the right kind of horse.

As the representative of a ho.rse-growing province, I have had occasion to bring the matter referred to by the hon. member (Mr. Neely) to the attention of the Government on more than one occasion. If my hon. friend from Humboldt were as anxious to obtain firsthand information as he apparently is to create some sort of prejudice in the minds of the people against the Government, he

would have learned that the Administration has been acting in this matter absolutely along the line that one -would expect, having regard to our responsibilities as a part of the British Empire. I ventured to bring the matter to the attention, of the Prime Minister himself on two or three occasions, iand I found that there were many aspects of the case which, because of certain imperial responsibilities and international complications in connection with the matter, he could not even discuss with a member of Parliament, much less with Parliament itself. I was content that the matter should be left entirely in his hands, and I know that other members of the House who are conscious of the enormous responsibilities that the Government of Canada has to carry at this time, were content that the matter should be dealt with by the Prime Minister as best he could.
I am sure that no farmer in Western Canada and no citizen of Canada will believe that the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) is any more anxious that the farmers of Western Canada should sell their horses, than is the Government of Canada. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Neely) said that the Government maliciously did this.
I said if they did it, it was a malicious thing to do.

Very well, and in the
very next sentence the hon. gentleman referred to the proud place that Canada is taking in this war. If Canada is taking a proud place in this war, it is because those who are responsible for the Government of Canada are acting in accord and in unison with the Imperial Government at Westminster. So far as I have been able to ascertain, having brought the matter to the attention of the Government on behalf of the horse-breeders of Alberta, the action which the Government has taken is in harmony with the imperial responsibilites of Canada.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me what he means by the action which the Government has taken? What action did the Government take?

The Government, so far
as I could ascertain from the inquiries I have made, was not in a position to disclose to me or to this House everything that might be connected with military operations. I was advised, as other members of this House who inquired were advised, that the Imperial Government thought that it 'was not an opportune time to purchase
horses in Western Canada, but that because of certain international possibilities horses [DOT]were being purchased elsewhere for the present. I was assured, not only by the Government but by a British officer whom I met, that we who live in Western Canada need not have the slightest fear but that every possible facility will be afforded us in due course to sell every horse we have that is suitable for military purposes or for any other purpose. That I believe to be so, and I accepted it because I believe that the Government is as well seized with a sense of its responsibility as is any private member of this House. The Government being possessed of large information wlhich we could not ask it to furnish us with, and which in the ordinary course of events it could not very well furnish to us, I conveyed to my constituents and to the people of the province in which I reside the information that everything that could be done by this Government, in view of the position we occupy, would be done in due course to give them an opportunity to sell their horses. That I believe to be the case. Perhaps Alberta is the greatest horse-producing part of Canada; but I have ascertained from inquiries I have made that the Ihorses we now have upon the ranges are not fitted without a great deal of training for either artillery, transport or cavalry purposes, and our ranchers are now training their horses, because an untrained horse that will shy at an automobile is not exactly the kind of horse to place near tfhe firing line beside big guns. In the ordinary course of events, a transport horse is not a very good transport animal if, coming into a city, he is afraid of an automobile. What would he do when he would be close beside the operations that are being carried on on the plains of Belgium or France? It requires months and years of training to make a cavalry horse. As regards the number of horses purchased, the hon. gentleman must have been misinformed, because horses have recently been purchased, not in hundreds but in thousands, in the western provinces. The number of. horses assembled at Brandon a!t one time was 1,800, and more are about to be purchased for the third contingent. The first thing we Ibave to do in Western Canada to find a market for our horses is to have them trained for transport, cavalry and artillery purposes, and my hon. friend from Maeleod (Mr. Warnock) will bear me out that the range

horse is not very well adapted for the purposes that I have mentioned. I am also informed that as the war progresses, the class of horses we have on our plains will be in the greatest demand, although just now that it is not the class that is required. In due course, if we faint not, our horses will command the highest possible price, and there will be no reason for us to have any complaint because of lack of opportunity to sell. The farmers that I have met in Western Canada, when they have understood the situation, have not ventured to complain in the terms in which the hon. gentleman has; but they have been content to accept the assurance of wie Government that every possible effort is being made to assure a ready sale for our horses consistent with the demands upon us by reason of the military operations of the Empire and its Allies.
I am sure 1 am very gratified to the hon. member for Calgary for his explanation-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to say a few words before he goes on. He will realize that the allied powers, in regard to horses, as to which the wastage is enormous, had to look pretty far ahead in the early months of the war, and certain arrangements were made, which I am not at the moment free to disclose to the House, hut which I would have no objection to mention privately to my hon. friend or to any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House; indeed, I have already communicated them to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), who desired some information on the subject. Not only was that the case, but it came to our attention some two or three months ago that the horses required by the various allied powers were not always horses of the same type or class; that one power, for example, might find use for horses which would not be required in the service of another power. Arrangements had to be made, as I understand, between the powers, as to where the provision of horses that would be required could be obtained, and with those arrangements, which were arrived at under a very distinct understanding, we could not very well presume to interfere. We did, however, make the suggestion some four or five weeks ago that there was a certain class of horses in Canada which were not required by one of the powers, but which might be found very useful for the purposes of another power, and that notwithstanding the

arrangements first entered into to which I have no more than alluded, we hoped it might be possible that an opportunity might be given for the purchase in Canada of horses of that type by the power to which I have last referred. The arrangements and conditions which have been brought to our attention are not only of a confidential, but , to a certain extent of a very complicated character, and I hope my hon. friend will do us the justice of believing that it has been our greatest desire to bring about a condition of affairs under which the farmers of Canada, whether in the East or in the West, will have an opportunity to dispose of their horses at remunerative prices. I would be very glad to supplement what I have said in a private interview with my hon. friend, if he will be good enough to give me an opportunity.

I am sure I am very
gratified for the trouble the right hon. the Prime Minister has taken to give us some explanation in regard to the situation, and I quite understand that there may be conditions surrounding this matter that cannot very well be given to the public or even to this House; but the information which was given to me and on which I based my remarks a few moments ago was not along the lines of the information given by my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and just now by the Prime Minister. My information was that the British Government actually sent their agent to Canada to purchase horses, and that the Canadian Government, wishing to retain the Canadian horses for itself, had requested the British buyers not to pursue the purchasing of horses on Canadian soil until the Canadian Government had itself secured at fair and reasonable prices a sufficient number with which to equip the Canadian contingents. If the Government says that there is no truth in that report, that settles the matter so far as I am concerned, and I am certainly quite ready and prepared to take the word of the Prime Minister to that effect. The Prime Minister was not here when I referred to the widespread impression that the Government of Canada was responsible for the withdrawal from Canada of British horse buyers, because of the necessity of the Canadian Government tp secure a sufficient quantity of horses at a reasonable price, which price of course, would be enhanced if this Govern-had to compete with the purchasers for the British and French Governments. If the Prime Minister will tell us whether that

information is right or wrong, that will clear up the matter so far as I am concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is no doubt whatever that persons who have been commissioned to purchase horses for the expeditionary forces wished to be in a position in which they could be absolutely certain of securing a sufficient number of the requisite type, not only to supply the first needs of the forces tout also to make good the enormous wastage that must necessarily take place as soon as these forces arrived at the front. But I can, I think, explain to my hon. friend that there was another predominating cause which led to the withdrawal, temporarily, from Canada of the British buyers. I should not feel free to enter into the reason for it tonight, but at some future day I may he able to explain it to the House. It would not be proper to do so at the moment, though I should have no objection to communicating it privately to my hon. friend, if he desires to know it.
Would the Prime Minister say if the Government has prohibited the exportation of Canadian horses to the United States?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With respect to horses and also with respect to other animals and commodities that were of a certain character, such as might make them useful to an enemy if they came into their possession, or the exportation of which might weaken the resources of the Empire for the purpose of carrying on the war, we received suggestions early in the succession of events after the outbreak of hostilities, and have received such suggestions from time to time since, from the Imperial Government; and with few exceptions -I think with no exceptions, but sometimes after a discussion by cable-we have carried out the view which they thought would be essential for the welfare of the Empire and the maintenance of our strength for the great conflict in which we are engaged. My recollection is that the exportation of horses, and other articles as well, was prohibited except to British possessions. There is an enormous list of articles embraced in the different orders in council. The same course was pursued here as was pursued in Great Britain. Recently, in Great Britain, all these Orders in Council have been consolidated into a general Order in Council for the purpose of convenience.
We have been engaged during 9 p.m. the last three or four weeks in consolidating our various Orders in Council, and the work is now practically done, so that we hope at a very early day to pass an Order in Council which will give a complete list of the articles the exportation of which is prohibited, whether to all countries other than British dominions or to specified countries. I might explain that arrangements have been made with the Imperial Government by which a certain discretion is to be exercised by the Governor in Council or a minister of the Crown, with regard to the exportation of certain articles-or the importation of certain articles, for that matter. If it should appear that the exportation of certain articles generally prohibited, is important for certain reasons to a particular country for a stated period or for some particular purpose, the Governor in Council or the minister may have the right to issue a license for that exportation. On the other hand, it has been found sometimes essential to permit the importation from German or Austrian sources of certain articles essentially necessary for some institution in this country, for instance, an agricultural college, or for the purposes of some industry in Canada, the maintainance of which is important in the public interest. These instances, however, are only occasional occurrences, and for the most part, the Orders in Council passed have been strictly observed and have not been departed from except with the general or special sanction of the Imperial authority.

The toon, member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) was in good company when he found fault with the Government for sending British buyers to the United States. I have heTe a copy of the Winnipeg Telegram which also finds fault because the British Buyers were sent to Chicago to buy horses. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) apparently did not quite know what sort of horses were required for cavalry purposes, or what sort were bought in the United States. He made the statement that the Alberta horses were not suitable, nor trained, for cavalry purposes. He is in conflict with the Winnipeg Telegram, for they make a statement that the horses bought in Chicago are wild horses from the southwestern prairies and that the stock men there have secured cowboys to train, them.
They train them in the yard after taking them from the prairie.
Not always.

That is the statement in the Winnipeg Telegram. Accepting the statements from the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and ithe Minister of Agriculture (Mir. Burrell) that they are responsible for comparatively few horses having been purchased by these British buyers in Canada so far, would it not be fair to the Canadian farmer, especially as he has carried his horses through the winter, at a time when oats were higher than they have been for many years in Canada, and hay also high and scarce, to advance the price for the horses bought hereafter in Canada? The price paid for the military horses that were bought is an arbitrary price fixed by the buyer, and the farmer was simply told he might take it or leave it. I do not -now find fault with that, for perhaps that is the only way it could be done. But would not the Government take it into consideration that the farmer has carried that -house through the winter though he could have sold his oati at a profit, and that he is entitled to a profit on the horse.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think there is force in what the hon. member suggests. I am not sure that the price is arbitrarily fixed at the present time. My recollection does not -agree with the statement of the hon. gentleman though I do not wish to speak with certainty, because it is only an impression, though a distinct impression. Of course, my hon. friend will understand that a Government buying a large number of horses over a great stretch of territory such as is comprised within Canada must endeavour to be pretty careful to get value for the money. It is said-I am not very familiar with the subject myself-that one may not always get good value unless he keeps his eyes open. I do not think that buyers have gone elsewhere, solely for the reason which the hon. gentleman suggests; indeed, I know to the contrary. But inasmuch as, owing to causes upon which I shall not
TMr. Robb.]
dwell at the moment and to which it is not desirable that I should refer, our farmers have kept and fed their horses during the winter, I really agree with the hon. gentleman that this is a circumstance which may fairly be taken into consideration, -and I think it will be taken into consideration.

Would it not be wise, now that the farmers are promised a market for their horses, for the Department of Agriculture to establish some sort of bureau by which the Government would (have information -as to the approximate number of horses there are available in Canada at the present time for war purposes? I understand that three weeks after the outbreak of war there was not a horse for sale in England, for the reason that a bureau (had been established and upon the outbreak of the war men were sent in every direction and all available horses in the whole country were picked up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member means that they took a census of the horses.

Yes, the facts concerning marketable horses are kept on record, as I understand it. I think that a somewhat similar system should be adopted in this country. I had occasion to go to Montreal to satisfy myself as to the situation with regard to horses, and I had the privilege of looking over 1,030 horses whidh- were turned into two large yards. As many of these horses had come from my own county, I asked the gentleman in charge what the cost of the horses was to the British Government, and I was amazed to hear that they were -paying $185 plus $5 for every horse in these yards. Horses may be taken from Glengarry to Montreal -at a cost of $1, and the -amount paid the Glengarry man for one of these horses was only $110 or $115, by reason of the fact that there was no competition. The matter was entirely in the hands of the gentlemen who came into the county to buy the horses. As hay and grain were scarce, the farmers were obliged to let the horses go at whatever they could get for them. The result was that for good, sound, young horses, suitable for military purposes, -the farmers obtained only $110 or $115. If you place the purchase of horses in the hands of any one man, he will take advantage of the situation and pay the farmers whatever he thinks fit. If the farmers had received the amount paid by the British Government for -the horses delivered in Montreal, they would be perfectly satis-

fled, but there was a difference of $65 in respect of every horse that left my county between the price paid to the person selling and the price paid in Montreal. While I was there I asked this gentleman also why he and his associates were leaving Canada- they were leaving next week-'and I was informed that they were leaving at the request of the Canadian Government, who had asked them to discontinue purchasing horses in Canada. He explained to me, when I asked him why this should be, that the Dominion Government required horses for their own military purposes in Canada, and that it would be unwise for the British Government to go into competition with them until such time as the Canadian Government should secure what horses they themselves required. It was pointed out that the price of horses would naturally be increased by competition. I do not propose to make any charges; I am willing to accept the statement of the Prime Minister that there was good reason for doing that, but if that is the situation, it is a serious matter, and one to which the Government should give their immediate attention. The price of horses should be allowed to advance, because at the present time an opportunity is offered by which we can restore this important industry to its proper standing. Unless you allow the British and French Governments to come into the market and buy up the surplus horses in Canada, after the war is over the price of horses will drop too low to make their sale profitable to the Canadian farmers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not absolutely clear as to the average price that has been paid for horses in Canada by the Canadian Government, but I am quite sure that it is much higher than the price mentioned by my hon. friend; I think it runs up to $170. I can assure my hon. friend that we have really had a great many complaints from various sources in the country because the Government insisted upon buying direct from the farmer instead of from dealers. I myself have been assailed with a great many complaints in this respect. It has been the policy of the Government to buy horses direct from the farmer, and if any different practice has been pursued in my hon. friend's county, I should like to know of it and to make inquiry. Sir Adam Beck has had charge of the purchasing of horses in Ontario, and 1 have seen him three or four times in regard to the matter. He assures me that the
policy of the department has been carried out throughout the province of Ontario.

I was referring to the purchase of horses by the British Government, and to the fact that there was a large difference between the price the farmer received and the price the British Government paid. I was suggesting that tne Government should look into this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was under
the impression that my hon. friend was referring to horses purchased by the Canadian Government. I do not deny that the persons who have been commissioned to buy horses for the Canadian Government were veiy anxious indeed that they should have an opportunity of obtaining a sufficient supply for the Canadian expeditionary force and of making some provision for wastage. The idea was that the horses lor our own expeditionary forces should be purchased in Canada and that a condition should not be brought about under which we would have tc go to some other country to obtain horses of the requisite type. So far as the purchase of horses by British buyers in the United States is concerned, three causes for this were operating. To these I have already alluded; I should be very glad to explain them to my hon. friend, and I am sure that he would recognize the force of them.
I have had several communications with purchasers of horses for the Canadian Government, more especially with Sir Adam Beck, as to having the British and French Governments come into this country and purchase horses, and I have endeavoured, to the best of my ability, to bring about an arrangement under which that could be done, so that the Canadian owner of horses should have the best possible opportunity to dispose of his animals at a remunerative price. While everything in that connection may not have been perfectly satisfactory in the past, for reasons which I have not fully stated, but to which I have alluded, I am strongly in hopes that in the future the conditions may be improved and that we may give to the Canadian farmer opportunities even more abundant than in the past of disposing of his animals.

Does my right hon. friend think that the department bought directly from the farmers after the appointment of Six Adam Beck or before? I think since his

appointment they have done so, but not before.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not speaking of the horses for the first contingent. I am not absolutely sure of that, but as soon as it was possible for us to make arrangements, after the strain and hurry and confusion of the early part of the war, the policy was proposed by the Minister of Militia to myse'lf and the other members of the Government that the purchases should be made direct from the farmers. We all acquiesced in that and that policy has been carried out ever since.

The horses bought in Nova Scotia were not bought directly from the farmers. It has been proven in the Public Accounts Committee that middlemen were employed in Nova Scotia and when the middleman had collected a certain number of horses he turned them over to the Government and a cheque was issued to him for a large amount of money to pay for the horses. It does not seem that the money that was paid to the middleman was the same as was paid to the farmer. There is no evidence of that before the committee. The evidence, in fact, is the other way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend must be alluding to some horses purchased in the early weeks of the war for the first contingent. The purchase of horses in the Maritime Provinces has been under the direction of Sir Adam Beck and has been carried on by persons selected by him. I am quite sure that the arrangement to which I have alluded has been carried out in Nova Scotia as elsewhere.

This matter is one of very great importance and it is evident that there is a condition whereby the farmers of Canada have not profited by the sale of horses to the extent they might reasonably have expected. The responsibility for this fact seems to be somewhat difficult to fix. Whether it was the policy of the Government of Canada, or whether the Government of Canada was merely carrying out the policy imposed on it by the Imperial Government, does not seem to be altogether clear. I would have understood from the statement of the Premier a few minutes ago that it was the policy of the Government of Canada that other buyers should not buy horses in Canada until the needs of the Canadian Government had been supplied. That was a matter of Canadian policy, not a matter of Imperial policy. Whatever the policy of the Imperial Government which was im-

posed upon the Government of Canada might be, we are quite willing to accept the judgment of the Imperial Government in that matter, provided due representations were made to the Imperial Government as to the conditions which existed and which were to be met in Canada by the Government of Canada. There being a superabundance of horses in Canada and an underabundance of money, it was desirable that there should be an exchange of horses for money wherever that could be satis-actorily accomplished, and it was, I take it, the business of the Government of Canada to place that Canadian situation emphatically before the Imperial authorities, so that it would be only in case the greater and more pressing needs of the Empire had to be met that the Canadian farmer would be forced to hold his horses through an expensive winter, with the probability of not being able to get better prices in the spring. We appreciate the necessity and the propriety of regulations being framed to the end that supplies or materials of any kind that might be of use to an enemy country should not be acquired by that country from Canada by indirect means. To that end regulations have been framed which apply to horses. But why should regulations be framed to apply to horses when such regulations are not framed to apply to nickel, which is just as much a necessity of war as horses, and is not only as much a product of Canada, but is very much more exclusively a product of Canada than are horses. While I do not wish to unduly criticise the Government at this time, I do not think I would be acting fairly by the people whom I represent if I did not say here and now that, as the ease has been placed before the House this evening, it does not appear to me that the Government has acted with the consideration towards the interests of the farmers of Canada that might reasonably have been expected. .

I wish to say a few words on this subject, because the various gentlemen who have spoken have confused four or five different episodes or occasions. It happens that I was here when a general officer of the British Empire was sent out first in connection with the purchase of horses. I know him very well, he has been many years in the British army, but he is a Canadian born, and I fancy there are thousands of people in this country who know him. The gentleman who opened this argument charged the Government here with some neglect in connection with his visit. The gentleman to whom I refer did

not come out to act for the Canadian Government; he was sent out by the British Government to see how far horses could be procured here for the British army. He went to Toronto, and, as he is a Canadian, he knows all about our part of the country.
I was asked by a member of the Government if I would go to Toronto and see this general officer and offer him any assistance I could afford him in the way of directing him to people he should see, or anything of that kind. I did see him. He had opened an office in Toronto, and had a small staff of junior officers with him, and was getting ready to buy horses. He was not asking this Government what he should pay for horses or anything of that kind; he knew all about that, I fancy, a great deal better than this Government or any member of this House. He is a thorough soldier, acquainted with his business. I had an interview with him. He was very thankful to the Government for having asked me to go to him and give him any assistance I could in the way of directions about seeing people, and I had a talk with him. He asked me to come and see him again. I saw him a few days afterwards, but I found that his orders had been countermanded.
They did not ask permission from this Government to countermand the orders, they simply changed their directions, and very much because of some change in the sale of horses in the United States, with which this Government had nothing to do and nothing to say. The gentleman at once found that his object in coming was cancelled, and he went home. If any one wants to know his name I can give it. It is a well-known name in Canada. The gentleman is not in any sense a Canadian officer or a Canadian official, but an officer in the British army. That is all there is to that part of the story, and all the rest of the story has been built on that. The horses that have been spoken of were not the horses that that officer of the British army was sent out to buy. All that came long after he went home.

We are discussing an item of $550,000-an increase of $150,000 over last year-for the development of the live stock industry. The Government is asking for this large amount of money and for this large increase for the purpose of developing the live stock industry. I 'do not know how you are going to develop the live stock industry unless you provide a market for the sale of the live stock after it has been produced. What is the use of producing live stock unless you can
dispose of it, and dispose of it profitably?
I do not wish to criticise the Government unduly, but, since my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has rushed to their rescue so valiantly, let me point out to him that if the British buyer came to Canada to get horses for the British army and afterwards was instructed by the Imperial authorities not to buy horses in Canada, it was certainly up to the Government of Canada to make strong and urgent representations to the Imperial Government that we had for sale in Canada horses that would be suitable for war purposes and which we would be very glad to sell.

Does the hon. gentleman not see that he has overlooked what I have said? Because of what happened in the United States, this officer got instructions from home not to buy horses in Canada. Having received those instructions his duty as an officer of the British army was to go home, and he did so.

This Government has
agents for the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the British Isles, and we have a Department of Agriculture whose business it is to promote the live stock industry. If we have any purpose at all in promoting that industry, surely it was the duty of the Government, with all tlhis multitude of councillors and means of publicity and argument, to represent to the Imperial Government that when they wanted to buy horses ' Canada certainly had horses that she wanted to sell. Does the hon. member- for Hamilton wish us to conclude that tlhe Government of Canada did not make any such representation?
I wish you to conclude that an officer of the British army came out here to buy certain horses. He had orders from home not to buy, and Ihe went home. I cannot say any more than that.

Perhaps the minister could give us some information about federal assistance to the horse breeding industry. I notice that the regulations fix the minimum service fee at not less than $12. Is that a misprint? Should minimum read maximum?

I will refer to that in a moment. Just before dinner I promised to get some information for tihe hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) in regard to the butter and cheese industries. He asked me if our cheese was sustaining its reputation, and what was the condition

in regard to exports. The report of our Commissioner is that the production is as it was a year ago. The exports of cheese for the nine months ending December, 1914, were 134,108,000 pounds. The home consumption is increasing. Our cheese never stood higher than it does at present. It is in a class by itself, so far as the export trade is concerned. Canadian butter, speaking generally, is improving in quality. Our exports are more than they were a year ago. Up to December, 1914, we exported 2,283,197 pounds, as against 1,011,653 pounds the previous year.
An increase of 100 per cent.

The .percentage is very gratifying. Our imports are heavier than our exports, but not quite so heavy as they were the previous year. My Ih'on, friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) asked me a question about the exports of cream. In the nine months ending December, 1914, we exported 1,776,000 gallons. This question is more or less related to the butter question, and my hon. friend will no doubt draw his own conclusions. The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) asked me a question about Mr. Giard. Mr. Giard is not exactly the Live Stock Commissioner for Quebec. He is a representative of the Live Stock Branch in the province of Quebec, and performs such duties as are assigned to him by the Live Stock Commissioner at Ottawa. He is principally engaged in the distribution of live stock to associations. He inspects the various associations, and also the animals that have been purchased and sent to them. He has recently been assisting in the organization of our lecture work in connection with the Patriotism-and-Production campaign in the province of Quebec. His headquarters are at Sherbrooke. His salary is $1,800 a year. He has no office, and no assistants. The hon. member for Renfrew also asked me a question about a cold storage company in Broekville. The contract was entered into with the St. Lawrence Produce Company, which has been reorganized and is now known as the Whyte Packing Company. In reply to my hon. friend from Huntingdon, the minimum service fee is not less than $12. I presume that he is familiar with the general scheme as outlined in this little pamphlet.

Yes, I have one of those.
My objection is that the Government are

practically raising the service fee by $2. I understand that the general fee throughout the country, at all events in our section, is $10 except where there is an extra good horse.
My hon. friend's district is much more fortunate than the West as regards really high-class animals.

We produce high-class animals in that part of the country. The objection I have to this is that the Government are giving a preference to the breeding of remounts. They are paying only $4 towards encouraging the breeding of draught horses that will sell anywhere from $200 to $250, while they are paying $4.80 to encourage the breeding of remounts that, as has been proved here to-night, will sell for from $110 to $175. It seems to me that the minister might very well revise that policy.

I discussed that matter very thoroughly with the Live Stock Commissioner last year and I am perfectly certain that it was after consultation with the men interested in the stimulation of the horse industry throughout the country that this scheme was finally adopted. It is a little on the lines of the English scheme. The 40 per cent for thoroughbred mares was partly a concession to the fact that remounts might be necessary. There was a great deal of criticism, some of it is possibly harsh and some of it possibly deserved, of the system which was in vogue before we took office, and as the feeling of the House seemed to be against it we adopted this modified form of assistance in regard to remounts which, in view of existing circumstances, was warranted. As to the general merits of the scheme I frankly admit that I cannot discuss it as intelligently as I should like to because it is some time since I have had an opportunity of looking into it. It was my earnest desire that the Commissioner of the Live Stock Branch should consult the horse people of the country, to get the best information he could, with the idea of giving that assistance which was most needed and most likely to improve the breed of horses. There may be some demerits, and I shall bear in mind the suggestions of my hon. friend and take them up with the Live Stock Commissioner.
Will the minister explain why a minimum service fee is fixed?

The chief object of that was to encourage the finest type of sires.

I do not know how it is in Quebec, but I know that in British Columbia, to get anything like a valuable sire, the service would be twenty-five dollars.
Mr. -GRAHAM: Has the minister any suggestion to offer as to the establishment of a bureau for taking the census of available horses in the country?

That is done in Great Britain by the War Office, and you can understand how in a small country like England which is not larger territorially than one of our western constituencies, the War Office, with its splendid machinery, can get accurate information. For Canada, so enormous in extent and with divided jurisdiction, there would, I think, be great difficulty in getting an adequate census of the available horses, but I shall have our officers look into it.
It might be done through some machinery in the different counties.
It might.

One of the members of the Horse Breeders' Association spent an hour impressing on me the idea of having a bureau for a census of horses, but I got more light to-night on the subject from the few remarks made by the hon. member for Glengarry than ever I had before.

If application is made to
the department for a bull, does the department take any steps to see what kind of animal is sent?
That is left to the association; usually we send whatever breed they ask for.
Is that wise?
I think so. If we started to dictate to the association what kind of animal should be sent, we would run up against serious criticism.
It should conform to the type of animal in the locality.
There are a great many localities in which they have not developed along special lines, and usually w<e send them the particular breed they prefer.
Generally speaking, is the quality of horses in Canada improving?'
I think it is.

In some parts of Ontario we have a splendid type of horse, while in others there doe's not seem to be any interest 133
taken in the horse-breeding industry. I remember that some years ago I was interested in exhibitions and I declined to allow prizes to be given in certain classes, for the reason that the judges allowed a horse that was not a carriage horse to be entered in that class because there were no other entries, but the Provincial Government which controls the exhibitions, has restricted that kind of thing in later years. I know two or three of our enterprising horsemen who lost a good deal of money in importing horses in an endeavour to improve the stock, and I look with a good deal of favour on any -aid that can be given to bring about a general improvement of the standard of different classes of horses. I am glad to see the Government moving along the line of improving horse-flesh, because I am very fond of a good horse and it is very important that it should be impressed on those who raise horses that it is easier to feed a good horse than a scrub, and a good deal more interesting, because the good horse shows some return for the care you give him. I have been very much interested, having attended some of the gatherings with the minister at different times and listened to the discussions. That is one jf the reasons why I referred to th-e question about the bureau, because I heard it discussed and it impressed -itself upon me. As I understand it, we have in Canada-I am speaking more particularly of the province in which I hve -different associations. There is the association of breeders of Clydesdales and Percherons, and there are associations of the breeders of the other different standard-bred horses. Have they each a different grant?
They all belong to the Canadian Live Stock Record.
Approximately how much does the horse industry get from the Dominion treasury every year?
I would not say that offhand, because as a matter of fact we give a lump sum to the Canadian Live Stock Record for the purpose of assisting the Record in keeping the breeds pure.

Does the department do anything in the way of education along the line of this new policy of supplying purebred animals; that is to say, does the department contemplate doing anything in the way of sending out men from the department to size up the situation through



Canada generally? How far does the minister propose t-o go with this policy?

We have officers who are following up this work in every province. As my hon. friend can understand-and I very much appreciate what he has said in connection with that work-the forming of tihese associations is an educational work in itself, and by following it up and inspecting the animals and answering continual questions in regard to the policy, we find it is educational work from the top to the bottom. We have such a tremendous response from all parts of the country, especially from the more newly settled portions, that it is pretty bard to keep up with the work.
What proportion of male animals are purchased in tlhe province in which they are distributed?
I cannot give the figures offhand. I can get it from the Live Stock Branch for the hon. member.

I have heard for
some time past that a large proportion of the animals distributed in each province is purchased in that province.

So far as possible we
have adopted that principle.

I think my hon. friend
is quite right, and the policy will work out in that way. We have adopted the principle of trying to encourage the breeders in the various provinces by buying their horses. Where we cannot do so, we generally have to fall back on the province of Ontario, which is so celebrated for its livestock production. If we buy in the other provinces, it simply means the stimulus of the breeding trade in Ontario, which goes out to the other provinces the more animals that are distributed. I think Ontario will reap some benefit indirectly.

Am I correct in
stating that the prices in the other provinces are higher than in Ontario?

I cannot speak positively about that, because I have not the figures.
Arts and Agriculture-to enforce the Seed Act, to test seeds for farmers and seed merchants, to encourage the production and use of superior seeds, and to encourage the production of farm and garden crop, $140,000.
What is the increase?

The amount is practically the same as that of last year, except that there is a little increase in the maintenance of seed laboratories for purity and germination tests. The work is increasing all the time; we are testing a very large number of samples sent from all parts of the country, and it is doing such a tremendous amount of good that we want to increase the strength of our laboratories. Then for seed inspection and enforcement of the Seed Control Act, including salaries and expenses of temporary inspectors, there is an increase from $12,000 to $15,000, and there is also an increase in the subventions to growers of field roots and certain garden seeds. We are doing something in the way of encouraging the production of high class seeds, so that we shall not have to depend so much upon supplies from outside. Otherwise, the work is practically the same. We are carrying on the same system of assistance, giving subventions to seed fairs and so on; that is

giving a proportion of the prize money that is given by the various provinces. We base the subventions, on the acreage under crop and the number of fairs held, and we also give supplementary assistance. The subventions have been immensely appreciated by the provinces.

The provinces hold the
seed exhibitions?
Yes, and we give them the subventions.
Has the minister's attention been drawn to the possibility of a scarcity of small seeds owing to the war in countries from which we have been importing seeds?

Yes, we have been looking into that matter, and it is for that reason a good thing that we have been giving subventions and assistance for the production amongst our own growers of such seeds, and we are getting very encouraging results.

What is this?

with the Agricultural Instruction Act, the agreements with all the provinces and the work connected witlx it ot inspection of the agreements and following up the work that is done.
There is no friction between the Government and the provinces?

Grant to Dominion Exposition, $50,000.
Who gets this $50,0.00 this year?

Last year that vote came by rotation to British Columbia. They were advanced one-third of the amount, something less than $17,000. But afterwards t'he Militia Department took possession of their exhibition building, and on account of the breaking out of the war they found it hopeless to attempt an exhibition. So they asked if I would let it stand over and give them the balance of the money this year. This year, by Tights, it would have gone to Nova Scotia- Halifax has put in a strong plea for it. It has been practically arranged, subject to the vote of the House; but there is a little doubt whether British Columbia or Nova Scotia would go on with it this year or next year. I think it will have to depend upon the developments of the war. As the vote is here, I think we had better leave it and see how it works out.
What has become of the proposition for a Winnipeg World's exhibition?

I have not heard anything about that.
Quarantine-salaries and contingencies of organized districts and public health in other districts, $225,000.

What relation has the medical department to the Conservation Commission? Can the minister tell me what

work the Commission of Conservation is doing in connection with public health ?_

I am afraid I cannot. Their work is generally of an investigative kind, with a view to use educationally and in the activities of the several departments. They carried on certain work with illustration farms, but they will drop that, feeling that it is better to leave it with the department. I suppose their medical work has nothing to do with the quarantine, but is rather work of investigation and education.

Has the Government
made up its mind as to the establishment of a health department with a medical man at its head? That has been discussed for a long time. Occasionally we see in the press that changes are to be made in the Cabinet, that a member of the Government is to be shifted to the head of a new health department and another gentleman appointed in his place. The country is anxious about this. Can the minister give us any information ?

Not any definite information. The matter has been under advisement. But, under the pressure of work, which seems to have been the lot of this Administration for the last year or two, these reorganizing matters have been left in abeyance. In Heaven's good time, I suppose, we shall be able to consider the matter.
I suppose we can take it for granted that a gentleman could be found willing to accept the management of that department?
Possibly.

I desire to speak of a matter which was brought forcefully to my attention a few weeks ago. The health of the people, whether conserved by Governments, by commissions or by
10 p.m. their own good common sense, is intimately bound up with the life insurance business. At a recent meeting I attended, one of the most interesting papers I have ever heard was read by a lady. She had entitled that paper "Live a little longer." I have brought it to the attention of the Commission of Conservation, and I think the ideas put forward in that paper are worthy of consideration by the Government. The young lady who read the paper is from Berlin, Ont., and is now a resident of Rochester. In that city, it seems, they have adopted the plan of having instruction given periodically- I think once a week-to all classes, not

only to young people, but adults as well, in the treatment of sudden illness until the physician can be summoned; how to prevent certain diseases, and generally how to care for health. These lectures are given by qualified physicians and nurses, and practical illustrations are given of attending to patients.
The St. John Ambulance Association is doing work of the same kind, and we give them a vote.

Yes, they work along that line. In Rochester, this instruction is very general. In this propagandist movement they use the school buildings, which are unused half the time, and could be put to no better use. The results, as indicated by the paper to which I have referred, are very marked. The people in all sections of that city, the poor as well as the wealthy, are taking an interest in the work. While the results do not interfere in any way with professional practice, a knowledge is cultivated among ordinary people of how to treat diseases, from some of which the patents would die if they were left without this attention.
I would advise the Government to get in touch with that organization in Rochester and see if this test could not be made in some of our large or even in some of our smaller centres. Thousands die in this and every other country through absolute ignorance of how to treat disease in its first stages, or before a physician can be secured.

How many physicians
have you there?

What is the Public Works Health Act?
It, is in connection with the sanitary condition of railway camps, and so on. We have two inspectors, and there is provision for another if the railway situation advises a readjustment.

I have already answered that question by pointing out that the matter as it now stands was left for the purpose of giving the exhibition to British Columbia. British Columbia had it last year, but owing to the fact that the Militia Department took over their buildings after the war broke out, they did not Ihold it. If British Columbia does not hold it this year, they will hold it next year, and Halifax will get it the year following.
I think representations have been made by the Halifax Board of Trade that the holding of the exhibition in Nova Scotia should be postponed until 1916.

I suppose the attention of many hon. gentlemen has been called to the fact that for attendance at the August session of Par' lament some of the employees of the Hout. of Commons, chiefly messengers, received s per diem allowance as usual, but the total amount received was comparatively so small that in some cases,
I understand, after paying disbursements for travelling expenses, these employees returned home out of pocket. I have not made any particular investigation into the matter, but it has been called to my attention by two or three persons on behalf of these employees.
I daresay it has also been called to the attention of Mr. Speaker. I am inclined to think that if the facts are as I state them, some little consideration should be given to their request, because if their disbursements exceeded the payment received for the August session it would be only fair that some allowance should be made. It may be quite true that some members of the House of Commons suffered in the same way in that session, but, of course, there is no objection on the part of hon. gentlemen. I mention this particularly to inquire of the Speaker if any request has been made to him concerning this matter and what his decision was.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
An application was made by the sessional employees of the House on the understanding that the session would only last for about two months. Their claim was that the amount received when the travelling and other expenses were deducted would leave a very small balance coming to them. As it was not known at that time how long the House would sit, it was thought well to defer decision for some time until we would have better knowledge of the duration of the session. I submitted their request to the Internal Economy Commission and after looking into it carefully it was decided that it could not be taken up and their request granted. To grant their request at the time would have in-

vclved a very considerable .expenditure. The daily payment to the sessional .staff is $627.24. They desired to be paid for 100 days whether the session lasted that long or not. If the session lasted 100 days they would not ask any additional payment, but they did ask that 100 days should be the minimum. That would call for an expenditure of $62,724 for the session. Up to April 1, the session had lasted 56 days. That would give them $35,125, and the balance to make up the 100 days would be $27,598. The commission thought, in view of the fact that if this was taken up and the request granted it would certainly result in a great many more applications being made to deal with other employees, it would not be well to grant the request at that stage of the session, if done at all. Of course it was not then known how long the session would last. It has already lasted some days past the 1st of April, and we do not know just when it will close. The decision was that the request could not be entertained, although it was admitted that many of the employees would have very little over their expenses, providing the session closed about the 1st of April.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN. I intended to say that my remarks would also apply to the Hansard amanuenses. There may be some objection to making an extra allowance calculating on the basis of a session of 100 days. That might be a bad precedent to establish. I should thjnk that some allowance might have been made in connection with the August session at least.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This included the debates amanuenses, 9 at $5 a day; 19 sessional clerks at $5 a day and 16 at $4 a day; four committee amanuenses af $5 a day; the stenographers, doorkeepers, bookkeepers, servants and charwomen. How were the Hansard staff and translators paid for the August session?	.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hansard staff and translators are paid by the year.

The clerks who
came here for the August session in some cases had to travel quite long distances and some of them did not receive enough to pay their expenses. I would suggest that they be remunerated in some way for that short session. The clerks who came from northern Ontario and from the Maritime Provinces
	-
were out of pocket. A Maritime Province clerk would have to pay railway fare and expenses of $25 or $30 and receiving $4 a day for seven days he would get $28. The messengers who would have the same expenses received only $22.75 for the seven days. They lost their time and were some of them out of pocket. I would suggest that something be done for these men. Those who receive higheT wages perhaps need not receive the same consideration as these men on small salaries. I would also suggest that as this is a short session they should be granted remuneration for at least 100 days.,

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: With reference to the short session, knowing it was likely to be a very short session, I instructed those whose duty it was to notify the employees that we were likely to have a short session and that-it was optional with them to come or not, so they were not exactly taken unawares. Of course, if anything was done it could not be done by enlarging this vote as we have not power to do that; but it might be paid in another way.

I do not think it would be advisable to fix a certain number of days like 100; but I do think, in all fairness, that some consideration should be given to these men for their services during the short session- in August. It does not seem to be dealing squarely with men to ask them to come down here when we need their services and pay them less than it costs them to come here. I think the country is big enough to at least give them something for their services over and above their expenses. Some consideration should be given to these officials for the session in August.

What is the practice with regard to the employment of messengers and members of the sessional staff? I gather from the remarks of the hon. member from Prince Edward Island that members of the staff are selected from points distant from the 'capital and that this is largely a grievance over travelling expenses. When I came down in August I was surprised, having in view the fact that we were to have a session of five or six days only, that the House was as fully manned as it was. As there was a great deal of expense going on I wondered if there was anything to justify their being here for such a short session. Perhaps the Speaker can tell us whether the whole staff was on at the opening of the session in August.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

I think they were all here with the exception of two or three. The

great bulk of the staff are located within a reasonable distance of Ottawa, but some come from Prince Edward Island, and others from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or the West.

There is a great deal of
reason in what has been said as to the small amount paid to the officers of the House during the short session we had in August. Of course we cannot very well correct that matter at the present moment, but I am sure that no member of the House would desire to see the staff come here and go home out of pocket, whether the session was long or short. I have never heard any complaint myself, but perhaps some other members of the Government have. I will bring it to the attention of the Government, and if anything can be done we shall be glad to do it.

The hon. gentleman's imagination is very strong; he is at sea, without rudder or compass. Mr. ,T. J. HUGHES:	The minister is
either not familiar with conditions in that part of the country, or he has been misinformed, because there is no question of a title to this land at all. Mr. Chairman, in the Estimates now before the House, both for the province of Quebec and for the other provinces, there appear a number of items for the construction of wharves, from which I conclude that the Government's policy is not antagonistic to the building of wharves in this country, and by which is deepened my regret at the minister's omitting to include in the Estimates of this session the amount necessary for the construction of a wharf at L'Assomption. I am not raising a new question. As early as 1911, the late Government had had plans prepared and had provided for this work, which is indispensable not only to the town of L'Assomption, but also to that whole district. The necessary amount was to be found in the Estimates of 1911-12 and 191213; but later was cut off, and the legitimate demands of L'Assomption were denied. The work had been started under the late Government, and a quantity of material had been brought on the ground; but with the coming into power of the present administration the work was discontinued notwithstanding that the money was again voted in 1912-13, and the material is still on the shore where it is going to waste. The other
day, when I advocated in this House the right of the town of St. Lin to a post office and taunted the minister for his indifference in the matter, the reply came, quite undeserved, that possibly I had not pressed my request sufficiently. In this particular case of a wharf for L'Assomption, I did repeatedly call the attention of the minister to it, and I know that representations have come to the Government from more welcome sources; I deem it my duty to warn the minister and this House that the Government's best friends at L'Assomption are disappointed to find that their claims have been heeded so very little by him. Joseph Edouard Faribault, K.C., perhaps the most prominent Conservative at L'Assomption, urged his leaders to action, but, only a few days ago, he confessed to me his vexation at having had to go a-begging to the dispensers of government patronage with no better result.
It is no matter of great surprise to me that the minister should show preferences to and be more favourably inclined towards his Tory supporters; but how comes it that he is so callous to the requests of his best friends at L'Assomption. All good movements for the betterment of conditions in my county find in me a staunch supporter; and the minister may feel sure that, unless he heed the claims of his good friends of L'Assomption, I shall not fail to take advantage of his indifference, and I shall succeed in proving to those good people that they need not expect fair dealing at the hands of the present Administration. Be fair towards all the citizens of the town of L'Assomption and of that whole section and, more especially, listen, to your best friends, if you do not want to provoke their just resentment.
In taking my seat, 1 would ask the minister if he intends to carry on this work?

I am very pleased to
know that my hon. friend notes with such satisfaction the large sums of money we are spending in the various public works that we are undertaking in the different counties of the province of Quebec. 1 must
acknowledge to the minister that he shows some willingness for the future. However, I must report that this work is of more immediate import than, judging from his statements, he seems to think. No tenders were called for; the price was named by the department, I fancy.	,
What was the reason for the change?
It was impossible to find the required length of timber in the native wood, and it was necessary to 'Substitute British Columbia fir.
What is the size of the wharf?
It is 150 feet long by 20 feet wide.
With a slip in the centre.
The other section is 200 by 40 feet.
Are there data in the department as to the number of boats that docked at that pier last year, or for the last four or five years?
Nothing has been docked there, because the work was under construction.
I am not sufficiently familiar with local conditions to give my hon. friend that information.

I want the House to get the information, and I can give it if you ' like. This is a little wharf situated at the mouth of the St. Maurice river in the county of Champlain. I do not think two steamers ever docked there, and it is easy to see from the length of the dock, 150 feet, that they could not be very large steamers. In the old days, when the wharf was first built, there used to be pilgrimages there, as there was a shrine. There was a little boat called L'Etoile, that used to dock there, carrying pilgrims to the shrine. But I understand that Cap de la Made-laine was a very expensive parish in elections. The hon. minister (Mr. Rogers) speaks of L'Assomption being expensive, but that was before the elections. In this case, this was done after the elections, and was done to square the present member's election accounts. That is my information; if the minister can give better, I hope he will supply it.

May I ask where this wharf is situated?
This is in Beauce county at the end of lake Aylmer on the Quebec Central railway, 52 miles east of Sherbrooke.
Is there any water there?

I presume there is; I hope there is.
Mr. TObIn : I would like to know. A few years ago statements were made by members of this House, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) being one, that there was no water in this lake and that this work was not useful. The hon. gentleman * went down on an excursion with
12 m. the late hon. member for Lennox, and some other gentleman, and had a photograph taken there, and returned with the statement that there was no water. What repairs is the minister going to make to this wharf?
The amount is required to replace the present wooden flooring 50 feet long by 36 feet wide with gravel and stone, and to effect other repairs, the estimated cost of which is $2,000.

I am sure the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) will be scandalized when he hears that the hon. minister is going on with these repairs. It was a useful work when the late Government took it up, and I approve the action of this Government in going ahead with it.
